what: Shuttle Discovery (STS-51-A) astronauts Allen and Gardner captured the stranded, written-off satellites Palapa B2 and Westar 6 and returned them to Earth for refurbishment and resale.
fit: Stranded, failed satellites drifting in the wrong orbit were found, caught and salvaged.

sources.title: NASA Activities December 1984
sources.quote: the retrieval of two wayward satellites, Palapa B-2 and Westar IV

sources.title: STS-51-A
sources.quote: Palapa B2 and Westar 6, meanwhile, had been deployed during the STS-41-B mission earlier in the year

note: Confirmed as the same STS-51-A event (Palapa B2 retrieved 1984-11-12, Westar 6 on 1984-11-14; landing 1984-11-16). Earlier candidates rejected: Gemini 10 (1966-07-20), where Collins left the spacecraft and removed a micrometeoroid package from the dead Gemini 8 Agena target (GATV VIII; NTRS 'Astronautics and Aeronautics, 1966'), because that was a planned pickup of an experiment deliberately left on a parked, still-owned target, not salvage of an abandoned or wrecked craft; Apollo 12 taking parts from Surveyor 3 (1969-11), which sat on the Moon rather than drifting; Solar Max repair (STS-41-C, 1984-04), a failed but NASA-owned satellite kept for rescue rather than abandoned; Skylab and Salyut boosts and Agena dockings (working craft). Salyut 7 revival (Soyuz T-13, 1985-06) and Syncom IV-3 repair (1985-04) are later. Palapa B2 and Westar 6 were insurer-owned write-offs returned to Earth and resold, which fits 'found, salvaged'. Gemini 10 is the nearest alternative and would move the date to 1966 if judged to fit.
searched: archive.org NASA Activities 1984-12; NTRS 'Astronautics and Aeronautics, 1966' chronology and the Gemini 10 press kit; Wikipedia Gemini 10, STS-51-A.

what: Britain suspended Bank of England convertibility of banknotes into gold (Bank Restriction Act 1797), lasting to 1821.
fit: Government stopped redeeming paper money in gold so notes circulated unbacked in place of gold coin; it was temporary.

sources.title: Bank Restriction Act 1797
sources.quote: removed the requirement for the Bank of England to convert banknotes into gold

note: Earlier candidates: Yuan China (13th-14th c.; Wikipedia says notes were first silver-backed then fiat, no precise date found), Song/Jin paper money, colonial and Continental American paper (not gold or silver redemption suspensions I could date). 1797 fits only partly since coin still circulated and notes were not legal tender until 1811; US greenbacks 1862 were not dated.
searched: Wikipedia Fiat money, Bank Restriction Act, Yuan dynasty coinage; web search on earliest inconvertible paper.

what: With the end of Bretton Woods (1971 US suspension of dollar-gold convertibility; Jamaica Accords 1976), all major currencies became fiat money.
fit: Many countries' currencies became unbacked fiat money, no longer redeemable in gold.

sources.title: Fiat money
sources.quote: Since the end of the Bretton Woods system in 1976 by the Jamaica Accords, all the major government currencies in the world are fiat money.

sources.title: Nixon shock
sources.quote: the unilateral cancellation of the direct international convertibility of the United States dollar to gold

note: The Nixon shock (1971-08-15) is the start; 1976 is when the system was formally fiat everywhere. Floating rates came by 1973. Earlier national abandonments in 1931-33 were not mass adoption.

what: Apollo 17 ended crewed lunar flights; budget cuts had cancelled further Apollo landings and no human went beyond low Earth orbit for over 50 years.
fit: Crewed exploration was cut back for years by cost and policy, leaving humanity in Earth orbit.

sources.title: Apollo program
sources.quote: Budget cuts forced the cancellation of three of these.

what: Grand Duke Leopold of Habsburg-Lorraine promulgated a penal code in the Grand Duchy of Tuscany abolishing the death penalty and ordering the destruction of execution instruments.
fit: A state abolished execution by law for all crimes and replaced it with other penalties, matching the definition's function and legal mechanism.

sources.title: Abolition of the death penalty
sources.quote: Leopold promulgated the reform of the penal code that abolished the death penalty and ordered the destruction of all the instruments

note: Joseph II abolished it in Austrian lands in 1787 (later); Tahiti 1824, Michigan 1846, Venezuela 1863 and San Marino are later. Tuscany reintroduced execution in 1790 but the abolition was in force 1786-1790, so it counts as the first. Earlier de facto halts (no execution after 1769) are not abolition by law.
searched: Wikipedia Abolition of the death penalty; Capital punishment by country

what: By the end of 2012 Latvia became the 97th country to abolish the death penalty for all crimes in law, about half of the world's states (98 by 2013).
fit: Abolition by law of execution for all crimes in a large number of countries, roughly half the world, i.e. common legal practice across many countries.

sources.title: New death penalty figures despite setbacks, 2012 trend toward global abolition
sources.quote: Last year Latvia became the 97th country in the world to remove the death penalty for all crimes

sources.publisher: World Coalition Against the Death Penalty
sources.title: Facts and figures 2014
sources.quote: 98 countries have abolished the death penalty for all crimes

note: No single year is when it became common; 97 of about 195 states in 2012 is the point at which roughly half had abolished by law. Counting abolitionist in practice would give an earlier year (140 countries in 2012) but that is not abolition by law.
searched: web search for Amnesty statistics; Amnesty UK and World Coalition pages

what: The French National Constituent Assembly abolished hereditary titles of nobility on 19 June 1790.
fit: A country legally ended hereditary noble titles and rank, so that status no longer rested on birth.

sources.title: French nobility
sources.quote: It was not until 19 June 1790 that hereditary titles of nobility were abolished.

note: Fiscal and feudal privileges were abolished earlier (August 1789) but titles and rank remained until June 1790. The US Constitution (1789) barred federal titles but never had a hereditary nobility to abolish in law. No earlier country found.
searched: Wikipedia French nobility, Abolition of feudalism in France

what: After World War I, Austria (law of April 1919) and other successor states and republics legally abolished nobility, so that hereditary rank with special rights largely vanished in the Western world.
fit: Many countries legally ended hereditary noble titles and privilege, so that rank no longer depended on birth.

sources.title: Nobility
sources.quote: Since the end of World War I the hereditary nobility entitled to special rights has largely been abolished in the Western World

sources.title: Austrian nobility
sources.quote: officially abolished in 1919 after the fall of Austria-Hungary

note: The year is a judgment: abolition came in waves (France 1790, 1848, 1919 Austria and Germany, Turkey 1934, Japan 1947, India 1971). The hereditary House of Lords seats were cut in Britain in 1999, which is a later partial case.

fit: A whole country ran without money or wages, with goods and labor assigned by the state and communes instead of bought and sold.

sources.title: Cambodian riel

sources.title: Khmer Rouge

note: Considered and rejected: Soviet War Communism 1918-21 (money devalued and rationing, but never abolished); Anabaptist Muenster 1534-35 (one city, not a country); Hutterite and other communes (not whole-country); Inca state (no market money, but never abolished money, it had none). what: Taborite Hussites at the new town of Tabor in southern Bohemia (founded spring 1420) held goods in common: arrivals sold their possessions and put goods in barrels and tubs in the town square, administered by priests-elected overseers, with private property declared abolished.
fit: A real town community ran an organized community of goods, replacing private ownership with common holdings for a time, as a small-scale trial of communal ownership.

sources.publisher: Canadian Journal of History (T. A. Fudge)
sources.title: Neither Mine Nor Thine: Communist Experiments in Hussite Bohemia
sources.quote: For a time in 1419 and 1420 the description is, in the main, accurate apropos to Tábor.

sources.publisher: Canadian Journal of History (T. A. Fudge)
sources.title: Neither Mine Nor Thine: Communist Experiments in Hussite Bohemia
sources.quote: At Tábor, barrels and tubs were set up in the main town square next to the church.

note: The earlier 1528 Hutterite date is replaced: Wikipedia's 'first communes in 1528 in Tyrol' is doubtful (Hutter reached Moravia only in 1533; the Anabaptist community of goods began 1528-29 around Nikolsburg/Austerlitz under Jakob Wiedemann and was formalized under Hutter after 1533), and Tabor in 1420 is about a century earlier and also a real community that ran. The Taborite practice was partial and brief ('sporadically in practice' per Fudge), so the date fits a demonstration, not a lasting society; the Hutterites (1528-29 onward, still existing) are the longer-running later case. Other candidates rejected: the early Jerusalem church (Acts 2, c.30 AD) and Pachomian and other monasteries (celibate religious orders, not a society reorganized with families and productive property), the Essenes/Qumran (same); Mazdak's movement in Persia c.488-528 (hostile and disputed sources, never enacted as law); Muenster 1534-35 (later); Plymouth Colony common stock 1620-23, Diggers 1649, Harmony Society 1805, New Harmony 1825 (all later).
searched: Wikipedia Hutterites, Jakob Hutter, Taborites, Tabor; WebSearch (worked) for Tabor 1420 community of goods and for Hutterite Nikolsburg 1528; Fudge's article PDF read in full via pipeline/sources.py; no source within two years of 1420 (chronicles such as Vavrinec of Brezova not found online in a readable form here), so the sources are references.

what: Soviet Russia abolished private ownership of land (Decree on Land, Nov 1917, restated Jan 1918), abolished inheritance (27 April 1918) and nationalized all large-scale industry (decree of 28 June 1918).
fit: A state abolished private ownership of land and of large productive enterprises and ended inheritance by law and by will, reorganizing the economy under state (socialist) ownership.

sources.publisher: Some aspects of the inequality of incomes in modern communities (Hugh Dalton)
sources.title: Some aspects of the inequality of incomes in modern communities
sources.quote: inheritance, whether by law or will, is abolished.

sources.publisher: Decrees and constitution of Soviet Russia (Nation / Soviet Russia pamphlet)
sources.title: Decrees and constitution of Soviet Russia
sources.quote: all private property in land is abolished, and the entire land is de- clared to be national property

sources.title: War communism
sources.quote: Following the June 28, 1918 Decree, the state nationalized all large-scale and some medium-scale industries, including sugar, oil, and the merchant fleet.

note: Date is when land (Nov 1917/Jan 1918), inheritance (Apr 1918) and large industry (Jun 1918) were all abolished. Earlier candidates rejected: Muenster 1534 and Hutterites 1528 and Tabor 1420 (communities, not a country, province or large city); Paris Commune 1871 (no abolition of property); Inca state and Jesuit reductions (state or mission ownership, not described as abolition of private property and inheritance); Mazdak (never enacted). Caveat: not total even in Russia, since small estates went to needy relatives under the inheritance decree, personal property remained, and small industry was nationalized only in Nov 1920. Total abolition of all private property never happened anywhere. The mass-adoption stage (communist bloc c.1949) is not part of this check.
searched: Wikipedia Decree on Land, War communism; Hitotsubashi RRC working paper (PDF); archive.org full-text search 1918-1920 found Dalton 1920 (decree text of 27 Apr 1918 quoted) and the 1920 Decrees and constitution of Soviet Russia; all quotes checked FOUND.

what: After the defeat of Macedon at Pydna, Rome stopped levying the tributum, its direct tax on citizens, living on war booty and provincial revenue.
fit: A government stopped taxing its citizens directly (the property levy that served as its income tax) and funded itself from the profits of conquest, though indirect taxes and duties remained.

sources.title: Tributum
sources.quote: After the defeat of Macedon in 167 BCE, Rome began to function without the Tributum because of booty accumulated through battle

note: This is only a partial fit: Rome kept customs and other indirect taxes and reinstated the tributum after Caesar's death, so it did not abolish all taxation. Considered: Alaska (state income tax repealed 1980, services partly funded by oil revenue and a resource dividend from 1982; still levies other taxes) and Gulf oil states (no personal income tax, funded by oil), both later. No state or country has been shown to raise no taxes at all.

what: In 1952 A. J. Menzies of Fettercairn Distillery claimed a process (circulating new spirit through active chemicals) that matures whisky in a few hours instead of 5-10 years; a trial analysis found the spirit had the character of a pot-still malt whisky (UK Board of Trade documents, Kew).
fit: A process matured a spirit to a long-aged character in hours instead of years.

sources.title: Super-fast whisky ageing was discovered and then abandoned in 1950s
sources.quote: claims his process reduces the maturing time from about five to 10 years to a few hours.

note: Replaces Lost Spirits 2014 for demonstration. Earlier candidates: a 12-hour whiskey aging process said to be in use and described in a US Government report over 40 years before 1934 (Scientific American 1934; the report was not found, so undated and unverified); 1934 post-Prohibition attempts with ozone, UV and catalysts (Chem. Eng. News 10 Apr 1934, Everyday Science and Mechanics Sept 1934) were research efforts and a 24-hour whiskey proposal, not shown to reach full maturity; Madeira estufagem heating (months), Roman fumarium and tobacco flue curing do not reach full maturity in hours/days. The 1952 trial is tied to official documents and a lab analysis, but the large-scale test failed and the results are a claim, so low confidence.
searched: WebSearch history of rapid whiskey aging; Drinks Business, Gizmodo (1934) pages; archive.org full text 1880-1936 for rapid aging of whiskey (Scientific American 1934 page found); Wikipedia Aging of wine, Madeira. Contemporary 1952 source not obtainable (Kew documents).

what: Lost Spirits (California) released Colonial American Inspired Rum in December 2014, the first commercial product made with its accelerated-aging reactor (days instead of years).
fit: A commercial spirit was sold after being matured to a long-aged chemical profile in days by a reactor process.

sources.title: California Distiller Makes 20-Year-Old Rum in Six Days
sources.quote: Lost Spirits Colonial American Inspired Rum, released in December 2014, was the first commercial product to fully undergo the accelerated aging process.

note: Date made precise from April 2015 to the December 2014 release named in the same Punch article. Earlier uses may exist: the 1890s 12-hour whiskey aging described as in use (undated, report not found), 1934 24-hour whiskey marketing plans (not shown to launch), and 1950s Fettercairn trial (abandoned). Whether these amounted to full maturity is unestablished, and Lost Spirits' equivalence to true aging is disputed.
searched: Punch page read; same searches as demonstration.

what: Le Verrier's Paris Observatory, with the Navy and the telegraph administration, began a service warning French ports by telegraph of approaching storms, installed from 1 April 1860 (his daily telegraphic weather bulletin from observation stations dated from July 1856).
fit: Storm approach was forecast ahead of time from simultaneous telegraphed barometer and wind measurements over a wide area and sent to ports.

sources.publisher: Études et lectures sur les sciences d'observation (Moigno)
sources.title: Études et lectures sur les sciences d'observation et leurs applications pratiques
sources.quote: service, installé à partir du i*' avril 1860

sources.publisher: Proceedings of the British Meteorological Society
sources.title: Proceedings of the British Meteorological Society
sources.quote: The probable approach of storms is signalled to the principal fishing stations and seaports

note: Replaced FitzRoy's 1861-02 gale-warning service: Le Verrier's French ports service predates it by about ten months and is the same kind of event (telegraphed measurements used to warn of coming storms). The first source's archive record is dated 1855 in the catalog, but its text refers to April 1860, so I give no date and call it a reference; the 1861 British Meteorological Society paper is contemporary and describes the Le Verrier system and FitzRoy's warnings. Also considered: Le Verrier's 1854-55 proposal and 1856 observation bulletin (observations, not warnings); Richardson 1922 hand forecast (failed); ENIAC 1950 and operational NWP 1954-55 (true calculation, but later, and the 1860 service already gives measured-and-charted storm warnings; days-ahead precision was modest in 1860 so confidence is medium); the Times forecast of 1861-08-01 (later). The date 1860-04 rests on a single source text.
searched: Wikipedia Weather forecasting, Robert FitzRoy, Urbain Le Verrier (en/fr), History of numerical weather prediction; archive.org full-text 1855-1862 in French and English for Le Verrier storm warnings; Presse Scientifique 1860, Moniteur scientifique, Cosmos 1860. Could not read The Times (refused) so no direct 1860-61 newspaper quote.

what: Dr Neil Arnott's hydrostatic bed, a water-filled trough under a rubber sheet and mattress, was first used for a bedridden patient and described in print in 1832, so that every point of the body is supported without local pressure.
fit: A bed that conforms by itself to the body lying on it, with equal support everywhere, so no adjustment by the user is needed (passive self-molding, not powered motion).

sources.title: The Hydrostatic Bed for Invalids
sources.quote: every point of his body is supported by the water immediately beneath it

sources.title: Waterbed
sources.quote: A form of waterbed was invented in 1833 by the Scottish physician Neil Arnott.

note: Replaces the Charcot vibrating chair (1892) and the 1954 massage chair: both move or vibrate against the sitter and neither fits itself to the user, so they are stand-ins. Dr Neil Arnott's hydrostatic bed (first used 1832) automatically takes the shape of whatever body lies on it, supporting every point equally with no adjustment by user or nurse; it is a passive, self-molding bed with no motors, so the fit to 'reshape, move or support themselves automatically to fit the user' is partial (support and conformity, not motion). Other candidates rejected: Gatch/Fowler hospital beds (user- or nurse-cranked, 1909 on); Noble's 1919 roller chair (user-operated); modern waterbeds (1968-71, later); memory foam (1960s-91, later); alternating-pressure and powered-turning beds (1950s, later); self-adjusting-firmness beds (Sleep Number, 1980s-2010s, later); robotic furniture (Ori, 2010s, later). A 1901 Chicago advertisement for a 'Comfort Chair' that 'automatically adjusts to any position' was seen, but it is a user-reclined chair and later than 1832.
searched: archive.org full-text for hydrostatic bed Arnott 1830-1860; Wikipedia Waterbed, Massage chair, Hospital bed; archive.org 'automatically adjusts' chair 1900-1960; alternating-pressure mattress 1950-65 (no hits). Contemporary source found: Penny Magazine Aug 1832.

sources.title: Flight 1914-10-16
sources.quote: exciting duel in the air which took place on the 5th inst. at Jonchery, near Rheims

sources.title: The First Aerial Combat Victory
sources.quote: Sgt. Joseph Frantz and his mechanic/gunner, Louis Quénault, shot down a German biplane near Reims

note: Contemporary Flight report (16 Oct 1914, quoting the Daily Telegraph of the 7th, vouched for by the French War Office) confirms date and result. Earlier candidates: Garros's 25 Aug 1914 damage-only exchange (counted as the demonstration; one could argue it is already wartime use), the disputed 1913 Mexican duel, and the Longwy 'first air battle' press myth of 3 Aug 1914; Nesterov's 7 Sept 1914 ramming rejected as not gun combat. Aircraft-versus-airship combat came later (1915). Mass adoption not claimed.

what: Navy engineers cooled and dried the air supplied to President Garfield's bedroom in the White House with an ice-brine screen cooler and blower (first cool air 11 July 1881).
fit: A machine cooled and ventilated a home bedroom to a comfortable temperature, though improvised and hand-managed rather than automatic.

sources.title: Reports of officers of the navy on ventilating and cooling the Executive mansion during the illness of President Garfield
sources.quote: On Monday, July 11, the air from this apparatus was for the first time admitted into the President's chamber and found to be cool

sources.title: Keeping Cool in the White House
sources.quote: Pumped through a duct into Garfield's bedroom, the device pushed the temperature down to 80 degrees and lowered the humidity.

note: Replaced 1929 with the earlier 1881 event. In July 1881 US Navy engineers (Jennings, Powell, Woodward's request) cooled and dried the air of President Garfield's bedroom in the White House with an ice-and-brine screen box and blower, ducted to the room; first cool air entered on 11 July 1881 and held the room at an agreeable temperature. It cooled a home bedroom for comfort, as the definition says, but was improvised and manually run (not thermostatic), so the fit is partial on 'automatic'. Rejected: Charles Gates's Minneapolis house (1914; may never have been used, house uninhabited); the 1896 Hungarian Rock/Ganz 'residential rooms' apparatus (only a Wikipedia claim, no checkable source); thermostat-controlled heating (Johnson 1883, Butz 1885), which automates heating only and is not the cooling/climate concept; 1902 Carrier and 1920s Carrier installations (factories, theaters, shops); 1929 Frigidaire room cooler (later).
searched: Wikipedia Air conditioning and Thermostat; WebSearch for Garfield 1881 cooling and for first residential air conditioning (1914 Gates the usual claim); archive.org full-text searches 1881-1883 (found the Navy report), 1915-1931 (Electrical Merchandising March 1929; Frigidaire room cooler 1929-31); energy.gov; whitehousehistory.org. No sourced working home installation found between 1881 and 1929.

what: The first five Chain Home radar stations, covering the approaches to London, were installed on the south-east coast of Britain by 1937, forming the first early-warning radar network (trials against the Bawdsey station in 1937).
fit: A chain of radar stations with transmitter and receiver towers and plotting displays watched for incoming aircraft over a region.

sources.title: Chain Home

sources.title: Chain Home
sources.quote: The first five stations, covering the approaches to London, were installed by 1937

note: Candidates rejected: London Air Defence Area (from Sept 1915: ground-observer reports telephoned to a central map room at Horse Guards) is the earlier regional system with a tracking display, but its detectors were human observers, so it is a precursor rather than a network of detectors in the radar sense; the definition's 'detectors, towers and tracking displays' fits Chain Home. 1920s-30s acoustic sound mirrors (short range, not a working network); Daventry test (Feb 1935) and the first aircraft detection (June 1935) were single-station tests; the 1936 Orfordness/Bawdsey exercises used two stations. Later: Freya (1938-39), SAGE and DEW Line. Chain Home work was secret, so no contemporary report within two years exists in public sources.
searched: Wikipedia Chain Home, London Air Defence Area, Acoustic mirror; archive.org full-text search 1936-1965 for Chain Home/radar early warning returned nothing usable; WebSearch worked (Marconi Family page, Warfare History Network); NDU Press page refused (403). No contemporary source exists because of wartime secrecy.

what: In August 1938 the first five Chain Home stations were declared operational and entered service during the Munich crisis, starting full-time operation in September 1938.

sources.title: Chain Home
sources.quote: In August 1938, the first five stations were declared operational and entered service during the Munich crisis, starting full-time operation in September.

note: Date made more precise (August 1938 declared operational; full-time from September). The Wikipedia lead says 'began full-time operation in 1938', consistent. Rejected as earlier: WWI London Air Defence Area (observer-based, see demonstration note); stations handed to the RAF in 1937 (Bawdsey May 1937, Dover July 1937) were not yet in operational service. Continental networks (SAGE, DEW Line) are later.

what: Croydon Airport, near London, commissioned the world's first aerodrome control tower on 25 February 1920; it gave pilots traffic, weather and location information, with wireless, direction-finding and signals (rockets, Very lights) used to control aircraft on the London-Paris, Brussels and Amsterdam routes.
fit: A tower and signals directing aircraft on the airfield and along defined air routes, which keep craft apart; assigned altitude levels and lanes came later, so only the tower, signals and route parts of the definition are met.

sources.title: Colourised images mark centenary of world's first control tower
sources.quote: designed to be 15ft in height with windows on its four walls – on 25 February 1920

sources.title: Air Conference visit to Waddon (Croydon aerodrome)
sources.quote: Rockets and Very lights are also used for signalling to and from aircraft.

sources.title: Air traffic control
sources.quote: It was commissioned on 25 February 1920, and provided basic traffic, weather, and location information to pilots.

note: Confirmed as the earliest strict fit for towers, signals and routes. The contemporary Flight report of 21 October 1920 describes Croydon's central control tower, signals, wireless direction-finding and hourly route weather reports for the London-Paris, Brussels and Amsterdam routes, but does not itself date the tower's commissioning; the 25 February 1920 date rests on Flight Global (2020, via NATS) and Wikipedia. Candidates considered: pre-1920 aerodrome flag and light signals at Hendon and military fields (no control of traffic by a tower, no dated source); the 1919 Paris air convention rules (rules of the air, not a working control service); later developments rejected as later, not earlier: the US air mail radio stations (1922), Cleveland's radio-equipped tower (1930) and the first airway traffic control center at Newark (December 1935), which first handled en-route separation by assigned altitudes and routes. Assigned altitude lanes at scale date to the 1930s and are not given a separate milestone because the definition is one concept with the tower as its first working piece.

what: By 1951 airlines carried 52 percent of all commercial transpacific (US-Orient) passengers, the ships 48 percent, so aircraft had become the main way to cross the Pacific; the air share rose to 68 percent by 1955.
fit: Aircraft carried the majority of long-distance ocean passengers on a major ocean route, taking over the main-carrier role from ocean liners (passengers only; cargo still went by ship).

sources.publisher: US House hearings on superliner legislation (American President Lines statement, Appendix C)
sources.title: Superliner Legislation, Hearings February-March 1958
sources.quote: In 1951 the airlines carried 52 percent of the total transpacific passenger traffic.

sources.publisher: US House hearings on superliner legislation (American President Lines statement, Appendix C)
sources.title: Superliner Legislation, Hearings February-March 1958
sources.quote: In 1955 airlines carried 68 percent; ships carried 32 percent.

note: Replaces the Atlantic 1957 parity. Candidates: (1) North Atlantic summer 1957 parity (Wikipedia 1957 in aviation): parity, not takeover, and later than the Pacific; (2) North Atlantic 1958: Flight, 20 Feb 1959, says 1958 'was the first year in which more passengers crossed the Atlantic by air than by sea' (1,292,166 IATA passengers by air), a contemporary source, but the Atlantic is later than the Pacific and was the given definition's most famous route; Atlantic 1949 was still ship 651,640 vs air 273,025 (American Aviation, 15 Apr 1950). (3) Transpacific: the 1958 statement says the air share already stood at 52 percent in 1951 and that 'upon reaching the 50-percent level' growth slowed, so the true crossing may be 1950 or earlier; 1951 is the earliest year with figures found, so the date may still be late. Not contemporary to 1951 (seven years later), hence reference. Caveats: route-level, passengers only, a small market (about 50,000 a year); cargo by air has never displaced shipping, so no mass-adoption claim. If the route-level Pacific event is judged too narrow, the fallback is North Atlantic 1958.
searched: archive.org full text 1949-1960 for Atlantic air vs sea passenger counts (Flight 1959-02-20, American Aviation 1950-04-15, Congressional Record 1959, New Statesman 1959), transpacific air vs ship share 1949-1953 (no contemporary 1950-52 source found), Wikipedia 1957 in aviation and Ocean liner; read the 1958 House superliner hearing for Pacific shares.

Considered and rejected: the Supermarine/Pemberton-Billing P.B.31E Nighthawk (first flew 1917; nose searchlight; later, and not used operationally); a German hydro-aeroplane with a searchlight captured by the Russians (Scientific American 1916-01-22, later); the January 1915 Zeppelin raid on Yarmouth where one airship 'seems to have carried a searchlight' (The Nation, 1915-01-23; hearsay, later); the 1913 German naval airship searchlight demonstration noted by the earlier researcher (Papers Past, never fetched, not used); the 1913 'phantom airship' panic reports (unverified sightings). The Leigh Light (1942) was the first aircraft-mounted searchlight in routine anti-submarine service but not the first airborne searchlight.

what: The AFTI/F-16 Automated Maneuvering Attack System (USAF Flight Test Center, Edwards AFB, General Dynamics) flight-tested an automatic ground collision avoidance function that computes when a flyup is needed and starts it automatically; flight tests ran from September 1984, with ground-collision avoidance development in 1985-86.
fit: A system using sensor altitude and flight data automatically initiates a fly-up maneuver to avoid hitting the ground.

sources.publisher: AFTI/F-16 Joint Test Force paper (DTIC ADA184941)
sources.title: AFTI/F16 Automated Maneuvering Attack System Test Reports
sources.quote: Initial flight test developaent of the empirically derived GCA flyup algorithm demonstrated problems with penetrations of minimum descent altitude

sources.publisher: AFTI/F-16 Joint Test Force paper (DTIC ADA184941)
sources.title: AFTI/F16 Automated Maneuvering Attack System Test Reports
sources.quote: then a flyup is automatically initiated.

note: Replaces the 1998 Auto-GCAS test, which the abstract itself says followed an earlier less sophisticated system on a research F-16 (this is it). Exact date of first GCA flight is not in the sources (Phase A Sept 1984-Apr 1985, Phase B from June 1985), so 1985 is approximate. Considered and rejected: terrain-following radar coupled to an autopilot (Cornell Autoflite 1950s, Canberra test 1962, F-111 1967), which holds a set low clearance for penetration rather than recovering from imminent collision (borderline; if the grader accepts it the date would be earlier); GPWS and TCAS only warn pilots; 1998 and 2009 Auto-GCAS tests are refinements.
searched: archive.org full-text search for automatic ground collision avoidance 1985-1999 and terrain following 1958-1968; read DTIC ADA184941, ADA216247 (cites AFFTC-TR-87-11 AFTI/F-16 AMAS GCAS Evaluation, Aug 1987), ICAS 1998 abstract; web search. AFFTC-TR-87-11 itself not retrieved.

what: The USAF fielded Auto-GCAS on its F-16 fleet during 2014, which automatically takes control and recovers the aircraft from imminent ground impact; it saved its first pilots within months.
fit: Sensors, terrain data and automation take over the aircraft and avoid ground collision with no pilot input, in operational service.

note: No earlier operational automatic system found that strictly fits: terrain-following radar (F-111 1967 onward) is automatic low flying but not collision recovery (rejected as borderline, see demonstration); six earlier F-16 systems were manual warnings. Month was September 2014 per the Air Force Magazine article (published year of 'last September' not clear from page, which shows 2016), 2014 per The Aviationist. The Aviationist text appears to be the 2015 article.
searched: web search, Wikipedia Auto-GCAS, Aviationist 2015, Air & Space Forces Magazine, NASA 2015 feature via Wayback.

what: Anastase Dragomir's catapulted, parachuted cockpit cell was tested in a Farman airplane flown by Lucien Bossoutrot at Paris-Orly, repeated 26 October 1929 at Baneasa near Bucharest in an Avia.

note: Date kept at 28 Aug 1929 (Wikipedia Dragomir and the Romanian engineers' journal AGIR agree; the Ejection seat article says 25 Aug). The AGIR page says the French press, including Excelsior of 29 Aug 1929, reported the test, but that paper could not be fetched. Neither source says whether a person or a dummy rode the cell, so it may be a weaker demonstration than it looks. Rejected earlier: 1910 bungee-assisted escape (not an ejection system); Calthrop 1916 compressed-air seat (patent only); Dragomir's 1928 patent filing (a patent); Heinkel He 280 and Swedish compressed-air seats 1940-41 (later); a plain parachute jump from a plane (the definition asks for a seat, capsule or pod).
searched: Wikipedia Anastase Dragomir, Ejection seat, Heinkel He 280; AGIR article; archive.org full text 1929-1931 for Dragomir (no hits); WebSearch for Gallica/Excelsior coverage (none reachable).

No contemporary source: the event was a secret wartime test, not reported at the time.
searched: Wikipedia Ejection seat and Heinkel He 280; archive.org full text 1942-1950 for Schenk He 280 ejection (no hits).

what: From 1920 RAF aeroplanes made vertical ascents in the UK for meteorological purposes, carrying instruments to record upper-air conditions.
fit: Aircraft flown to take atmospheric measurements for scientific data, showing the method worked.

sources.publisher: Royal Meteorological Society History Group newsletter
sources.title: History Group newsletter (talk by Brian Booth on RAF meteorological flights 1920-1959)
sources.quote: from 1920 until 1951, RAF aeroplanes were used to make vertical ascents for meteorological purposes

note: Candidates considered: Duckworth's 1943-07-27 AT-6 flight into a hurricane (a bet/training flight, no data, and long after routine sounding flights) and Wexler's 1944-09-14 flight (first recorded direct hurricane measurements, but storm-chasing is only one strand of the concept and routine aircraft sampling of the atmosphere is older); US Weather Bureau/Army Air Corps aircraft meteorograph network from 1925 to 1943 (later than the RAF Met Flight by about a year); 1935 hurricane search flights (searching, not measuring); 1913 Signal Corps San Diego airplane-meteorology work in Carpenter's 1917 book (instructional, not found to be routine sampling). Snow-survey and soil-sampling aircraft were not found earlier than these. Strict-fit caveat: the sounding flights sampled air temperature and humidity (clouds/atmosphere) for forecasting and research, which fits 'aircraft flown routinely to sample the atmosphere for data' but not snow or soil. The 1920 start rests on one retrospective talk report; no contemporary 1920 source was found.
searched: WebSearch (worked) for earliest aircraft meteorological flights, THUM/Duxford, 1943 hurricane flights; archive.org full-text search 1919-1928 (Nature, Flight, Meteorological Magazine); RMetS newsletter; NWS heritage; Carpenter 1917 book (Gutenberg timed out, archive.org text read in part); no contemporary source for 1920.

what: A periscope, designed with Lindbergh's help and installed by a former submariner at Ryan, gave forward vision in the Spirit of St. Louis, whose windshield was blocked by the fuel tank.

what: James McCurdy sent a wireless telegraph message from his Curtiss biplane in flight over Sheepshead Bay, New York, received by H. M. Horton on the grandstand, watched by Signal Corps officers and thousands of spectators.
fit: A radio (spark telegraph) link was established between a flying aircraft and a ground station and carried a message.

sources.title: The New York Times, 28 Aug 1910 (Sheepshead Bay aviation meet)
sources.quote: McCurdy in his flights carried a wire- less sending apparatus

sources.title: Aviation and Aeroplanes (Proceedings of the US Naval Institute, March 1911)
sources.quote: the first wireless message by Mr. J. B. McCurdy, on August 27, 1910

sources.publisher: Electronics in the West (Jane Morgan, 1967), on earlyradiohistory.us
sources.title: Wireless Begins to Talk and Fly
sources.quote: this is recognized as the first official transmission of a wireless telegraph message from the air to take place in the United States

note: Earlier candidates considered. (1) Elmo Pickerill's claimed solo flight with two-way wireless at Mineola on 4 Aug 1910: rejected, the claim rests on papers assembled from 1931, no contemporary report exists, and Air & Space (Smithsonian) reports new research suggesting the flight never happened. (2) Earle Ennis's unpublicized airborne transmitter test at Tanforan, spring 1910: date, pilot and flight are unknown (the 1967 book says only 'it is possible' it was around 29-30 May 1910), no contemporary record. (3) Balloon and airship wireless before Aug 1910: no pre-1910 wireless message from an aircraft turned up in searches; Clement-Bayard No. 2 (7 Sept 1910) and Wellman's America (Oct 1910) are later. (4) Ennis/Beck/Parmalee Wright flight at Tanforan (21 Jan 1911) is later. McCurdy's flight was publicly witnessed and reported next day.
searched: archive.org full text (NYT 28 Aug 1910, Naval Institute Proceedings Mar 1911, Applied Science Jan 1911 also names McCurdy); earlyradiohistory.us Ennis chapter; Air & Space article on Pickerill; Wikipedia Air-to-ground communication; WebSearch for pre-1910 aircraft wireless.

what: Walter Wellman's airship America, leaving Atlantic City on its transatlantic attempt, carried a Marconi wireless outfit run by operator Jack Irwin and sent position and progress reports to shore stations and ships (and the sponsoring newspapers) throughout the flight, from 15 October 1910.
fit: Aircraft radio was used for its real purpose outside the lab: routine reports from an aircraft in flight to shore stations and ships, in constant communication with the ground, over several days.

sources.title: The New York Times, 16 Oct 1910 (Wellman airship America sails)
sources.quote: the first wireless / messages ever received from an airship over the sea were pouring in

sources.title: The New York Times, 17 Oct 1910 (Wellman's wireless messages)
sources.quote: the shore and ocean liners, this proving con- clusively the efficiency of wireless in aerial navigation

note: Replaces the 1914-09-24 Royal Flying Corps artillery-spotting use (Marconi Heritage), which is a real deployment but about four years later; Lewis and James's sorties at the Aisne are the first use in warfare, not the first use. Wellman's flight is an expedition rather than a standing service, so the case is arguable, but it fits the definition (reports from an aircraft to the ground and ships, sent in earnest, not as a test). Other candidates rejected: McCurdy 27 Aug 1910 and the Jan 1911 Tanforan manoeuvres (mock war, demonstrations); Clement-Bayard No. 2 airship wireless tests (7 Sept 1910, tests); 1912-13 RFC wireless experiments (experiments); Italo-Turkish War 1911-12 not found documented; voice (1915 Brooklands) is later.
searched: NYT 16, 17, 18 Oct 1910 on archive.org; Marconi Heritage page (1914 date still checks); Thrower RFC radio history; WebSearch for first operational aircraft wireless (RFC, French Marne 1914, Italo-Turkish war; found nothing earlier than America except test flights); Wikipedia Air-to-ground communication. The RAF Museum page 404s.

what: United Air Lines' flying laboratory (H. M. Hucke) flight-tested trailing discharge wires in the Pacific Northwest in 1937 and found they gave improved radio reception in precipitation static by bleeding off the plane's charge.
fit: A fine trailing wire with a suppressor resistor let the charge on the aircraft leak off, the definition's trailing ground wire or leaker.

sources.title: Advance Against Snow Static
sources.quote: Trailing discharge wire gives improved reception through static

sources.title: Precipitation-Static Interference on Aircraft and at Ground Stations
sources.quote: Flights with this arrangement were made in the fall of 1937

note: Rejected: Blanchard's 1920 patent (proposal, not shown working); metallic shielded loop antennas of 1935-36 (shield the antenna, not the craft's charge); Bendix trailing-wire discharger 1940 and static wicks of WWII (later); no earlier airship or balloon bleed-off device found. Hucke's 1939 history shows no earlier discharger tests, only insulated antennas (1930, 1932) that failed.
searched: archive.org full-text 1925-1940 (Aviation Week 1937-08, IRE Proceedings 1939-05 history section, Air Force Magazine 1940-06, Gettysburg Times 1937-11-05 AP item on Sandretto's discharger), Wikipedia Static wick, WebSearch (worked; nothing earlier).

what: United Air Lines' commercial static-discharge cartridge system (ejectable fine wire with wind cone) was adopted and installed, usually two per plane, on airliners by 1939.

note: Hucke's May 1939 paper says commercial models were manufactured after two years of test flying; the exact start of airline service (probably 1938) was not found. Nov 1937 AP item calls it a new device. The Air Corps was only testing trailing dischargers in 1940; static wicks (WWII) are later.
searched: archive.org 1937-1940 for airline adoption (Gettysburg Times 1937-11-05, IRE 1939-05, Air Force Magazine 1940-06); no date for first installation found.

what: Zeppelin LZ 120 Bodensee began a regular passenger and mail service between Berlin and Friedrichshafen in Germany, first passenger flight 24 Aug 1919.

sources.title: Deception Island

note: Later cases: Argentine families at Esperanza Base (1978) and Chile's Villa Las Estrellas (permanently populated 15 Feb 1984, with school, bank and post office). what: Serbian private Radoje Ljutovac shot down an Austro-Hungarian aircraft over Kragujevac with a modified captured Turkish cannon, the first aircraft downed by ground artillery.
fit: A ground-based gun fired at an attacking aircraft in war and brought it down; the same event is both the demonstration and the first real use.

sources.title: Flight International Magazine 1915-10-08
sources.quote: Another aeroplane must, there- fore, have come down near Kragujevatz, besides the one which was brought down at Cragourvatl.

sources.title: Anti-aircraft warfare
sources.quote: During the bombing raid, private Radoje Ljutovac fired his cannon at the enemy aircraft and successfully shot one down.

note: Earlier candidates: Krupp Ballonabwehrkanone (1870, built against balloons, no kill credited) rejected, function not shown; Turkish rifle fire downing Lt Manzini's aircraft (25 Aug 1912) rejected as rifles, not a gun or battery; Serbian machine-gun air-to-air hit of 9 June 1915 (Flight 1915-06-18) is air-to-air; no ground-artillery kill before 30 Sept 1915 was found (a web search for 1914 claims found none; Nesterov's 1914 ramming is air-to-air). Radar-aimed AA (SCR-584, 1944) is a later refinement. The Kragujevac gun was a modified captured Turkish cannon on an improvised mount, which the definition (any ground-based gun that shoots down aircraft) allows. The nurse's diary names the day and a downed aeroplane but not who fired; the gunner's name rests on Wikipedia and the Serbian Ministry of Defence.

what: Watermarked paper first used for banknotes, by Berkshire paper maker Rice Watkins, so that forgers needed special paper and mould equipment.
fit: A watermark is a hidden marker built into special banknote paper that makes forgeries harder to make and easy to detect by holding the note to the light.

sources.title: Banknote
sources.quote: Watermarks for notes were first used in 1697, by Rice Watkins, a Berkshire paper maker.

note: Single reference source; other histories date the Bank of England's watermarked notes from Portal's Laverstoke mill to 1725, so 1697 is uncertain. Earlier candidates: Song dynasty jiaozi (11th century) were stamped with multiple banknote seals to combat counterfeiting, but visible seals are not special materials, hidden markers or automatic checking, so rejected as loose. Ancient coin milling and testing not dated to a strict fit. Automatic checking (coin and note validators) came later.
searched: Wikipedia Banknote, Counterfeit money, Security printing, Jiaozi and Huizi pages; WebSearch for Rice Watkins 1697 and Portal watermark (not corroborated).

sources.title: Banknote

what: At the US ambassador's residence in Moscow, State Department technician Joseph Bezjian found the Soviet passive cavity-resonator bug (The Thing) in the Great Seal carving during a radio countersurveillance sweep.
fit: A signal generator and receiver producing audio feedback detected a hidden listening device so the room could be cleared of it.

sources.title: The Thing (listening device)
sources.quote: They conducted a countersurveillance sweep of the ambassador's office

note: Kept. Earlier candidates considered: the Moscow embassy sweep at the end of WWII said to have found 120 devices (greydynamics.com; a manual physical search with no detection instrument named, no date or primary source); 1930s-40s detectophone/dictagraph hits in archive.org are bugs, not countermeasures; 1952 convention-hall searches for hidden microphones were manual searches; shielded rooms and TEMPEST (about 1960) are later. No dated pre-1951 detector sweep that strictly fits was found. The year is uncertain by one: Wikipedia says the bug was spotted by radio in 1951, the Ford/Bezjian sweep followed in March 1951 or later, and the exposure is 1952. The find was secret until 1960, so no contemporary source exists.
searched: archive.org full-text: detectophone, dictagraph detect, 'hidden microphones' 1900-1955, wire tap detector; WebSearch (worked) on early TSCM history; CIA Audiosurveillance PDF; Wikipedia The Thing and TSCM; counterespionage.com Great Seal page (no Bezjian text found). No contemporary source: discovery classified until 1960.

what: Kwajalein, 24 May 1963: a ground-launched Nike Zeus DM-15S (Project Mudflap) was tracked to and intercepted an Agena D target fitted with a miss-distance transmitter, after two failed attempts (21 March, 19 April).
fit: A ground-launched rocket guided to a real orbiting spacecraft and brought within the lethal radius of its nuclear warhead, the same standard (intercept in the kill radius) used for Kosmos 252.

sources.title: Nike Zeus
sources.quote: Success was finally achieved on 24 May 1963 against a real target.

sources.title: Nike Zeus
sources.quote: was carried out on 24 May 1963, and was a complete success.

note: Replaces Kosmos 252 (1 Nov 1968). Considered: Bold Orion (13 Oct 1959, air-launched, mock attack, no kill radius test); earlier DM-15S shots (17 Dec 1962 and 15 Feb 1963 intercepted fix points in space, 21 Mar and 19 Apr 1963 failed); Starfish and Thor 437 shots (no real intercept of a satellite); Kosmos 249 (20 Oct 1968, outside kill radius). The 24 May 1963 shot is the first complete intercept of a real orbiting target by a ground-launched rocket; like Kosmos 252 it destroyed nothing, since the target carried a miss-distance transmitter and no warhead detonated, so it is a 'would have destroyed' result. Low confidence: only secondary sources, and the test was classified (no 1963 public report found). If a reader requires an actual warhead detonation, Kosmos 252 (1968-11-01) is the fallback; contemporary report of that is the NYT 5 Feb 1970 reprint in the CIA journal, source CIA-RDP72-00337R000100040034-7.
searched: Wikipedia Anti-satellite weapon, Nike Zeus, Program 437; nuclearabms.info; WebSearch (worked) for Mudflap; NASA Astronautics and Aeronautics 1963 and 1964 chronologies (no public report of the Agena intercept; Zeus reports of 29 May and 14 Jun 1963 are ICBM-warhead intercepts); Army SMDC PDF refused (403, archive copy not a PDF).

what: On 27 June 1963 Secretary of Defense McNamara ordered a Nike Zeus missile kept ready at all times at Kwajalein with a live nuclear warhead, giving the US an operational anti-satellite capability (Program 505); it stayed on alert until 1964.
fit: A ground-launched interceptor system placed on alert for use against satellites in low orbit, the only practical use an ASAT has had, since none has been used in combat.

sources.title: Nike Zeus
sources.quote: Success was finally achieved on 24 May 1963 against a real target.

sources.title: Nike Zeus
sources.quote: From that point until 1964, one DM-15S was kept in a state of instant readiness

note: Replaces the Soviet IS declared operational in February 1973 (Wikipedia only), which is later. The second reader's point holds: the US Nike Zeus DM-15S was on instant alert from mid-1963 (nuclearabms.info: McNamara's order 27 June 1963), Thor Program 437 followed (NASA's 1964 chronology, from McNamara's 18 Sep 1964 news conference: 'usaf antisatellite system, utilizing Thor missile, completed successful operational testing and became operational'; contemporary, so a firmer but later date). The earlier researcher rejected these because they had not shown a kill; with the demonstration now 1963-05-24 that objection no longer applies. Low confidence: secondary sources only, no 1963 public report (the posture was secret; first public hints are NYT 20 Oct 1963 on a DoD ground-to-space weapons program).
searched: As for the demonstration; NASA chronologies 1963 and 1964 on archive.org for antisatellite/Zeus/Kwajalein; nuclearabms.info and Wikipedia Nike Zeus and Program 437.

what: On Apollo 8 (launched 21 Dec 1968) the Lunar Module Pilot took one Marezine (cyclizine) tablet for space motion sickness, with good results; his symptoms subsided.
fit: A pill taken by a space traveler in orbit relieved motion-sickness nausea, a drug countermeasure for space sickness.

sources.title: Apollo 8 Mission Report
sources.quote: The Lunar Module Pilot also took one Marezine tablet, with good results.

sources.publisher: NASA (Apollo 7 to 11: Medical Concerns and Results)
sources.title: Apollo 7 to 11: Medical Concerns and Results
sources.quote: Medication has been used in three of the six inflight motion sickness episodes.

note: Replaces Skylab 3 (July 1973). Apollo 8 (Dec 1968) was the first flight with space motion sickness and the first where a drug was taken for it. Apollo 9 (March 1969) was the first prophylactic dose (Marezine before liftoff and after insertion; Apollo 9 report), but the Apollo 8 dose is earlier and did relieve symptoms. Apollo 7 (Oct 1968) crew had no motion sickness. Apollo 8 Commander was told to take Marezine if nausea returned but did not. Gemini and Mercury and Vostok flights: no drug use found (no reported space motion sickness drug). Skylab 3 scopolamine/dextroamphetamine is later.

what: Albert Calmette (Pasteur Institute) told the Academie des Sciences on 27 March 1894 that the serum of animals immunized against snake venom is preventive, antitoxic and therapeutic; Phisalix and Bertrand had shown the blood of vaccinated animals neutralized viper venom in February 1894 (Societe de Biologie, 10 February).
fit: A specific counteragent (immune serum) that neutralizes and, given after the venom, reverses a named venom's effect in animals.

sources.publisher: Comptes rendus de l'Academie des sciences, vol. 118 (Phisalix and Bertrand note quoting Calmette, Comptes rendus 27 March 1894)
sources.title: Comptes rendus Academie des sciences 0118
sources.quote: le sérum des animaux ainsi traités est à la » fois préventif, antitoxique et thérapeutique

sources.title: Calmette on venoms and antivenom serum
sources.quote: sérum, la guérison est la régle

sources.title: Antivenom
sources.quote: announced that they had achieved treatment of a vulnerable animal with serum from an immunized one

note: Given milestone (1894, announced 10 February 1894) refined: the 10 February reports (Calmette; Phisalix and Bertrand) concerned immunization and the antitoxic action of the immune blood in vitro; the curative (therapeutic) serum was stated by Calmette on 27 March 1894, which is the earliest date the reversing function is documented in the sources read. Earlier candidates rejected: Bunsen and Berthold's hydrated iron oxide for arsenic (1834; the Lancet 1838-40 reports it as a new antidote, but it chemically locks arsenic in the gut rather than reversing a systemic effect, and I am not certain this is too loose, see concept note); atropine versus physostigmine (1860s, drug antagonism, later); Sewall 1887 immunization of pigeons against rattlesnake venom (prevention by prior immunization, not a counteragent given after); diphtheria antitoxin 1890-91 (counters a bacterial toxin, not a venom, paralytic or chemical agent). Later: first human use 1895.
searched: Wikipedia Antivenom, Antidote, Arsenic poisoning; PMC4898362 (Phisalix and Calmette discovery paper); archive.org full text of Comptes rendus vol. 118 (1894), Annales de l'Institut Pasteur 1895-04, Calmette's 1896 book; archive.org searches for Bunsen arsenic antidote 1834-1840.

what: Calmette's antivenom serum, made in donkeys and horses at the Pasteur Institute in Lille from 1895, was used on a bitten snake collector, the first person treated with antivenom; Calmette's March 1896 book also reports an Annamite bitten by a cobra at Saigon cured by a 12 cc serum injection.
fit: The counteragent was injected into poisoned patients and the venom's symptoms disappeared.

sources.title: Advancing antivenom

Calmette's 1897 memoir says the Lille institute had been preparing and distributing serum 'for more than a year', so routine supply began about 1896. Earlier candidates: none for an immune-serum antidote; arsenic antidote of 1834 and 1838 human cases (iron oxide) rejected as loose.

what: Hidemi Seno and Juzo Hori in Japan published a floating-raft method of growing oysters on hanging ropes, which replaced stakes in the ground and was soon used in farms.
fit: A working shellfish-farming method on rafts, adopted by commercial oyster farms.

sources.title: A Short History of Aquaculture Innovation
sources.quote: Hidemi Seno and Juzo Hori published a paper describing their new method for growing oysters by attaching them to ropes

sources.title: Aquaculture
sources.quote: Floating rafts have been used for mass production since the 1920s.

note: Replaces the 1969 Norwegian salmon date. Considered: Norwegian sea-cage salmon (Mowi release end of 1969, Grontvedt brothers 28 May 1970; laks.no notes trout was farmed in Norway in the 1950s-60s before), which is later; US trout hatcheries (1860s) and Roman or Hawaiian ponds, small scale or not industrial; Japanese yellowtail pens (about 1927-28) were small and low intensity at first (Bardach 1972). what: W. R. Amberson and colleagues (Marine Biological Laboratory, Woods Hole, and University of Pennsylvania) removed essentially all the blood from cats and dogs through cannulas and replaced it with a hemoglobin-Ringer-Locke solution, on which the animals lived, breathed and recovered consciousness for hours; announced in Science, 4 August 1933, full paper J. Cell. Comp. Physiol. 5 (December 1934).
fit: The animal's blood was replaced by a prepared fluid that carried oxygen and kept it alive, the same function as the definition's synthetic blood or special fluid.

sources.quote: all but the last traces of the normal blood may be swept out of the body

sources.quote: They recover consciousness and are able to walk and run.

note: Replaces the given 1968 Geyer fluorocarbon total perfusion of rats: Amberson's replacement of the normal blood of cats, dogs and rabbits by hemoglobin-Ringer solution is 35 years earlier, was a complete (to the last traces) blood exchange with survival, and is reported in Science in 1933 (contemporary) and reviewed by Amberson in Biological Reviews 1937 and in the 1935 Annual Review of Biochemistry. The solution is made from washed red-cell hemoglobin, so it is a fluid substitute rather than a fully synthetic one; the definition says 'synthetic substitute or special fluid', so it fits. Also considered and rejected: Kronecker and Sander's 1879 saline replacement in dogs and the 19th-century milk and saline transfusions (restore volume, no oxygen carrier, not checked by a fetched source); Sloviter and Kamimoto's 1967 fluorocarbon perfusion of isolated rat brain (organ, not a whole animal); Clark and Gollan's 1966 liquid-breathing mice (not blood replacement); Geyer 1968 rats (later; a PMC review gives 1968 but no contemporary page was found). The 1968 date and the earlier Geyer quote therefore drop.

what: Marvin Minsky and Dean Edmonds built SNARC at Princeton, a machine of about 40 Hebb-synapse neurons that learned to solve a maze by reinforcement (funded in summer 1951).

Earlier candidates rejected: McCulloch and Pitts 1943 (a mathematical model of neurons, nothing built, no learning); Hebb 1949 (a learning theory, no machine); Turing's 1948 'unorganised machines' (a paper design, not built); Ashby's Homeostat 1948 and Grey Walter's tortoises 1948-49 (a few valve units, not a neuron network that learns). Later: Farley and Clark 1954 (simulation on a computer), Rochester et al. 1956, Rosenblatt's perceptron 1957-58, Widrow's ADALINE 1960. The earliest contemporary record is Minsky's January 1952 Harvard report, 'A neural-analogue calculator based upon a probability model of reinforcement' (known only from citations, not online), and his 1954 Princeton thesis; neither was readable, so the sources are Wikipedia only and the exact month is unknown.

what: NASA's DART spacecraft struck the asteroid moonlet Dimorphos on 26 September 2022; NASA confirmed on 11 October 2022 that its orbit around Didymos was shortened by 32 minutes.
fit: An asteroid was deliberately moved into a measurably new orbit by a spacecraft; the match is on function (redirection) and the mechanism is kinetic impact rather than the gravity or thrusters in the definition.

sources.title: NASA confirms DART probe impact changed asteroid's orbit
sources.quote: shaving 32 minutes off the time needed to complete one orbit around a parent asteroid known as Didymos

sources.title: Asteroid impact avoidance
sources.quote: This mission constitutes the first successful attempt at asteroid deflection.

note: No earlier event strictly fits: no asteroid had been captured or moved by gravity tractor, ion-beam or thrusters (these remain proposals such as ARM, cancelled 2017). Deep Impact (2005) hit comet Tempel 1, a comet not an asteroid, with a negligible orbit change. Hayabusa, NEAR and OSIRIS-REx touched or orbited asteroids without altering their orbits. Mechanism differs from the definition (impact, not gravity or thrusters), but nothing else exists, so the function-level fit is kept. Dimorphos's orbit around Didymos changed, not the pair's solar orbit.

what: NASA chose the Mercury Seven (announced 1959-04-09) under a height limit of 5 ft 11 in and an age under 40, set by the capsule's size.

note: Confirmed: NASA's Mercury astronaut selection (criteria set late 1958, seven chosen and announced 1959-04-09) imposed a height ceiling of 5 ft 11 in and an age under 40, and 6 of the first 69 candidates were dropped for being over the height limit, so body size really selected people. Candidates considered: Soviet cosmonaut group of 1960 (height and weight limits, but later); USAF Man In Space Soonest 1958 (no selection was made, nothing found on size rules); the Mercury 13 women tests of 1960-61 (later, privately run); John Glenn's 1998 Shuttle flight at 77 (later, and the elderly-selection part of the definition). The rule is a maximum-size cap, so it fits the definition only in part (small people favored, not small people specially sought); no earlier real selection by size or age was found. Same event serves both kinds.

what: Friedrich Zibold, a Russian forester-engineer, built a stone-pile air-well condenser on Mount Tepe-Oba near Feodosia, Crimea, which began operating in 1912 and yielded up to about 360 liters of water a day from condensation of air moisture, until 1915.
fit: Moisture from the air condensed on a cooled mass of stones and was collected as water with no other source, matching condensation of drinking water from air.

sources.quote: Zibold's condenser began to operate in 1912 with a maximum daily production that was later estimated to have been 360 litres

note: Replaces the 1969 South African fog fences. Earlier or competing candidates: Chaptal's 1929 Montpellier concrete-and-limestone air well (1 to 2.5 L/day; its builder judged it a failure; no source fetched); Knapen's 1930-32 aerial well at Trans-en-Provence (Popular Science, March 1933, says first tests 'met with complete success', but the well fell far short of its hoped-for yield, and it is later than Zibold); Lavoisier/Cavendish water synthesis of the 1780s (a chemistry experiment, not a water supply); ancient Inca fog catching and dew ponds (undated, dew ponds are filled mostly by rain); Klaphake's unbuilt Cook, South Australia proposal (1930s) and an earlier coal-powered active condenser at Cook (undated, no source found). Zibold made no public record at the time and the 360 L/day figure was estimated later, and there is no contemporary source, so confidence is low; the date is the year operation began.

what: The USSR's Venera 4 descent capsule entered Venus's atmosphere on 18 October 1967 and descended by parachute, radioing temperature, pressure and atmospheric composition measurements from a thermometer, barometer, hydrometer, altimeter and gas analyzers; its magnetometer and plasma traps measured field and charged particles.

what: Heinrich Lamm, a medical student in Munich, transmitted an image through a bundle of flexible glass fibres bent around curves, aiming to look inside the body.

note: Dated alternative: image carried by light along a bent fibre bundle so a viewer sees around corners (Lamm, 1930). fit: Scalp EEG signals are filtered and detected by a machine, and the person sends coded commands to it by voluntary brain activity alone.

sources.title: Air Force Research Review 1964-11: Vol 3 Iss 9
sources.quote: Thus, by blocking his alpha rhythm in the appropriate manner, the user can send coded signals without moving a muscle.

sources.title: Air Force Research Review 1964-11: Vol 3 Iss 9
sources.quote: Dewan has successfully demonstrated his device to several doctors by operating it with his own alpha rhythm.

sources.title: Air Force Research Review 1963-11-02: Vol 2 Iss 17
sources.quote: This study has led Dewan to a proposed technique for using thought processes to operate switches

note: Kept at 1964. The same laboratory's Nov 1963 report calls the technique only 'proposed' with equipment on order, and the Nov 1964 report says it was built and demonstrated, so 1963 is excluded; wire stories of 25 Oct 1964 (Il Piccolo di Trieste) also report the working demonstration, bracketing it to Nov 1963-Oct 1964. Earlier candidates rejected: Berger's 1924-29 EEG (recording only, no machine control); Kamiya's 1962 alpha feedback training (subject reports a state; no device); Grey Walter's 1964 slide-projector experiment (patients with implanted electrodes; I could not find a dated primary report, and the cursor-like control ran on premotor signals before a button press, so it is unverified and not earlier than Dewan); Lucier's Music for Solo Performer 1965 (later, an artwork); Fetz 1969 (monkeys); Vidal 1973 (later). One organization's reports only (plus the wire story), hence medium.

what: W. Gilman Thompson of New York University exchanged and transplanted pieces of brain tissue between dogs and between cat and dog; a piece of cat brain grafted into a dog's brain survived seven weeks, firmly united to it with blood vessels, and he published it as 'Successful brain grafting' in the New York Medical Journal of 28 June 1890.
fit: Part of one animal's brain was surgically moved into another animal's brain and survived, which the definition allows ('a whole brain, or part of one, from one body into another').

sources.title: Successful brain grafting
sources.quote: successful brain grafting has not heretofore been performed

sources.title: Successful brain grafting
sources.quote: firmly adherent to the dog's brain, with the pia mater intact

note: Added: the earlier researchers had no milestone. The definition includes 'part of' a brain and the aliases include 'brain graft', so Thompson's grafts fit; the weakness is that it is a tissue graft, with no function restored or intended, and the experiment day is not given (published 28 June 1890, the dog lived seven weeks, so the year only). If only whole-brain or whole-head moves count, the demonstration is Guthrie's 1908 dog head transplant (JAMA 14 Nov 1908: 'I have transplanted dogs' heads with preservation of cerebral and bulbar function'; the head showed reflexes for hours, Wikipedia), then Demikhov 1954 (dog head and forelegs, up to 29 days) and Robert White 1970 (monkey head onto another monkey, about 8 days; the second reader's candidate): all later than 1890, so not used. Earlier brain-tissue attempts (Del Conte 1907 and others) are later than Thompson.

what: BIOS-3, Institute of Biophysics, Krasnoyarsk: crewed closure experiments began in December 1972, the longest a three-person 180-day run (1972-73) in which algae and wheat renewed the air, water and urine were recycled (urine fed the wheat), and inedible plant matter was recycled, with most of the food grown inside.
fit: A sealed, crewed habitat that regenerated its air and water, reused crew urine and plant waste, and grew most of the crew's food for six months, which is the function and mechanism of closed-loop life support (a ground habitat standing in for an outpost).

sources.publisher: Persson, Closed Ecological Life Support Systems (Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences thesis)

sources.quote: The longest experiment with a three-person crew lasted 180 days (in 1972-1973).

note: Replaces Lunar Palace 1 (2014). The earlier rejection of BIOS-3 rested on Wikipedia's remark that dried meat was imported and feces were dried and stored; but the thesis (citing Salisbury, Gitelson and Lisovsky 1997 and Gitelson 2003) says the later set-up used urine in the wheat nutrient solution, recycled plant waste, produced most of the crew's food in the system and reached about 95 percent closure; only solid human waste was dried and stored, and some food and plant nutrients came from outside. That is as closed as the 2014 Lunar Palace 1 run, which also regenerated food only in part.
