searched: archive.org full text (armed helicopter Algeria 1955-57, Korea); Wikipedia Armed helicopter wikitext citations (acig.org, dead); WebSearch on Korea armed helicopters found only transport use.

what: Halley's Comet reached perihelion on 13 March 1759, delayed 618 days by Jupiter and Saturn, as Clairaut, Lalande and Lepaute had computed (within a month).
fit: Planetary perturbation of a comet's orbit was predicted by calculation and confirmed by observation, which establishes the orbit half of the claim.

sources.title: Halley's Comet
sources.quote: the attraction of Jupiter and Saturn having caused a delay of 618 days

note: I dated the orbit-perturbation half. Considered Halley's 1705 prediction (no perturbation test yet) and Lexell's comet (1770). The composition half (dirty snowball, Whipple 1950; nucleus imaged by Giotto and Vega 1986-03) was not dated separately; the definition bundles both, so this is a partial fit, hence low confidence.
searched: Wikipedia Halley's Comet

what: General Electric opened its research laboratory in Schenectady in 1900, the first industrial research facility in the United States, with research done by salaried scientists for a corporation.
fit: Scientific research was placed under corporate control and funded by a business for its commercial ends rather than done by independent individuals.

sources.title: General Electric Research Laboratory
sources.quote: General Electric Research Laboratory was the first industrial research facility in the United States. Established in 1900

sources.title: Laboratories
sources.quote: Around 1900, General Electric (GE) and AT&T established the first industrial research laboratories in America.

note: Considered Edison's Menlo Park laboratory (1876), often called the first industrial research lab, but it was one inventor's own enterprise, not corporate or state control. Search results also say German dye and pharmaceutical firms (BASF, Bayer, Hoechst) set up research laboratories in the 1870s and 1880s; I could not fetch a page dating one, so an earlier German date may exist. Chose GE 1900 as the earliest I could verify for a corporation.
searched: WebSearch for first industrial research laboratory; Wikipedia GE Research Laboratory and Bayer; encyclopedia.com Laboratories; sharpgiving Edison page.

what: After the Manhattan Project (1942-1946), governments became the chief patrons of science, especially in the United States and the Soviet Union, and big science became the norm.
fit: Research came under state big-project control and funding in the leading countries.

sources.title: Big science
sources.quote: After the success of the Manhattan Project, governments became the chief patrons of science

note: The page gives no single year; 1945 is the end of the war when state patronage became general. Corporate laboratories had spread through American industry in the 1920s (encyclopedia.com: a 'fever of commercialized science').
searched: Wikipedia Big Science and Manhattan Project; encyclopedia.com Laboratories.

what: The euro was introduced on 1 January 1999 as a common currency issued under the European Central Bank for 11 countries, replacing their national currencies as money of account and electronic payment.
fit: One currency set by a common authority replaced separate national currencies across many sovereign states.

sources.title: Euro
sources.quote: introduced to world financial markets as an accounting currency on 1 January 1999

note: Dated the euro as the first common currency of many sovereign states issued by one common authority that replaced national money. Rejected: Latin Monetary Union 1865 and Scandinavian Monetary Union 1873 (national mints, no common institution); the West African Currency Board 1912 and East African Currency Board 1919 (one currency across several British colonies, but colonies not countries, set by the imperial power); CFA franc 1945 and the 1962 West African Monetary Union (a currency shared by newly independent states: not a replacement of separate national money, and it fits only loosely). Cash circulation began 1 January 2002.
searched: Wikipedia Euro, West African Currency Board, Latin Monetary Union, CFA franc, East African Currency Board.

what: Euro banknotes and coins entered circulation on 1 January 2002 in 12 countries, replacing national cash in everyday use.
fit: A single currency issued by a common authority circulated in the hands of ordinary people across many countries.

sources.title: Euro
sources.quote: Physical euro coins and banknotes entered into circulation on 1 January 2002

note: Everyday cash use began on this date; see the first_practical_use note for earlier schemes rejected.
searched: Wikipedia Euro.

what: In Sparta, boys of citizen families entered the state-run agoge at age seven, living in barracks groups and restricted from contact with their birth families until adulthood.
fit: A state raised and educated children in groups in an institution, with the family no longer the unit of child care for boys over seven.

sources.title: Agoge
sources.quote: Participants were required to live in the open or in barracks, and were restricted from contact with birth families or wives.

sources.title: Agoge
sources.quote: modern scholars have dated its inception to the 7th or 6th century BC.

note: Date is the start of the 7th century BC (source gives only 'the 7th or 6th century BC'). Later: Owen's New Lanark infant school (1816), the first crèches (Paris 1844), kibbutz children's houses (1910s), Soviet nurseries. Partial fit: Sparta boys over seven only; girls and infants were raised at home.
searched: Wikipedia Agoge.

what: Degania Alef, the first kibbutz, was founded in 1910; kibbutz members ate meals together in the communal dining hall.
fit: A real community ran with a common dining hall as its normal custom, as an organized trial of communal life.

sources.title: Kibbutz
sources.quote: The first kibbutz was Degania Alef, founded in 1910.

sources.title: Kibbutz
sources.quote: Up until recently, members ate meals together in the communal dining hall.

note: Earlier communal communities (Shakers from the 1780s, Harmony Society, Oneida 1848, Owenite and Fourierist communities) probably ate together, but no fetched page stated that their meals were communal in place of home cooking, so none is dated. The Shaker page found dates only a first meal at Canterbury in 1795.
searched: WebSearch for Shaker and Oneida dining; Wikipedia Kibbutz, Degania Alef, Shakers, Harmony Society.

what: In China's 1958 people's communes, more than 3.4 million communal kitchens fed about 90 percent of the rural population by the end of 1958.
fit: Households stopped cooking at home and ate from public dining halls as the norm across most of a large country.

sources.title: State Repression and Selective Expression: Communal Canteens and the Collective Memory of China's Great Leap Famine
sources.quote: By the end of 1958, more than 3.4 million communal kitchens fed roughly 90 per cent of the country’s rural population.

note: Considered Petrograd 1919: a 1919 account says over 400,000 inhabitants received one meal a day in communal restaurants, with take-home allowed, so households still cooked: partial, rejected. Soviet factory-kitchens of the 1920s-30s (partial). Kibbutzim (a community, not a country, state or large city). 1958 is the first case I verified where the custom covered most of a large country.
searched: WebSearch for Petrograd 1919 and Chinese canteens; Wikisource Life in Petrograd in 1919; Wikipedia Factory-kitchen, Great Leap Forward, People's commune; China Quarterly.

what: Same event: by the end of 1958 about 90 percent of China's rural population ate in commune canteens.
fit: Most of one large country took meals from public kitchens instead of cooking at home.

sources.title: State Repression and Selective Expression: Communal Canteens and the Collective Memory of China's Great Leap Famine
sources.quote: By the end of 1958, more than 3.4 million communal kitchens fed roughly 90 per cent of the country’s rural population.

note: Lasted only until about 1961 (the Great Leap famine); one country only, but a large one. See first_practical_use.
searched: Same as first_practical_use.

what: Greek athletes competed and trained nude in the Olympic Games and gymnasia; Orsippus of Megara is traditionally the first to run naked at the Olympics, 720 BC.
fit: Going without clothing in shared spaces (athletic grounds and gymnasia) was normal for Greek men.

sources.title: Orsippus of Megara
sources.quote: Orsippus won the stadion of the 15th Olympic Games in 720 BC.

sources.title: Nudity in sport
sources.quote: Historically, the ancient Olympic Games were nude events.

note: Many prehistoric and indigenous societies were habitually unclothed but have no source dates. Others claim Acanthus introduced athletic nudity. Modern naturism (Germany, 1890s onward) is later.
searched: Wikipedia Orsippus of Megara, Nudity in sport, Naturism.

what: At the outbreak of the Indian Rebellion (Meerut/Delhi, May 1857) the mutineers cut the telegraph wires, leaving British stations cut off from news.
fit: Enemy forces cut telegraph lines at the start of an uprising, isolating the region from outside communication.

sources.title: The Examiner 1857-07-04
sources.quote: the telegraph wires were cut at the commencement of toe outbreak we know nothing of what is occurring elsewhere

note: Considered: Confederate cutting of telegraph lines into Washington after Fort Sumter (April 1861; Wikipedia 'Electric telegraph'), later than 1857; British cable cutting of Germany (Aug 1914) and Egypt's 2011 internet shutdown, later. The 1857 case is an enemy (rebel) cut, not a government act, and I did not find an earlier one (1848 revolutions, Crimean War) in the quick search; an earlier case may exist.
searched: WebSearch on earliest telegraph cutting; Wikipedia Electric telegraph, Indian Rebellion of 1857; archive.org full-text search for wires cut 1857 (found The Examiner 1857-07-04).

what: Project SCORE (launched 18 Dec 1958) received a taped message and retransmitted it from orbit, including President Eisenhower's Christmas greeting.
fit: An orbiting satellite received radio signals and retransmitted them to distant points on Earth, using an onboard tape recorder and transmitter.

sources.title: Project SCORE
sources.quote: used as a platform for a communications relay experiment to demonstrate the feasibility

sources.title: Victoria Daily Times 1958-12-20
sources.quote: its architects planned to again broadcast from it President Eisen- hower's Yuletide message of goodwill

note: Considered: Echo 1 (Aug 1960) passive reflector, not a receive-and-retransmit relay; Moon-bounce relays (1946, 1956) use a natural body; Sputnik 1 and Explorer 1 only transmitted telemetry; Courier 1B (Oct 1960) and Telstar are later. SCORE operated about 12 days. The AP report of 20 Dec 1958 shows the message had already been broadcast from the satellite.
searched: Wikipedia Project SCORE and Communications satellite; archive.org search for SCORE 1958 (Victoria Daily Times); searches for earlier relay satellites found none.

what: Telstar 1 (launched 10 July 1962) relayed the first live transatlantic television pictures and telephone calls; live TV programs between US networks and Europe followed on 23 July.
fit: An orbiting active repeater carried real television, telephone and data traffic between North America and Europe.

sources.title: Post Office Telecommunications Journal Volume 14 Part 3
sources.quote: the first television picture was flashed across the Atlantic by way of the artificial satellite Telstar

sources.title: Telstar
sources.quote: Telstar 1 was launched atop a Thor-Delta rocket on July 10, 1962, and relayed the first television pictures, telephone calls, and telegraph images through space.

note: Considered: SCORE (1958) and Courier 1B (1960) carried only test or military messages; Echo 1 (1960) was passive; Early Bird / Intelsat I (service from 28 June 1965) was the first commercial satellite and is the alternative if 'first service' means commercial. Telstar was experimental but carried real public telephone calls and live TV broadcasts between networks and PTTs, so it is kept. The Post Office journal says the first picture was flashed on 11 July 1962 (UK time), the public programs on 23 July.
searched: Wikipedia Telstar; archive.org Telstar 1962-1963 (Post Office Telecommunications Journal, NBC trade releases, BBC R&D report).

what: Bell Telephone Laboratories (F. S. Chen, J. T. LaMacchia, D. B. Fraser) showed a single crystal of lithium niobate used as a holographic storage medium, holding up to about 1000 holograms that could be read back and thermally erased.
fit: A small solid crystal stored large amounts of optical information in volume holograms and gave it back on readout.

sources.title: Holographic storage in lithium niobate
sources.quote: Single-crystal lithium niobate has been used as a holographic storage medium.

sources.title: Single crystal stores 1,000 holograms
sources.quote: The lithium niobate crystal can temporarily store up to 1000 different holograms.

note: Confirmed: same event as before. Earlier candidates: Poulsen's magnetic wire recorder 1898 and delay-line wire memories of the 1950s (a wire stores audio or a few thousand bits, not large amounts of data); Van Heerden 1963 theory of optical storage in solids (a proposal); a 1967 index entry for a nondestructively optically read bismuth titanate single-crystal memory device (A67-39261, seen only as an index line, a small bit-array memory, abstract not read); photochromic crystal memories of the 1960s (not verified). 1000 holograms is not a proven large capacity, so fit is partial. Later: 5D fused-quartz (Southampton 2013), a glass disc.
searched: Wikipedia holographic data storage and 5D optical data storage (earlier work); archive.org full text 1962-1968 for photochromic and holographic crystal memories; Crossref for the Chen/LaMacchia/Fraser paper; quotes re-checked (Crossref record 1968-10-01, Electronic Engineer Jan 1969).

what: The USB flash drive (M-Systems DiskOnKey, IBM and Trek ThumbDrive) was first offered for sale in late 2000: a small solid stick storing megabytes of files for later retrieval.
fit: A pocket-sized solid object that stores large amounts of a person's data for retrieval on any computer, in everyday use outside the lab; it matches the function but is a flash-memory chip in a stick, not a crystal, cube, rod or wire of the fiction.

sources.title: USB flash drive
sources.quote: Since first offered for sale in late 2000

sources.title: Editor's Choice, Portable Storage
sources.quote: Portable Storage: DiskOnKey (M-Systems, www.diskonkey.com)

note: A judgment call: the definition says 'such as a crystal, cube, rod or wire', so a flash stick fits loosely (small solid object, large amounts of data); the earlier researcher excluded flash as a chip. Drop this if strict material forms are required, in which case there is no practical use before the 5D quartz archives (2016 Southampton discs, 2018 Asimov Foundation disc launched on Falcon Heavy), which are glass discs and later. Earlier candidates: wire recorders 1940s-50s (audio, not data), magnetic core memory 1950s (small capacity), none strictly a small data-dense object.
searched: Wikipedia USB flash drive (sale date, M-Systems patent); archive.org 2000-2001 for DiskOnKey and ThumbDrive (Macworld Dec 2001, MacHome Aug 2001); no 2000 contemporary found, the MacHome 2001 review shows it in use.

what: Tiger Electronics showed the working Furby, an electronic robotic pet toy that reacts to touch, light and sound and 'learns' to speak, at the American International Toy Fair in New York.
fit: A small motorised, sensor-equipped robot built to act as an affectionate pet-like companion that responds to its owner; a loose match, with no romance or sex function.

sources.publisher: Mary Beth's Beanie World: Furby Edition
sources.title: Mary Beth's Beanie World: Furby Edition
sources.quote: completed the sam- ple Furby just in time for the annual eight day Toy Fair festival held in New York

sources.title: Furby
sources.quote: Furby's first public appearance was at the 1998 American International Toy Fair held in New York City.

note: Kept, with the fit caveat that Furby is a talking, moving toy and 'animatronic' toy in contemporary words. Considered and rejected as earlier: Sony's research robot-dog prototype (a 'robotic pet' picture caption in The Japan Times index, Aug 1997, and the 1998 Zrehen/Kitano/Fujita 'pet robot' paper) because it was a research prototype with no companion product, not built to give companionship and shown with only an index caption; Petster (1996 toy dog on wheels), Omnibot (1984) and Teddy Ruxpin (1985), toys sold for play, not companionship; Tamagotchi (1996, virtual pet, not a robot); RealDoll (1996-97, a doll, not a robot); Elektro/Sparko (1939, exhibits); Paro (designed from 1993, first exhibited late 2001, sold from 2004). Later and stricter alternative: Sony AIBO ERS-110, announced 1999-05-11 and sold 1999-06-01. No earlier romance or sex robot found; those come in the 2000s-2010s.
searched: archive.org full text for 'robotic pet', 'companion robot', 'pet robot' 1985-98 (mostly fiction and game magazines); Furby Toy Fair 1998 (newspapers and Beanie World); Wikipedia Furby, Paro, AIBO, Social robot; re-checked all quotes (FOUND).

what: Furby went on general sale in the United States (launched 2 October 1998, press event at FAO Schwarz, New York) and was a 1998 Christmas craze.
fit: The robotic pet toy was bought and kept by ordinary families as a companion that responds to touch and sound.

sources.publisher: Mary Beth's Beanie World: Furby Edition
sources.title: Mary Beth's Beanie World: Furby Edition
sources.quote: for his grand arrival at the flagship FAO Schwarz store in early October

sources.title: Furby
sources.quote: The product officially launched on October 2, 1998

sources.title: 1998-10-15 W5YI Report
sources.quote: Your kids will be wanting the new interactive Furby “animatronic” toy this Christmas!

note: Same fit caveat as the demonstration (a toy, accepted as a loose companion robot). AIBO (sold 1999-06-01) is later; Paro's handmade sales from 2004 are later. No earlier product sold as a robot companion was found; Petster (1996), Omnibot and Teddy Ruxpin were play toys.
searched: Same as demonstration; Furby launch in Wikipedia, Beanie World and the W5YI Report of 1998-10-15; newspaper hits from Dec 1998 confirm the Christmas sales.

what: Swedish prospectors used a magnetic compass to locate iron ore near Kiruna by its local deflection of the needle
fit: Local ore magnetism deflecting a compass was observed and exploited.

sources.title: Magnetic Methods in the Search for Iron Ore
sources.quote: recorded geophysical prospecting was the use of a magnetic compass to locate iron ore in the Kuruna region in Sweden as early as 1640

note: Candidates: Kursk Magnetic Anomaly 1773 (Inokhodtsev; later, and page does not describe compass). 1640 is a 'first recorded' prospecting claim; earlier unrecorded noticing of local deflection (and Gilbert 1600 on iron ore effects) is likely but undated. Discovery: first_practical_use and mass_adoption not applicable.
searched: WebSearch for earliest compass deflection by ore; Wikipedia Kursk Magnetic Anomaly; AusIMM 1951 paper; Parasnis 1975 cited in search result.

what: Andraud and Tessie du Motay ran a rail carriage for eight passengers on compressed air on a test track at Chaillot, Paris.
fit: A carriage driven by an engine running on stored compressed air.

sources.title: Compressed Air Trams - 1
sources.quote: with a car running on a test track at Chaillot on the 9th July 1840

note: Sources give 1838 for the vehicle and 1840 for the trial. German Wikipedia mentions a 1833 Henschel locomotive proposal, unverified so not used. Graces Guide also calls it the first authentic compressed-air carriage (about 1840).
searched: Graces Guide, tramwayinfo, web search.

what: Louis Mekarski's compressed-air trams entered regular service on the Nantes tramway after a Paris trial in 1876.
fit: Tramcars run by stored compressed air carried the public in regular service.

sources.title: Mekarski system
sources.quote: The system was tested in Paris in 1876 and introduced to the Nantes tramway in 1879.

note: Pneumatic locomotives were also used on the Gotthard tunnel works from 1872 to 1882 per Wikipedia, but no date of first use was found, so that was not used.
searched: Wikipedia Mekarski system, Compressed air vehicle, Fireless locomotive.

what: Light-bulb makers including Osram, Philips and General Electric incorporated the Phoebus cartel in Geneva on 15 January 1925, setting a 1,000-hour bulb life (down from 2,500) and fining makers whose bulbs lasted longer.
fit: Producers deliberately shortened product life so customers had to buy replacements more often, the planned-obsolescence half of the definition, by private cartel rather than by government.

sources.title: Phoebus cartel
sources.quote: The cartel lowered operational costs and worked to standardize the life expectancy of light bulbs at 1,000 hours (down from 2,500 hours)

note: Considered: General Motors annual model changes suggested by Alfred Sloan in 1924 (the page gives no date of first implementation; a suggestion, and style rather than product-life obsolescence); Bernard London's 1932 proposal of government-imposed legal obsolescence (a proposal only); state destruction of goods to support prices (US 1933 crop and livestock destruction, Brazilian coffee burning in the early 1930s; not checked or fetched). The cartel is private and the definition says government or economy; not a compulsion by a state. No mass_adoption date given.
searched: Wikipedia: Planned obsolescence, Phoebus cartel.

what: Indiana passed the world's first eugenics-based compulsory sterilization law in 1907.
fit: A state law ordered sterilization of people judged criminal or hereditarily unfit.

sources.title: Eugenics in the United States
sources.quote: In 1907, Indiana passed the first eugenics-based compulsory sterilization law in the world.

note: Considered Michigan's 1897 bill (failed), Pennsylvania's 1905 bill (vetoed) and Dr. Harry Sharp's sterilizations at the Indiana reformatory from 1899 (one doctor's practice, not a law or board). Indiana's law is the first in force. No separate first_demonstration given: the law and its use are the first organized program.
searched: Wikipedia Eugenics in the United States, Compulsory sterilization, Eugenics.

what: By 1933 laws existed in about thirty US states and Denmark (1929), and Germany passed its sterilization law in July 1933; Sweden followed in 1934.
fit: Governments in many countries sterilized people judged unfit under eugenic laws and boards.

sources.title: Compulsory sterilization
sources.quote: to pass the Law for the Prevention of Hereditarily Diseased Offspring (Gesetz zur Verhütung erbkranken Nachwuchses) in July 1933

sources.title: Eugenics in the United States
sources.quote: Thirty One U.S. states would soon follow their lead

sources.title: Compulsory sterilization
sources.quote: 11,000 people were sterilized in Denmark from 1929 to 1967

note: 1933 is a marker for when the practice was law in a large country (United States, mostly states), Denmark and Germany; the exact count of states at that date was not verified.
searched: Wikipedia Compulsory sterilization and Eugenics in the United States.

what: Italian city authorities issued health passes certifying that a traveler came from a plague-free place; the earliest known example is from Milan in 1484.
fit: A state authority required a health certificate of individuals before they could travel or enter.

sources.publisher: Social History of Medicine (White Rose repository)
sources.title: Health passes, print and public health in early modern Europe
sources.quote: Initially health passes were manuscript sheets akin to a letter of presentation, the earliest known example of which dates to Milan in 1484.

note: Health passes certify travel origin and are a limited form of health certification, not monitoring or classification of workers and citizens; the date is the earliest surviving example, and compulsory certificates may be older (searches mention 14th-century Italian bollette di sanita; not verified). Considered Wisconsin's 1913 marriage medical certificate law (later, and limited to men) and smallpox vaccination laws (1853 England; certificates not shown). No mass_adoption found.
searched: WebSearch for health passes and Wisconsin 1913; Bamji paper; Wikipedia Vaccination policy and Eugenics in the United States; UVM Wisconsin eugenics.

what: New Zealand passed the Industrial Conciliation and Arbitration Act in 1894, the world's first compulsory system of state arbitration.
fit: Disputes were settled by a Conciliation Board and an Arbitration Court whose rulings bound registered unions, which could not strike against them.

sources.title: Industrial Conciliation and Arbitration Act 1894
sources.quote: it was the world's first compulsory system of state arbitration.

sources.title: Industrial Conciliation and Arbitration Act 1894
sources.quote: If a union registered, it was bound to comply with the rulings of the Arbitration Court and could not, for example, strike

note: Date is the year the Act passed; it may have taken effect in 1895 (not checked). Earlier voluntary boards (e.g. state boards of arbitration in the US from 1886) were not compulsory. Mass_adoption: Australia's federal act 1904 and state systems followed, but I found no source showing many countries; none given.
searched: Wikipedia Industrial Conciliation and Arbitration Act 1894, Compulsory arbitration, Industrial Disputes Investigation Act.

what: GM Research's 'Digital Design' (later DAC-1) interactive graphics design system shown working at General Motors, 1959

sources.title: DAC-1
sources.quote: The system, known as Digital Design, was demonstrated and improved throughout 1959.

note: Rejected later candidates: DAC-1 full demo at IBM Kingston Dec 1962, Sketchpad (Sutherland, Jan 1963 report), DAC-1 public unveiling 1964; Hanratty's PRONTO (1957) is numerical-control programming, not interactive design by computer. The 1959 date rests on one Wikipedia statement and the early system's scope is unclear.

what: Production DAC-1 went live at GM in Warren, Michigan, used to design automobile parts (trunk lid modelled Nov 1963)

sources.title: DAC-1
sources.quote: The production DAC-1 system went live in Warren in April 1963.

note: Sketchpad (1963) was a thesis research system, not production. Earlier numerical-control tools (PRONTO 1957) are machining aids and were not counted. Not exhaustive for other countries (e.g. Citroen SPAC, Renault, 1960s).

what: Alex Bernstein's IBM 704 program for the full 8x8 board was in partial operation from about early 1958 and by September 1958 had played one full game against a human (and lost).
fit: A computer program that plays complete games of standard chess on the full board, shown working.

sources.publisher: RAND Corporation (Newell, Shaw and Simon, P-1319)
sources.title: Chess-Playing Programs and the Problem of Complexity
sources.quote: This program has been in partial operation for the last six months, and has now played one full game plus a number of shorter sequences.

note: Same event as the earlier researcher's (Bernstein, IBM 704) but the date moves from 1957 to 1958: the only contemporary report (RAND, 4 Sept 1958) says the program took two years to build, had been in partial operation for six months and had played one full game; no source shows a full game in 1957. Candidates rejected: El Ajedrecista (1912, king-and-rook endgame machine, not a program); Turing's Turochamp (1948-52, never run on a computer); Prinz's 1951 Ferranti Mark 1 program (mate-in-two only); Los Alamos MANIAC I chess (1956, 6x6 board without bishops, a variant, 'we can beat a beginner' only); the Soviet BESM program (about 1957-58) has no contemporary source found. If a 1957 Bernstein game is documented, 1957 would stand.
searched: archive.org full-text search for Bernstein/IBM 704 chess 1957-1959 (found RAND P-1319, Proc. Western Joint Computer Conference 1958 contents, Scientific American June 1958 index entry 'Computer v. Chess-Player', whose text is lending-only); Wikipedia Computer chess.

what: Peter Jennings of Toronto finished Microchess for the 1K KIM-1 microcomputer and put it on sale (Micro-Ware), the first chess program sold commercially.
fit: A chess-playing program sold to and used by people for play on their own computer, which is the practical use of a chess program.

sources.title: KIM-1/6502 User Notes, Volume 1 Issue 3
sources.quote: Peter Jennings says that his chess playing program is now available, runs on the basic KIM with no additional memory

sources.title: Computer chess
sources.quote: In December, Canadian programmer Peter R. Jennings releases Microchess, the first game for microcomputers to be sold.

note: Replaces Fidelity Chess Challenger (March 1977, dedicated hardware) with the earlier sale of Microchess (completed Dec 1976, announced as available in the Jan 1977 User Notes; the November 1976 issue 2 only said Jennings planned to market it). Rejected: Chess Challenger (March 1977) and Boris (1977) are later; ACM computer chess championships (from 1970) are program-versus-program competitions, not a product; Kaissa and Chess 4.5 (mainframe tournament programs) are not products. Exact Dec 1976 sale date rests on Wikipedia and the January 1977 report only.
searched: Wikipedia Microchess, Computer chess; KIM-1 User Notes issues 2 and 3 on archive.org; Creative Computing 1978, Byte, Kilobaud and MICRO hits on archive.org (later than 1977, used only to confirm the product).

what: St. Louis Metropolitan Police Department brought its IBM 7040/7740 police computer system into use (installed Oct-Dec 1964), giving officers fast access to wanted-person and stolen-vehicle records.
fit: A computer system built to assist crime detection, letting officers and detectives check suspects and vehicles against stored police records in seconds; a database, not evidence analysis or prediction.

sources.publisher: Digital Computer Newsletter (Office of Naval Research)
sources.title: Digital Computer Newsletter, Vol. 17 No. 2
sources.quote: The first components of an advanced police computer system were installed in October 1964

sources.publisher: Digital Computer Newsletter (Office of Naval Research)
sources.title: Digital Computer Newsletter, Vol. 17 No. 2
sources.quote: This computer system is designed specifi¬ cally to assist in crime detection and control

sources.publisher: ICMA / NCJRS (Computers and the Police Revisited)
sources.title: Computers and the Police Revisited
sources.quote: The first real-time police computer system was installed in the United States only ten years ago in the St, Louis police department.

note: Same event as the first practical use: the St. Louis system was an operational police tool from the start, with no separate earlier laboratory demonstration found. Replaced NCIC (1967): the St. Louis Metropolitan Police Department's IBM 7040/7740 police computer system, installed from October 1964 and put into use in 1965, gave patrolmen and detectives near-instant lookups of wanted persons and stolen vehicles to identify suspects, so it predates NCIC but is the same kind of event (a crime database, a loose fit to analysis and prediction). The Newsletter (April 1965) says it would need several months of testing before it was fully operational, so the use date is 1965, not 1964. Other candidates: NCIC (Jan 1967) later; New Orleans arrest and warrant computer system (1955) seen only in a secondary snippet, not checked or fetched; LAPD 'Computerized Crime Information' and SDC 'Computer Based Justice Identification and Intelligence System' are listed in the same 1965 newsletter without detail; San Diego 1967 clearing of cases and Kansas City ALERT II (1968) and the Police Beat Algorithm (about 1965-68, pattern recognition, suspect profiling and patrol positioning, described only in a 2022 retrospective) are later or unverified; NYPD 'Computer-Aided Crime Detection' (1966) is later; PredPol (2011) is the first predictive-policing product. True analysis of evidence or prediction was not found earlier than the late 1960s.
searched: WebSearch (early police computers, predictive policing history); Wikipedia Predictive policing and NCIC; archive.org full text 1956-1967 for police computers and suspects; read DTIC Digital Computer Newsletter 1965 and 1966 and an NCJRS 1974 article; slate.com article read for the Police Beat Algorithm; Task Force report (1967) is a lending item whose text was not available (HTTP 401). No newspaper report of the St. Louis go-live date was found.

fit: A computer system built to assist crime detection, letting officers and detectives check suspects and vehicles against stored police records in seconds; a database, not evidence analysis or prediction.

True analysis of evidence or prediction was not found earlier than the late 1960s.

what: The UK Post Office began prosecuting subpostmasters on the strength of Horizon accounting data; over 900 were prosecuted or convicted between 1999 and 2015.
fit: Computer records were treated as authoritative and the people they implicated suffered when the records were wrong.

sources.title: British Post Office scandal
sources.quote: Between 1999 and 2015, more than 900 subpostmasters were wrongfully convicted of theft, fraud and false accounting based on faulty Horizon data

sources.title: Post Office scandal: What the Horizon saga is all about
sources.quote: prosecuting 700 people between 1999 and 2015

note: Considered and rejected earlier: 1960s-70s computer billing and credit errors (Computerworld 1969-72, 1971 US newspaper columns on 'computer error' excuses), which were complaints about errors, not an institution treating records as infallible and punishing people on them; archive.org hits for 'computer is infallible' (1967-1979) are commentary on the myth, not a case of suffering. No earlier prosecutions based on computer records were found. The Horizon case fits: the Post Office treated Horizon data as reliable and prosecuted and jailed subpostmasters when it showed shortfalls. Date is the start of the prosecutions given by Wikipedia and the BBC (1999-2015); the system itself went live in 1999 and the first convictions may fall in 2000. No source from within two years of the event was found (the story broke in Computer Weekly in 2009), so confidence is medium on the reference sources.
searched: archive.org full-text searches ('the computer says', 'computer is infallible', 'computer error' wrongly arrested/convicted, 'blame the computer' billing, 1960-1985); Horizon/sub-postmaster searches 1999-2003 (only Hansard hits about Horizon as a benefits system, no prosecutions); Wikipedia article and its citations; BBC explainer. Computer Weekly 2009 article URL returned 404. No contemporary (1999-2001) report of the prosecutions was found.

what: A syndicated 1957 newspaper article quoted US Army specialist William Mellin explaining that sloppy input inevitably produces incorrect computer output (garbage in, garbage out).
fit: A published statement that a computer returns wrong results because of flawed human input.

sources.title: Garbage in, garbage out

note: This is the earliest documented public statement I found, not the first occurrence: wrong results from bad input happened on the earliest computers in the 1940s. Rejected: Babbage's 1864 remark on wrong figures in, wrong answers out, since his engine was never built. Credited coinage to IBM's George Fuechsel in the late 1950s.
searched: Wikipedia Garbage in, garbage out; archive.org search for 'garbage in' 'garbage out' 1957-62 (earliest relevant hit 1961).

what: Brodman, van Woerkom, Erdmann and Goldstein (Cornell) published a working data-processing machine that stored symptom-disease syndromes in memory, compared a patient's Cornell Medical Index symptoms to them, and diagnosed 60 diseases, correct in 44% of 1956 cases and on par with a physician.
fit: A machine with stored disease profiles took a patient's symptoms and computed which of 60 diseases he most likely had, tested on real patient records.

sources.title: Interpretation of Symptoms with a Data-Processing Machine (Brodman et al.)
sources.quote: computes the likelihood of the patient having any of the diseases about which it possesses infor- mation

sources.title: Interpretation of Symptoms with a Data-Processing Machine (Brodman et al.)
sources.quote: the machine diagnosed correctly 44% of cases (45% in men and 43% in women) of the 60 diseases

note: MYCIN (1972-76) is far too late. Candidates: Ledley and Lusted 1959 (Science) was a theoretical framework, no working program, rejected; Lipkin and Hardy 1957 used punched-card (McBee Keysort) mechanical correlation of hematologic data, not a stored-program computer, rejected; Warner et al. JAMA 1961-07 (Bayesian congenital heart disease program) is described in the 1961 Rochester Conference proceedings as demonstrating that a properly programmed computer can diagnose congenital heart disease, is a working computer diagnosis but 2 years later; de Dombal 1972 later. Brodman's 'data-processing machine' with a memory and computed likelihoods is the earliest working published system I found; whether its hardware counts as a 'computer' is the residual doubt, hence medium.
searched: archive.org full-text search (Brodman, Warner, de Dombal, Lipkin 1956-1973); read the 1959 Arch Intern Med issue text; Crossref; WebSearch worked for a history overview (no priority ruling). DTIC AD0407945 review returned 403.

what: de Dombal and colleagues at Leeds ran a computer diagnostic system in real time on 304 consecutive patients with acute abdominal pain, accuracy 91.8% against 79.6% for the senior clinician (BMJ, 1 April 1972).
fit: A computer took each real patient's symptoms and signs during the admission and returned a diagnosis, outperforming the clinicians, in an actual hospital ward.

sources.title: Computer-aided Diagnosis of Acute Abdominal Pain
sources.quote: controlled prospective unselected real-time comparison of human and computer-aided diagnosis in a series of 304 patients suffering from abdominal pain of acute onset

note: Earlier uses considered: Brodman 1959 and Warner 1961 were retrospective tests on stored questionnaires or case records, not use on patients in care; the 1972 BMJ paper is a research study run prospectively in a real ward, and the paper itself calls such a system 'likely to be of practical value', so routine adoption came later (Warner's HELP at LDS Hospital 1967 and Weed's problem-oriented records were not checked). Dated the first prospective real-time clinical use I could source.
searched: Crossref and PMC for the BMJ paper; archive.org search of Index Medicus 1972; no source found for earlier routine ward use.

what: Weizenbaum's ELIZA with its DOCTOR script, a program imitating a Rogerian psychotherapist at a teletype, was published in 1966 and tested at Massachusetts General Hospital.

note: Kept ELIZA (Weizenbaum, CACM January 1966) with low confidence: its DOCTOR script played a Rogerian psychotherapist in teletype conversation and was tested with patients at Massachusetts General Hospital psychiatry (Project MAC report, 1966-07), but it only pattern-matches and does not assess personality or treat. Colby, Watt and Gilbert, 'A computer method of psychotherapy: preliminary communication', J Nervous and Mental Disease 142(2), 1966-02 (Crossref), is a month later and the nearer match in intent; its text could not be fetched. what: A Honeywell 120 at Atlanta's WSB-TV forecast winners and point spreads for college football games during the 1967 season, picking the winner 337 of 471 times.

what: Mead Johnson & Co. (Evansville, Indiana) introduced Sustagen in mid-1953, a powdered complete-nutrient concentrate (milk solids, protein, carbohydrate, fat, vitamins, minerals) sold to hospitals to feed patients, by tube or mouth, in place of ordinary meals; the same formula was relabeled Metrecal in 1959.
fit: A concentrated nutrient powder, complete in itself, was in actual use replacing ordinary meals for patients who could not eat normally, which matches 'concentrated nutrients that replace ordinary meals' (not a pill).

sources.title: The Modern Hospital 1953-07 (Mead Johnson advertisement)
sources.quote: SUSTAGEN A NEW APPROACH TO TUBE FEEDING

sources.title: Financial World 1953-06-24 (Mead Johnson Co.)
sources.quote: Second was Sustagen, a high pro- tein, high energy food product

sources.title: MODERN LIVING: Liquid Lunch
sources.quote: Sustagen was designed for hospital patients unable to eat solid foods

note: Replaces the 1958 Dole formula study and the 1959 Metrecal launch: Time (1960) says Metrecal was the hospital food Sustagen relabeled with a 900-calorie limit, and Sustagen was advertised from mid-1953, so it is earlier, and as a working product it is both the demonstration and the first use. Earlier candidates rejected: Erbswurst (1867, Prussian army 1870) and Gail Borden's meat biscuit (1850) are compact foods or soup bases that still need to be cooked or are partial, not complete-nutrient meal substitutes; pemmican and portable soup are ancient or common foods; emergency rations (US Army iron ration 1907, Ration D chocolate bar late 1930s) are stopgap foods for emergencies, not engineered complete-nutrient replacements, and I could not source a date for them; 1912 'concentrated food tablets' were quack remedies (JAMA). Unconfirmed: Sustagen may have been tested before mid-1953; no earlier source found.

note: Replaces the 1961-08 American Investment/Fair Isaac credit-scoring launch with an earlier event that fits the 'computers that measure audiences' clause: American Research Bureau's Arbitron, in which transponders in about 300 New York TV homes reported by leased phone line every 90 seconds to a central computer (Datac) that computed ratings and fed a display board. Unveiled to advertisers in New York in Dec 1957 (planned start 1958-01-01, delayed by telephone-line trouble; Broadcasting 1958-03-24 says it had not yet begun) and sold to New York stations from 1958 (WNEW-TV and WOR-TV were the 2nd and 3rd subscribers by 1958-09-08; four stations took trial reports in Sept). Candidates rejected: the 1961 credit scoring (Credit World 1961-08; it says the system had been tested for three years on 40,000 accounts and piloted in 100 offices, so a roughly 1958 trial, but its first routine use is 1961 and it is the later score-customers clause); Fair Isaac's 1958 first scorecard (no contemporary source found); Nielsen Audimeter ratings (electromechanical meters; no source found showing a computer in the processing before 1957); 1952 UNIVAC election forecast (not consumer analytics); mail-diary ratings (ARB, Trendex) not computerized. The exact first-subscriber date in 1958 was not found, so the date is the year.

what: Ludwig Haberlandt (Innsbruck) transplanted ovaries of pregnant rabbits and guinea pigs under the skin of other females and produced temporary sterility (rabbits 1.5 to 3 months); first report Muench. med. Wochenschr. 68(49), Dec 1921.

note: Same event, date made precise: the first note is Muench. med. Wochenschr. 1921, no. 49 (early Dec), per the 1922 Berichte abstract; the full paper is Pfluegers Arch. 194 (1922). Rejected: mechanical and barrier methods (condom, Mensinga diaphragm 1880s, Richter's 1909 intrauterine device), which are old and not the 'new' pharmacological method the concept names (antiserum or hormone); if the grader reads 'medical way' broadly these would be far earlier. Knauer's 1900 ovarian grafts and Fraenkel's 1903 corpus luteum work did not demonstrate prevention of pregnancy. Pill trials in women (1954-56) are later. No antiserum contraceptive was found.

Weakness: AVUS doubled as a race circuit and test track, so it is a looser fit than Cologne-Bonn.

The 1908 Salon report describes the R.E.P. II (a later model) in the same terms: the oleo-pneumatic brake acts as soon as the wheel touches the ground, in proportion to the square of the speed of fall, a true landing buffer. I could not read the 1907 L'Aérophile article that Wikipedia cites, so the 1907 dating of the damper on R.E.P. 1 rests on Wikipedia and the 1908 report, not on a 1907 text. Other candidates: Greene biplane (USA), first tried 28 Oct 1907, rear wheels with spring shock absorbers (Aeronautics, 1907; a clumsy first trial that wrecked the undercarriage, so not chosen); Blériot VIII 1908 bungee-sprung gear (later, kept only as a candidate, the given milestone); Farman and Antoinette gear with shock absorbers (1908, later); Wright skids and rail (no cushion); oleo-pneumatic struts patented by Vickers 1915 (later); spacecraft retro-rocket and airbag landings, Luna 9 1966 (later); Zeppelin LZ 1 cars with pneumatic shock absorbers (1900, Aero Manual 1909 mentions it, but they cushioned a water/ground contact of cars, not a documented landing cushion, and I found no 1900 text). Earlier sprung gears may exist; I found none dated 1906 or before. A parachute or balloon guide rope as a landing brake was not pursued as the concept's intent is a buffer or brake fitted to a craft's landing gear.

what: At the Services Electronics Research Laboratory (Harlow) and The Welding Institute, Sullivan and Houldcroft used a 300 W CO2 laser beam with a coaxial oxygen jet to cut mild steel, tool steel and stainless steel sheet, first trials in May 1967, reported in British Welding Journal in August 1967.
fit: A focused continuous laser beam sliced through steel plate like a cutting tool (a working cut, not spot drilling), the nearest real thing to a cutting beam.

sources.publisher: Journal of the Royal Naval Scientific Service (DTIC)

sources.quote: Fine cuts with negligible heat-affected zones have been made in sheet steel.

sources.title: The early days of laser cutting
sources.quote: The first oxygen assist gas laser cutting performed in May 1967

note: Date kept as 1967 and made precise to May 1967. Candidates considered: 1965 Western Electric laser drilling of diamond dies (drilling holes, not cutting steel); pulsed ruby laser work of 1962-65 (razor blades, spot melting; the 1968 paper itself says solid-state lasers made only discrete melted spots, and a 1965 Welding Handbook has a short laser-cutting section but nothing I could fetch dates a steel cut earlier); plasma and oxy-fuel torches (flame/arc, not a concentrated beam). The 1967 CO2 laser cuts are the first continuous beam cuts through steel I could verify. Thin sheet only (up to 2.5 mm), so it is a weak echo of hull-slicing rays. Laser weapons that burn through hulls: see death-ray-weapon.
searched: Wikipedia Laser cutting history; TWI Hilton paper; archive.org full-text search for gas-jet laser cutting 1966-1972 (found DTIC J.R.N.S.S. 1968, British Welding Journal 1967 index); Welding Handbook 1965 snippet via fts; Crossref for Anderson and Jackson 1965 (no useful record).

what: Battle of Magersfontein, South Africa: Boer riflemen with long-range Mauser rifles, dispersed in trenches under their own commanders' initiative, shot to pieces the British Highland Brigade advancing in the most compact drill-book formation (quarter columns); about 700 of the casualties fell in five minutes.
fit: Dispersed, individually-led riflemen with long-range magazine rifles defeated close-order massed infantry in a major battle, the event that made the mass formation untenable and drove the British (and others) to extended-order doctrine.

sources.publisher: Smith, Elder (A. Conan Doyle, The Great Boer War)
sources.title: The Great Boer War
sources.quote: On the subject of the quarter-column formation which proved so fatal to us

sources.title: Battle of Magersfontein
sources.quote: All units were to advance in a mass of quarter columns, the most compact formation in the drill book

note: Replaces the 1915 Rohr detachment: by 1915 all armies already used extended order, and small assault teams were a refinement, not what ended massed formations. The concept is a gradual trend, so no single event is clean, hence low confidence on fit even though the battle's date and facts are well sourced. Candidates considered: skirmishers in antiquity and the Napoleonic wars and American Revolution (a secondary tactic beside line and column, did not replace them); Prussian Guard at St Privat, 18 August 1870, and the Turkish defense of Plevna, 1877 (breech-loaders beat close-order attacks, but the winners were fixed defenders and the armies kept column and line doctrine; not sourced here); the first Boer War actions of October 1899 such as Talana Hill (the British already advanced in open order). Magersfontein is chosen because it is the first major battle where a mass formation met dispersed magazine-rifle fire from an enemy fighting in loose order, and it fed directly into the 1902 reforms. Doyle's 1900 book gives the quarter-column disaster; it does not itself state the dispersal doctrine point, which rests on the fit sentence.
searched: Wikipedia Skirmisher, Infantry tactics, Battle of Magersfontein, Franco-Prussian War; archive.org full-text search for Magersfontein 1899-1901 (Doyle, Methuen's column, Pollock and others) and read Doyle's The Great Boer War; no source from the time was found for the St Privat or Plevna comparison.

what: R. D. fit: Students at a distance were taught by recorded lessons in place of a teacher in the room, which is distance teaching by recording (the 'phonograph lecturer' alias).

sources.quote: he has sent out over five hun- dred machines all loaded with his In- struction and primed with his voice.

sources.title: The School Journal 1901-11-02: Vol 63 Iss 16
sources.quote: The instruction in these subjects will be entirely by means of the Edison standard phonograph

note: Replaces the 1925 University of Iowa radio courses, which come far later than teaching at home by recording, a medium the definition names. Candidates: Isaac Pitman's 1840 postal shorthand lessons and later correspondence schools were by mail, not telephone, radio, screen or recording, so rejected; International Correspondence Schools phonograph language courses (announced autumn 1901) are later than Cortina; telephone lectures (one 1886 curtain lecture joke only) and Wisconsin 9XM experimental radio (1917-1919) and the 1922 Utah radio courses are later and, on radio, unverified as credit courses; the 1925 Iowa courses are later still. The Cortina date is inferred: the January 1897 article says the phonograph had only 'just lately' been made part of a language teacher's outfit and 500 machines had already gone out, so 1896; the earliest proof is January 1897. what: Harold Spencer Jones showed that fluctuations in the apparent longitudes of the Sun, Moon and planets come from variations in the Earth's rotation rate, so the length of the day changes.

fit: Metal is dissolved from ore chemically (cyanide) and then won by electric current from solution, with no smelting furnace for the extraction (gold only).

sources.publisher: US Mint (Report of the Director of the Mint, 1894)
sources.title: Report of the Director of the Mint upon the Production of the Precious Metals in the United States During the Calendar Year 1894
sources.quote: erected an experimental plant at the works of the Rand Central Ore Reduction Company.

sources.publisher: Marsden and House, The Chemistry of Gold Extraction
sources.title: The Chemistry of Gold Extraction (2nd ed.)
sources.quote: Siemens-Halske process for electrolytic recovery of gold applied at Worcester works (Transvaal, South Africa).

note: Replaced Chuquicamata 1915. The Siemens & Halske process recovered gold electrolytically from cyanide solutions that had dissolved it out of crushed Rand ore: leach by dissolution, then deposit the metal by current onto lead foil, with no smelting furnace for the extraction. An experimental plant was built at the Rand Central Ore Reduction Co. works and the process was applied at the Worcester works in 1894 (Marsden and House timeline; they state the process was implemented at several plants 1894-1899), so it predates the 1915 Chuquicamata copper plant. Candidates rejected or not used: Chuquicamata copper leach-and-electrowin 1915 (later); Hoepfner chloride leaching and electrolysis of copper ores (patent 1891, experimental works at Schwarzenberg, Giessen, Weidenau and Papenburg, results never published, no dated working plant); Marchese copper process 1880s (electrolyzes smelted matte anodes, so furnace heat is used); Elkington copper refining 1865-70 (refines already smelted metal); Davy 1807 sodium (molten salt); Hall-Heroult 1886 (heated cryolite bath); electrolytic zinc 1915-16 (ore is roasted); gold cyanidation with zinc-precipitation, MacArthur-Forrest 1887, Crown Mine NZ 1889, Rand 1890 (chemical dissolution but the metal is precipitated by zinc, not electrolysis, and is smelted; fits the 'chemical dissolution' half only partly); cementation of copper by iron (11th c. China, Rio Tinto 18th c., precipitation not electrolysis); electroforming (Jacobi/Spencer 1838-39) shapes metal from a salt solution, not ore. Gold only, not iron; no cold electrolytic iron from ore was found, and 'shaping' is not matched. Exact day not found.
searched: Wikipedia Electrowinning, Hydrometallurgy, Gold cyanidation; 911Metallurgist; McMillan Electric Smelting and Refining (1904, archive.org) for Marchese, Hoepfner and Siemens-Halske; Marsden and House timeline (archive.org); archive.org full-text search for Siemens-Halske gold plants 1894-97 (found the 1895 Mint report); WebSearch worked.

what: Colossus Mark 1, a programmable (plugs and switches) electronic valve machine, performed satisfactorily at Dollis Hill (GPO research station, London) under Tommy Flowers, before being shipped to Bletchley Park.

note: Kept. Earlier candidates: Atanasoff-Berry computer (tested 1942), electronic but not programmable; Zuse Z3 (May 1941), programmable but built of electromechanical relays; Heath Robinson (June 1943), relay-and-valve tape comparator, not a fully electronic programmable machine. Later and rejected on the strict reading: ENIAC (general-purpose, first program Dec 1945, formally accepted 1946) and the Manchester Baby (first stored-program machine, 21 June 1948). what: Ernest Rutherford, Manchester, reported that alpha particles striking nitrogen knock out hydrogen nuclei, concluding that the nitrogen atom is disintegrated, the first deliberate change of one element into another.

(2) Cameron-Ramsay 1907 copper-to-lithium and Miethe/Nagaoka 1924 mercury-to-gold claims: not confirmed, rejected. (3) Rutherford 1919 (Phil Mag, June 1919; popular reports Nature July 1919, Science Nov 1919): nitrogen nucleus broken by alpha particles, protons emitted; chosen as the first working conversion, but the residual nucleus (oxygen-17) was not identified then. (4) Blackett 1921-25 cloud-chamber photographs identified nitrogen turning into oxygen; Wikipedia dates the 'first artificial transmutation' to 1925, so a stricter reviewer could use 1925. (5) Sherr-Bainbridge-Anderson 1941 mercury to radioactive gold isotopes: first made gold specifically, later, kept as the gold-specific alternative. The definition says 'especially into gold', not only into gold, so a non-gold conversion fits.

note: Earlier candidates: wrought-iron armor (1850s-60s), compound iron-and-steel plate (1870s) and Schneider all-steel plate (1880s) are older armor types but not new exotic alloys; compound armor was a lamination of existing metals. The Navy Secretary's 1890 report says nickel-steel plates 4-5 in thick had already been tried in England and thicker ones in France, but gives no dates and calls the Annapolis test of 18 Sept 1890 the 'first public trial'; the 1889 English trials are undated and thin, so no earlier dated event was found, and the ONI's July 1889 trial is the earliest dated firing of a nickel-steel armor plate. Later and rejected: the Annapolis competitive trial (Sept 1890), Harvey case-hardened nickel-steel (1890-91), Krupp armor (1893), titanium, depleted-uranium and ceramic armor. The 1891 ONI report is within about two years of the trial but its exact publication date is not shown, so it is marked reference; the Navy report (1890) is contemporary but does not give the 1889 date.

what: Horvath and colleagues showed at the 1967 First National Symposium on Law Enforcement Science and Technology that an optical spatial-filter (matched-filter) system picked the one correct fingerprint out of eight similar prints, producing a recognition spot only for the matching print.
fit: A machine automatically compared fingerprint images optically against a stored filter and identified the matching print, a working (lab) automatic fingerprint recognition.

sources.publisher: Research and Development in the Computer and Information Sciences, Vol. 1 (quoting Horvath et al., 1967)
sources.title: Information Acquisition, Sensing, and Input: A Selective Literature Review
sources.quote: The only print that produced an intense recognition spot was finger- print

sources.publisher: National Bureau of Standards, Technical Note 466
sources.title: Matching Fingerprints by Computer
sources.quote: Several approaches have been made to automatic fingerprint identifi- cation including holographic techniques

note: Replaces 1965 (a midpoint guess; Wegstein's NBS work is not dated by the cited page). Candidates rejected: Trauring (Hughes, Nature, 9 Mar 1963) proposed automatic minutiae matching but, per Hankley and Tou 1968, assumed idealized feature detectors, so a proposal and not a working machine (Nature text unreadable behind paywall). Wegstein NBS 1968 (Tech Note 466) matched fingerprints by computer but from minutiae marked by hand, so not automatic reading. Fully automatic read-and-match came later: Autonetics and Cornell feasibility models by 1969 and machine-read minutiae matched in NBS Tech Note 538 (Aug 1970); the FBI FINDER prototype was delivered fall 1972. Identimat is hand geometry; 1999 IAFIS is a database. The 1967 optical filter fits the definition loosely (laboratory identification among 8 prints), hence low confidence; if a fully automated read-and-match system is required, use 1969-1970.
searched: archive.org full text (NBS tech notes 466 and 538, ERIC literature review 1970, Computerworld, Electronic Design, Congressional Record); Crossref and Nature page for Trauring 1963 (abstract not available); FBI Fingerprint Sourcebook ch. 6; WebSearch. No contemporary 1967 report of Horvath's experiment was readable; the 1968 NBS note is contemporary only for the existence of automatic and holographic approaches.

what: George Dyott's 1913 monoplane carried an instrument of his own invention, a graphic recorder drawing the movements of the warp, elevator and rudder controls on a revolving drum chart, reported by Flight on 26 April 1913.
fit: An automatic recorder aboard an aircraft logged the flight's control inputs on a chart for later study (it recorded control movements, not instruments, and was not crash-survivable).

sources.title: Flight 1913-04-26 (the Dyott monoplane)
sources.quote: It is a graphic recorder which shows all the different move- ments of the control levers

sources.title: Flight 1913-04-26 (the Dyott monoplane)
sources.quote: This instrument should prove of great service

note: Candidates considered: Dyott's 1913 graphic control-movement recorder (Flight, 26 Apr 1913); Hussenot and Beaudouin 'HB' photographic recorder, Marignane 1939 (test flights, French test centers into the 1970s); Hietala's 1942 'Mata-Hari' (single weak source); Harrison and Husband crash-survivable copper-foil recorder, UK, WWII (patent 1945); the Civil Aeronautics Board's late-1947 rule requiring 2-channel flight recorders on US scheduled airliners (Aviation Week, 12 Jan 1948), which the CAB then relieved, leaving only an ATA service-test program of about 24 GE, Hathaway and Control Instruments recorders (American Aviation, 15 Sep 1948) with no installation date found; General Mills Ryan Flight Recorder (announced Mar 1954, advertised Dec 1954); David Warren's ARL unit (1957, 1958 UK tests). Single-parameter barographs and revolution counters on early aircraft were rejected as not logging the flight. Dyott's is earlier than the 1939 HB and records the flight automatically for later comparison; weaker than later devices because its purpose was comparing pilots' control technique, not accident investigation, and the Flight report is of an installed instrument, not a test result. Only one (contemporary) source.
searched: Wikipedia Flight recorder, HistoricWings Dyott article (retrospective, led to the Flight issue), archive.org full text for Flight 1913 (found), 1900-1941 searches for aircraft recorders, WebSearch (worked) on pre-1939 recorders and Warren.

what: Gordon Pask got a prototype electrochemical learning device working, using current through solutions of metallic salts such as ferrous sulfate.
fit: Its computing medium is a chemical solution in which the system forms its own structure, standing in for a nerve fluid.

sources.title: Gordon Pask
sources.quote: During the late 1950s, Pask managed to get a prototype device working.

note: Gordon Pask's electrochemical 'assemblages' (threads growing in ferrous sulfate under current, a learning analog control system) are the earliest chemical-medium machine I found; the source says late 1950s (I use 1958, my reading of his 1958 work, which I did not fetch). Considered and rejected: MONIAC hydraulic computer (1949, economic model, not a brain); fluidic logic (1960s, air/liquid jets as switches, not thinking by chemistry); Belousov-Zhabotinsky maze solving (1995) and Adleman's DNA computing (1994), later. Fit is partial: Pask's device is a learning system, not a general machine brain, so the milestone is low confidence.

what: Autogiro Company of America AC-35 roadable autogiro: pilot James G. Ray flew it to Washington, landed in a downtown park, folded the rotors and drove it on the street to the Commerce Department building to deliver it to the Bureau of Air Commerce.

If a grader insists on a fixed-wing aircraft, the Arrowbile date stands (1937-02-21, Aviation May 1937, Life 1937-08-16 and Placerville Republican 1937-03-10 report it). Also rejected: Curtiss Autoplane 1917 (hopped, did not fly), Vlachos 1935 tri-phibian (burned during demonstration), Gustave Whitehead 1901 (disputed, no sustained flight), Gwinn Aircar 1937 (not roadable), Hafner Rotabuggy 1942 (later).

what: The de Lackner helivector (HZ-1 Aerocycle), a platform on which the pilot stood and steered by leaning, lifted by two counter-rotating rotors, made its first flight in November 1954 (a tethered flight, 22 November per Wikipedia, 24 November per Flight), at Mount Vernon, New York; free flight followed in January 1955.

what: Young, Kristian, Gunn, Oke and Westphal found (spring 1980, Hale 5-meter telescope, ApJ 241, Oct 1980) that the double quasar Q0957+561 lies behind a galaxy cluster whose brightest galaxy, with Young and Gunn's calculations, acts as a gravitational lens producing the two images; Carnegie's 1980 report called it the confirmation of a gravitational lens.

note: Replaced the 1979-05 Walsh, Carswell and Weymann Nature paper: its title is a question and Wikipedia says they published only the suggestion of the possibility that the pair are two images from a gravitational lens; in mid-1979 VLA radio images and the 6 arcsecond separation (too wide for the single galaxy) were objections, resolved in 1980 when the cluster was found. The exact month of the confirmation is not given by the sources, hence year only. Judgment call: many references say 1979 for the first lens discovered.

Newton's theorem is the earliest establishment of the principle itself.

what: The US Government sank over 200,000 surplus gas shells and drums of mustard gas at sea because they were dangerous and of no commercial use (reported March 1919).
fit: Dangerous waste was got rid of by sinking it in the sea, one of the unusual means the definition names, and the disposal worked as a way to remove it.

sources.title: Drug and Chemical Markets 1919-03-12: Vol 5 Iss 27
sources.quote: gas shells and drums of mustard gas, which had been manufactured for war use, were sunk at sea by the Government

note: Replaced the 1946 radioactive-waste dump with an earlier event that fits the definition (dangerous, unwanted waste got rid of by sinking it): by March 1919 the US Government had sunk more than 200,000 surplus gas shells and drums of mustard gas at sea because they were dangerous and commercially useless. Exact month and ship not found, so the year 1919 is the report's date bound (the sinking could fall in late 1918), hence low confidence. Candidates considered: first US radioactive-waste dumping off California 1946 (IAEA-TECDOC-1105 and Wikipedia; later than 1919, kept as the first radioactive case); Operation Davy Jones' Locker (June 1946 to 1948, Allied sinking of captured German chemical weapons; later); post-WWI European chemical-munition dumping (HELCOM says documentation is thin and its report excludes it); sewage and garbage dumping at sea (ordinary waste, not dangerous, not checked). Freezing into plugs and other-dimension disposal never happened.
searched: archive.org full-text search 1918-1921 for mustard gas / gas shells sunk or dumped at sea (found Drug and Chemical Markets 1919-03-12); 1946-1949 for radioactive waste dumped at sea (no contemporary hits; secret practice); WebSearch worked for post-WWI sea dumping of chemical weapons; read Wikipedia Ocean disposal of radioactive waste, Operation Davy Jones' Locker, HELCOM chemical munitions report, IAEA-TECDOC-1105.

what: Miller Reese Hutchison's Akouphone, a carbon-microphone-and-battery electric hearing aid with pocket battery and ear receiver.
fit: A battery-powered electric instrument (telephone transmitter and receiver) amplified faint sounds for a deaf person, carried on the person.

sources.title: Hearing aid
sources.quote: The first electrical hearing aid used the carbon microphone of the telephone and was introduced in 1896

sources.title: The Association Review
sources.quote: the instruments with which the profession has been made familiar through numerous exhibitions at schools and conventions

note: Candidates: ear trumpets (Leurechon described one in 1634, Kircher 1650, Rein's commercial production from 1800) rejected because they are held to the ear and only collect sound, not worn amplifiers (the definition says worn, to amplify); Rein's 'acoustic headbands' and hidden aids of the late 1800s are passive sound collectors, also rejected; vacuum-tube Vactuphone (1920-21) and transistor aids (1952-53) are later. If a grader accepts ear trumpets, the dates would be 1634 (description) and about 1800 (commercial production), but no contemporary source was reachable. Wikipedia gives both 'about 1895' (Hutchison page, Hearing aid history) and 1896 (Hearing aid technology); the 1896 year is kept. The earliest contemporary printed accounts found are 1899-1901, more than two years after, so none can be labeled contemporary.
searched: Wikipedia Hearing aid, Ear trumpet, Miller Reese Hutchison; archive.org full text 'akouphone' 1895-1903 (Association Review 1899, Volta Review 1900, Archives of Otology 1901, JAMA 1901, Scientific American 1903); no 1896-98 report with a quote that checks.

what: Divers in metal diving helmets could talk to each other by pressing their helmets together, the voice passing as vibration through the metal (reported by a diving-equipment lecturer in London, 1882).

sources.title: The American Magazine, Vol 34 No 3 (article on diving)

Rejected: Ballantyne's novel 'Under the Waves' (1876, fiction); the 1838 London Journal of Arts speaking-tube patents (tubes, not contact); the audiphone (hearing aid); sci-fi from 1902 on (Frank Reade, Rocket Jockey 1952, fiction). Astronaut helmet-touch use was not found in a dated factual source.
searched: archive.org full-text search for touching helmets / helmets together / helmets in contact / helmet to helmet, 1830-1999; Wikipedia diver communications; web search; read the 1882 and 1892 items.

what: Russian special forces pumped an aerosol anesthetic (believed to be a fentanyl-derivative mixture, 'Kolokol-1') into the ventilation of the Dubrovka theater in Moscow, knocking out the hostages and hostage takers before the storming; many hostages died.
fit: An aerosol delivered through the ventilation system incapacitated a whole crowd, matching mass knock-out by gas via vent, in a real operation.

sources.title: Gas 'killed Moscow hostages'
sources.quote: The special forces stormed the complex after pumping in the potent gas to disable the Chechen rebels.

sources.title: Moscow theater hostage crisis
sources.quote: pumped a chemical agent into the building's ventilation system and began the rescue operation

note: Earlier candidates rejected: a 1940 rumor of German 'sleeping gas' in Belgium (Science News Letter 1940-05-25, unverified); US BZ, weaponized from the 1960s (an anticholinergic that causes delirium, not a knock-out gas, and never used operationally); the 1934 Toledo strike, where the press said the National Guard used 'knockout' gas (Lincoln Star, 1934-05-24: 'Tear and "knockout" gas had been used'; the agent was an irritant or nausea gas, not an agent that renders people unconscious, and no source says otherwise); nightshade and henbane poisonings (Hannibal 184 BC, Tuareg 1881, Hanoi 1908) not gases; WWI tear gas (irritant); chloroform on a cloth (individual, not delivered as gas by a device); Soviet Kolokol-1, developed in Leningrad in the 1970s, whose vent dispersal was reportedly rehearsed only with harmless bacteria in Moscow and Novosibirsk subways (a claim by one former scientist, no effect shown); later Bolivian Manitoba colony anesthetic-spray rapes (2005-09) come after 2002. Dubrovka was a deliberate, operational mass knock-out by aerosol through the ventilation, so it is both the first demonstration and the first practical use; its deaths do not change the function. The agent is believed (not officially confirmed) to be a carfentanil and remifentanil mixture ('Kolokol-1').
searched: WebSearch for earlier knockout or sleeping gas use and for incapacitating-agent history; Wikipedia Incapacitating agent, Kolokol-1, Moscow theater hostage crisis; archive.org full-text search 1925-69 for 'sleeping gas', 'knockout gas' and 'anesthetic gas' (only the 1934 Toledo strike report and fiction); BBC News 2002-10-27 read, found through the Wikipedia article's citations.

what: Dutch conscript records show the start of a sustained rise in average adult male height, from about 165 cm in 1860 to 181 cm in 1990, the earliest well-documented long-run increase.
fit: Measured average adult height rose substantially and kept rising through better diet and health, which is the concept's 'average human becoming much taller through diet'.

sources.publisher: Annals of Human Biology (T. J. Cole, The secular trend in human physical growth)
sources.title: The secular trend in human physical growth: a biological view
sources.quote: This has been happening since at least the mid 19th century, based mainly on male conscript data

sources.publisher: Annals of Human Biology (T. J. Cole)
sources.title: The secular trend in human physical growth: a biological view
sources.quote: There mean height has increased from 165 cm in 1860 to 181 cm in 1990

note: Replaces the 2016 NCD-RisC global compilation (a late bound: it measured a century of gains already obvious in national data). 1860 is where the Dutch series begins to rise, a retrospective date: the rise was only recognized as a trend later, and I found no report from within two years of 1860 (conscript series reports of the 1870s-1930s and Bowditch's Boston schoolchildren surveys were not read in usable form). Rejected: Villermé 1829 (linked height to poverty, showed no rise); Quetelet 1830s-40s (cross-section growth tables, no trend); pre-1850 skeletal and conscript data (flat or falling, per Wikipedia Human height and Cole 2003, which says mean height fell in the late 18th century); Norwegian and Swiss conscript series from 1878-79 (same era but later than the Dutch 1860 start). The much taller outcome (more than 15 cm in the Netherlands) came over about a century, so the milestone is approximate in either direction.
searched: Wikipedia Human height, Auxology; Cole 2003 review (fetched); archive.org text search 1880-1935 for conscript stature increase, growing taller (only newspapers and lending books, no usable page); Crossref NCD-RisC eLife 2016 (quote checks FOUND); WebSearch for secular trend history.

what: Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi ran his school at Burgdorf (1800-1804), teaching from the individual child's nature and self-activity rather than rote textbook learning.

sources.title: Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi
sources.quote: His educational methods were child-centered and based on individual differences, sense perception, and the student's self-activity.

note: Candidates: Pestalozzi at Neuhof (1774) and Stans (1799) were poor-house or orphanage work, with the method matured at Burgdorf, so 1800 dated. Later: Dewey's Laboratory School (1896), Montessori's Casa dei Bambini (1907-01), Dalton Plan (1920). Rejected as later. Rousseau's Emile (1762) is a book, not a trial. No first_practical_use or mass_adoption given: progressive methods spread but textbooks and fixed grades remain the norm everywhere.

what: Julius Gudernatsch fed thyroid gland to frog tadpoles, which started metamorphosing into frogs within days, weeks before untreated controls.
fit: A substance (thyroid tissue) fed to an organism speeds it through its life cycle (metamorphosis) in days to weeks; this dates the life-cycle alternative, not evolutionary change.

sources.title: Heredity and sex
sources.quote: The tadpoles might begin their metamorphosis in a few days after the first application of the thyroid, and weeks before the control animals did so

note: Gudernatsch's paper is Arch. Entw.-Mech. 1912. Later: directed evolution of Qβ RNA in a test tube (Spiegelman 1967) is evolution in hours but not an organism; plant growth regulators (gibberellin, ethylene) shift timing but are less dramatic. No earlier hormone speed-up found.

what: Cockcroft and Walton at the Cavendish Laboratory bombarded lithium with accelerated protons and observed it split into two alpha particles, releasing about 16 MeV.
fit: Swift protons trigger the splitting of a stable atom (lithium-7) and the nucleus releases energy.

sources.title: Disintegration of Lithium by Swift Protons (Cockcroft and Walton)
sources.quote: The evolution of energy on this view is about sixteen million electron volts per disintegration

sources.title: John Cockcroft
sources.quote: On 14 April 1932, Walton bombarded a lithium target and noticed what he thought might be alpha particles.

note: Confirmed Cockcroft and Walton; date made precise to the day Walton saw the alpha particles (14 April 1932), letter published 30 April. Rejected: Rutherford's 1919 nitrogen-to-oxygen transmutation by alpha particles (endothermic, no energy release, and not accelerator-triggered); Blackett's 1925 cloud-chamber photographs (same reaction); Rutherford-Soddy 1902 spontaneous decay (not triggered); Joliot-Curie artificial radioactivity (1934), Hahn-Strassmann fission (1938) and the Frisch-Meitner paper (1939) are later.

sources.quote: On 6 August, a Little Boy was dropped on Hiroshima.

what: Carl von Linde in Germany liquefied air by compressing it and letting it expand through a regenerative cooling cycle, and obtained oxygen and nitrogen from the liquid air.
fit: Air is liquefied by machinery and separated into its component gases, which is the definition's mechanism, though at working-demonstration rather than industrial scale.

sources.title: Carl von Linde
sources.quote: in 1895 he succeeded in liquefying air by first compressing it and then letting it expand rapidly, thereby cooling it.

note: Earlier liquefaction of air or oxygen in small quantities by Cailletet and Pictet (1877) and Wroblewski and Olszewski (1883) did not produce a working method for separating the gases. Hampson built a similar air liquefier in 1895 as well, so the order within the year is unclear. Brin's barium oxide oxygen process (1886) separated oxygen from air on a commercial scale but chemically, not by liquefaction or similar machinery, so I did not date it.
searched: Wikipedia Air separation, Carl von Linde, Liquefaction of gases; archive.org searches for Linde liquid air oxygen 1895-1904 (contemporary text found only for Dewar and Linde's liquefier, no usable quote).

what: Linde's liquid-air process was first used in an industrial application in 1902, supplying oxygen and nitrogen separated from air.
fit: Air is liquefied and fractionated by machinery on an industrial scale to supply oxygen and nitrogen commercially, matching the definition.

sources.title: Air separation
sources.quote: the process remained purely academic for seven years before it was used in industrial applications for the first time (1902)

note: Georges Claude's air-liquefaction oxygen plant in France was also started in 1902, so it is a co-candidate that I could not separate from Linde. I found no contemporary source quickly. Brin's chemical process (1886) is rejected as above. Mass adoption not claimed: I found no source for the year it became routine for ordinary people.

what: Castaways from the wrecked ship Grafton on the Auckland Islands (1864-65) built a forge and made charcoal to work metal, burnt shells for lime mortar and made soap from what they could salvage or gather.
fit: Survivors re-created small-scale metalworking and soap-making with local materials after losing industrial supplies, though it was a craft forge and soap, not smelting or steel.

sources.title: Grafton wreck and Epigwaitt
sources.quote: Published accounts detail how the party built their own forge to work metal and made charcoal to fire it.

note: This is a documented example, not a verified earliest: similar shipwreck improvisation (e.g. the 1565 French wreck forge in Florida, Sea Venture at Bermuda 1609, Invercauld and General Grant 1864-66) is older or contemporary, and none produced glass or smelted ore. Fit is partial (salvaged iron reworked, not smelting from ore); no source found for an earliest event, so treat as a representative case.

what: Unimate, the programmable robot arm built by Consolidated Controls Corp. (Bethel, Conn.), was shown working a forging-press job (picking up a billet, placing it in the two-stage die) and reported in the trade press in March 1961 as a machine to replace human labor in factory jobs.
fit: A programmable arm with a 200-step drum memory, taught by leading it through the task and then repeating it unattended, doing a real factory task (forging press feeding) in place of a worker.

what: Lockheed Missiles & Space Co. (Roger K. Summit) completed the DIALOG online retrieval system, a computer searched from a remote terminal, tested on NASA data at Ames.
fit: A computer stores a large bibliographic file and returns references matching keyword queries interactively from a remote terminal in minutes or seconds.

sources.title: Dialog (online database)
