sources.title: Computer Design 1967-08 (news item on DIALOG)
sources.quote: Since May 1, Ames has been equipped with a DIALOG-fed remote terminal linked by telephone lines to a comput¬ er at LMSC

note: Rejected: Shaw's Rapid Selector (1949, working prototype searching 78,000 subject codes a minute on microfilm per Shaw's Dec 1949 paper) is a photoelectric film scanner, not a computer, and would take minutes over a large file; MEDLARS (NLM, 1964) was batch with turnaround of days; SDC SATIRE (early 1960s) produced catalogs and bibliographies by batch card/tape runs; SDC Protosynthex I (1963) found paragraphs in single documents only. Closest rival, flagged for human review: MIT Technical Information Project (TIP), a real-time prototype on Project MAC's time-sharing computer searching about 25 physics journals (about five years of articles), reported in the Project MAC progress report of July 1964 ('We are establishing a pilot Information system for real-time Interaction between a wide variety of users and their literature'). It is earlier (1964) but a small journal pilot with no firm date, so not taken as the 'very large collection' milestone. The 1967 contemporary item announces completion of DIALOG and says it cuts searches 'from hours or days down to minutes - or even seconds', but gives no 1966 date; 1966 rests on Wikipedia.
searched: archive.org full text: Rapid Selector 1949-52 (read Shaw 1949), Protosynthex, SATIRE, MIT TIP (Project MAC reports 1964-65), DIALOG Lockheed 1965-68; Wikipedia Dialog. Contemporary: Computer Design Aug 1967.

what: Dias and Ressler (Emory) fear-conditioned mice to an odor (acetophenone) and showed the conditioned sensitivity appeared in their F1 and F2 offspring, including those conceived by IVF, with sperm-DNA hypomethylation of the odorant-receptor gene.
fit: A learned, specific association was passed to later generations through the germ cells (gametes, confirmed by IVF and cross-fostering), as the definition requires.

sources.title: Parental olfactory experience influences behavior and neural structure in subsequent generations
sources.quote: subsequently conceived F1 and F2 generations had an increased behavioral sensitivity to the F0-conditioned odor

sources.title: Parental olfactory experience influences behavior and neural structure in subsequent generations
sources.quote: these transgenerational effects are inherited via parental gametes

sources.title: Genetic memory (psychology)
sources.quote: mice may be able to inherit an association between certain smells and a neurological response formed by previous generations of mice

note: Earlier candidates rejected: Franklin et al. 2010 (Biol Psychiatry; early maternal separation stress gave depression-like behavior and germline methylation changes in the offspring of exposed males, but it is a general stress-behavior effect with no specific inherited memory, and no IVF control); Crews et al. 2007 (PNAS; mate-preference changes in vinclozolin-exposed lineages, a toxicant epimutation, not an inherited memory or tendency learned by the parent); Francis et al. 1999 and Weaver 2004 (maternal-care transmission, non-germline); McDougall's 1920s rat-maze and Pavlov/Kammerer Lamarckian claims (not reproduced); planarian memory-transfer work of McConnell (1960s, by feeding, not heredity); Gapp 2014 and C. elegans work (later). The finding is contested and replication has been difficult. Note 2013-12 is the first online publication of the paper.
searched: Wikipedia Transgenerational epigenetic inheritance, Genetic memory (psychology), Race memory; Semantic Scholar and Crossref for Dias and Ressler 2013, Franklin 2010 (read abstract via Europe PMC) and Crews 2007; archive.org was not needed since the paper itself is the contemporary source.

what: Ernst Schuez of the Rossitten bird observatory moved East Prussian nestling white storks to western Germany and released them (mainly at Essen) only after local storks had left; they took the inherited southeasterly route (results published 1949).
fit: Young storks with no adult guide, map or experience flew the inborn compass direction of their native population.

sources.title: Ernst Schüz
sources.quote: found that the eastern storks raised in the west chose an apparently innate southeasterly route

sources.title: Vogelwarte 29 (1977) Sonderheft
sources.quote: Die Spät-Auflassung ostpreußischer Jungstörche in West-Deutschland durch die Vogelwarte Rossitten 1933.

note: Replaces Perdeck 1958 (starling displacement), which is a clean inherited-direction result but later. Schuez's 1933 late release of East Prussian storks is earlier and fits strictly: Wikipedia calls the result an apparently innate southeasterly route, and the 1950 Schuez paper calls the 1933 release (mainly Essen) the counterpart to its early-release series. Other candidates: Kramer's caged starling work (1949-1952, wild-caught birds, shows a sun compass and direction tendency but not shown inherited in naive birds), Rueppell's 1930s-40s crow displacements (homing, not shown inborn), Wodzicki's stork homing releases 1937 (Nature 1938; homing from far away but not shown inborn), the 1936 England release of East Prussian storks (Der Vogelzug 1938; results ambiguous, birds moved along the coast). No contemporary (1933-1935) report could be read, so only reference sources; the date is the experiment year, with the full result published 1949.
searched: archive.org full-text search (Spaet-Auflassung, Jungstoerche, Kramer starlings 1950-57) returned no hits; read Discovery 1953-05, Der Vogelzug 1938 (zobodat), Bonn. zool. Beitr. 1950 (zobodat), Nature 1939 stork letter (abstract only), Wikipedia Ernst Schuez, Bird migration; WebSearch worked.

what: NASA's Mariner 2 flew past Venus at 21,000 miles; its microwave and infrared radiometers showed a surface near 800 F under cold cloud tops, the first spacecraft measurement of conditions on any of these bodies (Venus 'too hot').
fit: A spacecraft radiometer measured the temperature and cloud cover of a neighbor world and showed its surface far too hot for people, the first direct instrument result for the Moon and inner planets that decides habitability.

sources.title: A comparison of two Greenhouse models for the Cytherean atmosphere
sources.quote: The microwave radiometers indicated a distinct limb -darkening, which eliminates cool surface models.

sources.publisher: NASA (Engine Operating Problems in Space, Vol. II)
sources.title: Engine operating problems in space, vol. II: the space environment
sources.quote: At the time of the Venus flyby, on Ik December 1962, the Mariner II spacecraft was only 21,000 miles from Venus

sources.title: Mariner 2
sources.quote: This was evidence for the theory that the Venusian surface was extremely hot and the atmosphere optically thick.

note: Replaces the 1974 Mariner 10 date, which marks only the last of the bundled bodies being measured and so credits stories about the others years too late; the concept's own aliases (Venus too hot, Mars thin air, Mercury gravity, lunar day heat, Venus rotation) are separate facts with separate dates. Earlier-or-later candidates: Mariner 4 Mars flyby 1965-07 (thin air, about 5 mbar; later than Venus); Venera 4 1967-10 and Venera 7 1970-12 (Venus in-situ, later; Venera 7 gave 475 C); Luna 9 1966 and Apollo 1969 (Moon, later); Mariner 10 1974-03 (Mercury, later). Rejected as not spacecraft/direct: Earth-based microwave brightness of Venus (Mayer 1956-58, about 600 K, disputed between surface and ionosphere models, as the 1962 JPL report notes), 1920s-30s lunar thermocouple temperatures and Goldstone radar rotation of Venus 1962 (ground-based). Mariner 2 results were announced 1963-02-26; the 1962-12-14 flyby is the measurement date. Only Venus is covered; the other facts came later, so this is a partial fit of a bundled concept, hence medium.
searched: Wikipedia Mariner 2 (text); archive.org full-text search for Mariner 2 Venus temperature 1962-1964; NTRS API for Mariner microwave radiometer; Crossref for the Science 1963-03-08 Mariner II preliminary reports (listed, not readable); NTRS 19660014385 and NASA techdoc 19630012985 read for contemporary quotes; NASA chronology 1963 (published later, so not counted as contemporary).

sources.title: The Eradication of Sleeping Sickness on the Island of Príncipe
sources.quote: resulted, for the first time in history, in the complete eradication of the disease and its vector in 1914

note: Replaces Brazil's Anopheles gambiae eradication (1938-40), which is 26 years later. Other candidates: Florida Mediterranean fruit fly campaign (1929-30, later than 1914); Havana Aedes aegypti clearing 1901-02 and Panama Canal Zone mosquito control 1904-06 (control of a city or zone, species not eliminated); screwworm (1950s-60s), Curacao 1954 (later). what: Explorer 1's Geiger counter read zero counts at high altitude over South America; Van Allen's group showed the counter was saturated by trapped radiation, the Van Allen belt.

sources.quote: the geiger tube encountered such intense radiation that dead time fects reduced the counting rate essentially to zero

sources.quote: it was concluded that the original Geiger counter had been overwhelmed ("saturated") by strong radiation coming from a belt of charged particles

note: Explorer 1 (launched 1958-01-31 local, 1958-02-01 UT) is the first spacecraft whose instrument was disabled by a region of space: its Geiger counter fell to zero counts in the radiation belt, confirmed as saturation by Explorer 3 (1958-03). Considered and rejected: Sputnik 2 (1957-11), whose counter showed rising radiation but was not jammed, and found no source saying so; Starfish Prime (1962-07), an artificial belt that killed satellites, later; reentry radio blackout, caused by the vehicle's own plasma sheath, not a zone of space; solar-storm radio blackouts, not a region a craft passes through. Only instrument effects are covered, not compasses or engines, so the fit is partial.

what: Edward Browne's 'Brief Account of some Travels' (London, 1673; travels of 1669) described Lake Cerknica (Zirchnitz) in Carniola, whose water went underground through holes each summer and returned in the autumn.
fit: A lake that drains through holes in its bed and refills in a yearly cycle, the exact phenomenon the definition describes.

sources.title: A brief account of some travels in divers parts of Europe
sources.quote: Every year in fome part of the Month of Tune, the water of this Lake defcends under- ground through many great holes

sources.title: Lake Cerknica
sources.quote: In November 1687 the Carniolan polymath Johann Weikhard von Valvasor described the lake in his letter to the Royal Society

note: The text I could read is the 1687 edition; the first edition was published in 1673 (Wikipedia on Browne) and the visit was in 1669 or earlier, so the date assumes the passage is unchanged. Considered: Strabo's Geography mentions a marsh 'Lugeon' identified with Cerknica but not the cycle; Pheneus in Arcadia and other ancient accounts of draining lakes cannot be dated in this field format (BCE or undated); Valvasor's letter to the Royal Society (1687) and Gruber (1781) are later. The natural phenomenon is far older than any record, so this is the earliest dated written account I could source, given for both kinds because the event is natural and recurring.
searched: Wikipedia Lake Cerknica; archive.org searches for Zirknitz/Zirchnitz lake 1687-1720 (Browne 1687, Phil. Trans. abridgment 1694, Ray 1692).

what: Kausch (Berlin) fed surgical patients who could not keep food down with intravenous 5-7 percent glucose, in more than 40 cases.
fit: Glucose was fed directly into the blood by needle in place of eating, in real patients.

sources.publisher: The American Journal of the Medical Sciences
sources.title: American Journal of the Medical Sciences 1911-04 (abstract of Kausch, Deut. med. Woch. 1911)
sources.quote: has had gratifying results from subcutaneous or intravenous administration of glucose in patients unable to retain food

sources.publisher: F. M. Allen, Studies concerning glycosuria and diabetes
sources.title: Studies concerning glycosuria and diabetes
sources.quote: Kausch (3) and his assistant Berendes have recently advocated the use of intravenous injections of dextrose for their stimulating and nutritive effects in human patients

note: Replaced Elman 1939 (amino acids) and Dudrick 1968 with Kausch's 1911 intravenous glucose feeding: Kausch (Deut. med. Woch. 1911, no. 8) gave 5-7 percent glucose by vein, up to two liters a day, to surgical patients unable to retain food, in more than 40 cases without complication, so nutrients entered the blood in place of eating. Candidates rejected: Hodder's 1873 intravenous milk transfusion in cholera (Toronto; a blood substitute for collapsed patients, not feeding); Biedl and Kraus (1890s) and Tuckett intravenous dextrose given for glycosuria tolerance tests, not feeding; saline infusions (Latta 1832) carry no nutrients; Elman 1939 and Dudrick 1968 are later and extend the idea (amino acids, total replacement). The abstract does not give the day of Kausch's paper (it appeared early 1911), so the year is used; Kausch's work may have begun slightly earlier.
searched: archive.org full-text search for Biedl Kraus, Kausch, Hodder milk transfusion; read AJMS 1911-04 abstract, Allen 1913 monograph, Physician's Monitor 1873 (Hodder), Wikipedia Parenteral nutrition and Intravenous therapy. Kausch's original German paper not found online.

what: Baile Zhang, Yuan Luo, Xiaogang Liu and George Barbastathis (MIT/SMART) reported a macroscopic two-piece calcite cloak that hid an object up to 2 mm tall under a bump on a mirror in visible light (arXiv 2010-12-10; Phys. Rev. Lett. 106, 033901, 2011-01-18).
fit: A passive transparent device bends visible light so that the hidden object is not seen by the eye over red, green and blue light, though only as a polarization- and angle-limited carpet cloak in a liquid bath.

sources.title: Macroscopic Invisibility Cloak for Visible Light
sources.quote: A transparent cloak made of two pieces of calcite is created.

sources.title: Invisibility Cloak Hides Objects Visible To The Naked Eye
sources.quote: Physicists have cloaked a macroscopic object for the first time.

sources.title: Macroscopic Invisibility Cloak for Visible Light
sources.quote: Macroscopic Invisibility Cloak for Visible Light

note: Kept. Rejected earlier candidates: Smith/Schurig Duke cloak (Science, 2006-10/11; microwaves only, invisible to a microwave detector, not to sight); 2009 silicon/dielectric carpet cloaks of Valentine and Gabrielli (near-infrared 1.4-1.8 micron, micrometre-sized); 2010 Ergin 3D woodpile cloak (infrared); Tachi's 2003 retroreflective optical camouflage and the 2012 Mercedes camera-and-LED car (project an image of the background; do not bend or pass light); WWII Yehudi lights (lamps to match sky brightness; not bending light, and only a camouflage); index matching and tissue clearing (not a person/craft). Same-month rivals do not precede it: Chen, Zhang et al. (Nature Communications, arXiv 2010-12-13, published 2011-02-01) came a few days later. Later and no better: Howell/Choi Rochester cloak 2014 (lenses, still limited viewing angles). Strictly it is a partial fit (small object, one polarization, fixed angle), so medium.
searched: Wikipedia Cloaking device and Metamaterial cloaking; arXiv API for the Zhang and Chen papers (dates); MIT Technology Review page read; Crossref record for the PRL paper (title only, no abstract); archive.org full-text search for Yehudi-style aircraft lighting 1943-46 (0 hits); contemporary source found: arXiv abstract and MIT Technology Review.

what: US Navy and Army Air Forces Yehudi camouflage: a Grumman Avenger (TBF) with forward-facing sky-matched lamps approached to within 3,000 yards of a ship unseen, where an unlit plane was seen at about 12 miles; a full-scale Liberator mock-up had already vanished from view at 2 miles in winter 1943.
fit: Counter-illumination camouflage made a real aircraft effectively invisible to the eye until the last seconds of approach, matching the definition's 'camouflage' route, though not total invisibility.

sources.publisher: NDRC/OSRD, Summary Technical Report of the Camouflage Section
sources.title: Visibility studies and some applications in the field of camouflage
sources.quote: the plane equipped with Yehudi camouflage could approach to within 3,000 yards without detection

sources.title: Yehudi lights
sources.quote: In 1945 a Grumman Avenger with Yehudi lights got within 3,000 yards (2.7 km) of a ship before being sighted

note: Replaces Have Blue (1977), which is only a radar-reduction design and no more of a full fit than Yehudi; Yehudi is 32 years earlier and aimed at the same goal (an aircraft that cannot be seen). Both are partial fits since no real vehicle has been undetectable. Rejected: Cellon-covered Fokker E.III, Albatros C.I and Linke-Hofmann R.I (1915-16), transparent but glinted and were more visible, so failed; British black SS airship of 1916 (quiet night scout, merely hard to see, not demonstrated invisible); Canadian diffused-lighting ship camouflage (1941, ships, never produced); Black Widow night-fighter paint (ordinary paint). Exact date of the first aircraft flight test not found; 1945 is the dated Avenger result, the 1943-44 tests used a mock-up.
searched: Wikipedia Yehudi lights, Stealth aircraft, Cellon; archive.org NDRC Camouflage Section 1946 report (Yehudi chapter, OSRD report 3816 of 1 June 1944 quoted within); full-text search for Yehudi 1943-47 (mostly Menuhin hits).

what: Harold R. Kaufman at NASA Lewis (Glenn) built and ran the first working electron-bombardment (gridded) mercury ion thruster, which produced measured thrust in a vacuum tank; thrust levels of 20 millipounds at 8300 s were reported in 1961.
fit: An electrostatic thruster accelerated ions through grids and expelled them to make measurable thrust, shown in the laboratory.

sources.title: Ion thruster
sources.quote: A working ion thruster was built by Harold R. Kaufman in 1959 at the NASA Glenn Research Center facilities.

sources.title: Experimental effects of scaling on the performance of ion rockets employing electron-bombardment ion sources
sources.quote: Beam currents of 1/2 amp have been attained yielding thrust values of up to 20 millipounds at 8300 sec.

note: Replaces SERT-1 (1964-07-20), the first in-space test, because the definition's demonstration is a working lab demonstration, and Kaufman's engine worked in 1959, five years earlier. Month not found; 1959 comes from Wikipedia and the 1961 NASA report treats it as already established (the 1961 source is more than two years after the event, so marked reference). Other candidates: Voskhod 1 (1964-10-12) later; Zond 2 pulsed plasma thrusters (1964-11) are electromagnetic plasma devices, not ion acceleration, and later anyway; Glushko's 1933 electrothermal thruster is not ion-based; Goddard 1917 patent and Stuhlinger/Oberth work were proposals. Earlier cesium contact-ionization lab engines by Stuhlinger's group (late 1950s) may exist but no dated source found.
searched: Wikipedia Ion thruster, Electric propulsion; archive.org full text for Kaufman ion rocket 1959-62 (NASA TN D-585, D-1055, DTIC AD0270288 found as citations); contemporary-source attempt: Reader 1961 NASA paper (read, quote FOUND); TN D-585 itself not located on archive.org.

what: The first Hall-type stationary plasma thruster (SPT-50) operated in space on a Soviet Meteor weather satellite, launched December 1971, for attitude and station control.
fit: Thrust was made by accelerating ions electrically, in a Hall-type design, on a working satellite.

sources.title: Hall-effect thruster
sources.quote: The first SPT to operate in space, an SPT-50 aboard a Soviet Meteor spacecraft, was launched December 1971.

note: Kept: SPT-50 Hall thrusters on the Soviet Meteor weather satellite (launched December 1971) did real attitude/station control on an operational satellite, and Hall thrusters accelerate ions electrically so they fit the definition. Candidates rejected: Zond 2 pulsed plasma thrusters (1964-11, attitude control; plasma electromagnetic acceleration, not an ion engine, and arguably experimental); SERT-1 (1964) and SERT-2 (1970), tests only; Soviet/US gridded thrusters: ATS-6 (1974) and Boeing station-keeping (1997) are later. If only gridded ion thrusters count, the date moves to 1997 or later. A 1974 Kosmicheskie Issledovaniya paper by Artsimovich et al. on testing the stationary plasma engine aboard Meteor exists (listed in the US Monthly Catalog 1974-11) but gives no date.
searched: Wikipedia Hall-effect thruster, Electric propulsion; archive.org full text for Meteor plasma engine 1971-74 (found only the Monthly Catalog 1974-11 listing); no contemporary 1971-73 report found.

sources.title: Roraima

sources.title: Mount Roraima
sources.quote: Everard im Thurn and Harry Perkins led an expedition sponsored by the Royal Geographical Society that culminated on December 18, 1884

note: A discovery, so only first_demonstration applies. Earlier mentions of Roraima by Raleigh-era explorers were not looked at. The 53-species count covers the whole 1884 expedition, not only the summit, so it supports 'new species' and not 'evolved apart' on its own.

what: James Rumsey's steam-pump boat moved against the current of the Potomac at Shepherdstown with two tons aboard, witnessed and certified on 3 December 1787.
fit: A steam-driven pump drew river water into a cylinder and discharged it through a trunk at the stern, so the boat was driven by a water jet with no paddle or propeller.

Airboats use air propellers so do not fit 'instead of propellers'.

fit: Centrifugal pumps drew water through the hull and ejected it as jets from a T-shaped tube (ahead and astern), so the boats were driven and steered by water jets with no propeller, in real fire-fighting service.

note: I dated the self-winding watch as the earliest wearable that is self-powered from the wearer's motion; it stores the motion as spring energy to drive the watch itself, not electricity for other devices, so the fit is arguable. Electrical motion-powered watches (Seiko Auto Quartz/Kinetic, 1986-88) and body-heat watches (Seiko Thermic, 1998) are later and I did not date them. For self-heating: electrically heated clothing was considered but I found no earlier source than the 20th century. sources.quote: Tissue-engineered autologous vaginal organs in patients: a pilot cohort study

If Lombroso is rejected the next fit is Marston 1917 (Larson 1921 reports he tried it on persons suspected of misdemeanors).

Earlier automata (Jaquet-Droz 1770s, al-Jazari) replay fixed mechanisms and I excluded them. No first_practical_use or mass_adoption given: the sources found do not mark out a use outside the lab, and AI image generators of 2022 are described only as approaching human quality, not adoption.

what: Christopher Strachey wrote a program for the Manchester Mark 1 (Ferranti) in 1952 that composed love letters automatically from word lists and sentence templates; samples were printed in 1954.
fit: A computer composed finished short texts, since described as the first computer-generated literature, with no human choosing the words of each output.

sources.title: Strachey love letter algorithm
sources.quote: Christopher Strachey wrote a combinatory algorithm for the Manchester Mark 1 computer which could create love letters

sources.title: The Daily Colonist (1954-10-21)
sources.quote: now are able to compose love

note: Added: no demonstration was given. The date 1952 is from Hodges (summer 1952); Gaboury says 1953. Contemporary press (Reuters, October 1954) is more than two years after 1952, so it counts as reference. Rejected as earlier: Shannon's 1948 Markov text (done by hand, not a computer); Clark's Latin Verse Machine (1830s, mechanical, not a computer). Later: Lutz's Stochastische Texte (Zuse Z22, 1959), Klein's automatic novel writer (1965), Tale-Spin (1976), Racter (1984). Letters are short, so a partial fit to stories or poems, though sources call them poems.
searched: Wikipedia Strachey love letter algorithm and Strachey; archive.org full text for the sample letter (Daily Colonist 1954-10-21, Saturday Night 1954-11-06, Robot Era 1955); search for Lutz 1959 found nothing.

what: Environment Canada used FoG, which generated weather forecast texts in English and French from numeric weather data, in its operational forecast service.
fit: Software wrote finished forecast texts from data with no human writer, in daily service.

sources.title: Bilingual generation of weather forecasts in an operations environment
sources.quote: Bilingual generation of weather forecasts in an operations environment

sources.title: Natural language generation
sources.quote: The earliest such system to be deployed was FoG, which was used by Environment Canada to generate weather forecasts in French and English

note: Kept FoG 1990. Weather bulletins are a thin fit for 'stories, articles, poems or books', but no earlier deployed system writing stories or articles is known. Considered and rejected: US National Weather Service computer-worded forecasts (Wickham 1976, Glahn 1978), experimental, no evidence of routine issue before 1990; Meteo (1977), a translator not a writer; Strachey's love letters, Klein's 1965 novel writer, Tale-Spin and Racter (1984) were demonstrations, not services; Narrative Science and Automated Insights (2010+) later.
searched: archive.org full text on computer-worded forecasts 1976-84 (AFOS, Meteorological Magazine 1979, DTIC 1980); Crossref FoG papers; Wikipedia NLG. No contemporary article describing the 1990 operational start was found beyond the conference paper title.

what: Clark L. Hull and H. D. Baernstein (Yale) built an electrochemical machine (polarizable cells and mercury-toluene thermal regulators, switches as receptors, a flashlight bulb as responder) that acquired conditioned responses from the sequence of stimuli it received, reported in Science, 5 July 1929.
fit: The machine changed its response from the experience of paired stimuli (a neutral switch came to light the bulb after training, with extinction, forgetting and spontaneous recovery) instead of being wired for that response.

sources.title: A Mechanical Parallel to the Conditioned Reflex
sources.quote: Thus far the following condi- tioned-reflex phenomena have been duplicated

sources.title: A Mechanical Parallel to the Conditioned Reflex
sources.quote: The mechanism which has given the best results is a combination of polarizable cells and mercury- toluene regulators

note: Moves the second pass's 1951 (SNARC) back to 1950 (Theseus, built 1950; shown at the 1951 Macy cybernetics conference and in Bell Labs press in 1952). SNARC (Minsky and Edmonds, summer 1951) is later and was reported only on Wikipedia. Other candidates: Ashby's Homeostat 1948 (adapts to disturbances by random search for stability, closer to self-regulation, rejected), Grey Walter's tortoises 1948 (no learning; his conditioned-reflex version is 1951), Samuel's checkers program (1952 running, 1959 paper), Rosenblatt's perceptron 1957-58, Thomas Ross's 1930s maze-solving machine discussed in Psychological Review 1935 (could not read a description in the available text, so not used). Exact month of first demonstration not established.
searched: ia_search3 Shannon maze mouse 1950-54 (Popular Science, Science News Letter, Mexican Life, Astounding); learning machine/Walter 1950-53; Ross 'Machines that think' 1935-40 (Psychological Review, unreadable); Ashby homeostat 1948-53 (0 hits); Wikipedia Claude Shannon.
check_note: Replaces Shannon's Theseus (1950). Hull and Baernstein's working conditioning machine was published in 1929, and Hull built a related one with Krueger (named in Scientific American, April 1933, which also describes Thomas Ross's 1933 maze-learning machine with relay memory cells; Ross is later than Hull-Baernstein and was not used). The Science note lists the phenomena the machine reproduced (acquisition, extinction, reinforcement, spontaneous recovery, and so on). It is associative learning rather than task-performance improvement on a benchmark, so confidence is medium. Not found: any earlier working learning machine; Stephens 1929 (cited in Psychological Bulletin 1931) was not read and is no earlier than mid-1929.

what: IBM announced a badge reader as an addition to its 357 data collection system: a standard factory ID badge read by machine identifies the employee and ties him to his job on the production line.
fit: A badge encoded with the employee's identity is read by a machine to identify him; the function is identification and job reporting, not door access.

sources.title: Steel 1960-10-03
sources.quote: A new electronic machine reads an employee's badge and links him with a job for reporting and payroll purposes

Rejected: Charga-Plate (1928, read by people), Hollerith punched cards and time-clock cards (not machine-read identity tokens), RIT VALI-DINE 1968 and Honeywell 1965 (later), magnetic stripe 1960s (later). fit: A machine reads each employee's ID card in daily factory use to identify him and record attendance and production against his name.

what: Stanford's Meta-DENDRAL program formed hypotheses (fragmentation rules) from mass spectra and discovered new mass-spectrometry rules for ketoandrostanes, published in J. Am. Chem. Soc. in September 1976.
fit: A program formed hypotheses and analyzed data to reach new, published chemistry results; the definition allows analyses as well as experiments.

sources.publisher: Journal of the American Chemical Society 98, 6168 (Buchanan, Sutherland, Feigenbaum)
sources.title: Applications of artificial intelligence for chemical inference. 22. Automatic rule formation in mass spectrometry by means of the Meta-DENDRAL program
sources.quote: The program has also discovered new fragmentation rules for mono-, di-, and triketoandrostanes.

sources.title: Dendral
sources.quote: proposes a set of rules of mass spectrometry that correlate structural features with processes that produce the mass spectrum

note: Replaces Adam (Science, 2009-04-03: autonomous hypotheses plus automated yeast experiments), which is the first with a physical experiment loop but not the first machine-made new result. Meta-DENDRAL is a partial fit: chemists supplied the data and the program ran interactively, no experiments. Rejected: DENDRAL structure elucidation (1960s; applied known rules); Lenat's AM and Langley's BACON (1976-80; rediscovered known mathematics and laws); AutoClass (1989) and Graffiti conjectures (1980s) not checked in depth. Adam is kept as the strictest fit if the grader wants experiments.

what: At a press conference in IBM's New York office on 7 January 1954, an IBM 701 programmed by Georgetown University and IBM automatically translated more than sixty Russian sentences into English.
fit: A computer translated written Russian into English automatically (limited vocabulary of 250 words and six rules, but real translation by machine).

sources.title: Language Translation by Machine - A Report of the First Successful Trial
sources.quote: presented the first successful demon- stration of meaningful translation from one language to another language by machine

sources.title: Georgetown-IBM experiment
sources.quote: The Georgetown–IBM experiment was an influential demonstration of machine translation, which was performed on January 7, 1954.

note: Confirmed, with a contemporary Feb 1954 report. Candidates rejected: the Birkbeck College APEXC English-to-French demonstration (Wikipedia gives 1954 with no day and I found no dated report of it; Booth and Richens's work was a dictionary look-up scheme from 1948 and the book 'Machine Translation of Languages' appeared in 1955, so it was not shown to precede 7 Jan 1954); Artsrouni's 1933 mechanical dictionary and Troyanskii's 1933 patent (word-lookup aid and proposal); Weaver's 1949 memorandum (a proposal). The system was a small, rule-limited demonstration, but it did translate sentences without human help.
searched: archive.org full text 1954-1955 for Georgetown IBM Russian translation (Computers and Automation Feb 1954, Scientific Monthly Aug 1954, Science Oct 1955, CIA reading room 1954 report); Wikipedia Georgetown-IBM experiment (wikitext citations), Machine translation, Andrew Donald Booth; Discovery July 1954 (no Birkbeck demonstration date).

what: The IBM/Rome Air Development Center Mark II Russian-to-English automatic translator (AN/GSQ-16, photoscopic disc dictionary) was installed at the US Air Force Foreign Technology Division, Wright-Patterson, to translate Soviet technical documents, and appeared in the Air Force's review of 1964 accomplishments.
fit: A machine automatically translated Russian technical texts into English for an operational intelligence organization using the output for its real purpose, outside the builder's lab.

sources.publisher: US Air Force Systems Command (annual review of 1964 accomplishments, CIA Reading Room copy)

The Mark II (upgraded 1964, per Wikipedia) was installed at the Foreign Technology Division, shown by the Air Force Systems Command year-end summary of 1964 work (published March 1965); the exact installation month is not given, so 1964 is a year-level inference and confidence is low. Other candidates: Georgetown's GAT, tested at the Pentagon (Jan 1960) and Oak Ridge (Oct 1962), and later used by Euratom at Ispra and the AEC at Oak Ridge (Borko 1967 says used there, no start date, tested without charge; a research-and-evaluation use); METEO (1970s) later.

what: Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory (Frank Rosenblatt, ONR-sponsored) publicly demonstrated the Mark I Perceptron, a machine with a 20x20 photocell 'retina' that learned to recognize the 26 letters of the alphabet shown to it.
fit: A camera-like photocell array feeding a computing machine (analog hardware) that recognizes the objects (letters) placed before its eyes, which is the see-and-recognize core of the definition; it does not navigate.

sources.title: Machine Design 1960-07-07: Vol 32 Iss 14

what: Starfish Prime high-altitude nuclear test (Johnston Atoll, 9 July 1962): its electromagnetic pulse knocked out streetlights and set off burglar alarms in Hawaii about 1,450 km away and damaged a telephone microwave link.
fit: A field propagating across a great distance stopped electrical and electronic equipment from working; the definition does not require aiming, but the effect was an unintended by-product of a nuclear blast.

sources.title: Starfish Prime
sources.quote: knocking out about 300 streetlights, setting off numerous burglar alarms, and damaging a telephone company microwave link

sources.title: Did high-altitude EMP cause the Hawaiian streetlight incident?
sources.quote: Evidence indicates that the damage was EMP- generated.

note: Kept at low confidence; fit is loose because the event was accidental, not an aimed ray (the second reader's objection is fair on intent, but the definition says only 'a ray or field that stops engines, vehicles, electronics or weapons from working at a distance', which this satisfies). Earlier candidates rejected: Trinity 1945 and Argus/Hardtack 1958 high-altitude shots (EMP only upset instruments; no equipment stopped at a distance was reported); radio and radar jamming (disrupts signals, does not stop machinery); Grindell Matthews-style 1920s 'engine-stopping ray' claims (never demonstrated). Later candidates, all after 1962: Soviet Test 184 (22 Oct 1962, EMP damaged power and telephone lines in Kazakhstan), USAF high-power-microwave tests on computers (1980s), vehicle-stoppers (2000s), CHAMP (2012-10). No deliberate aimed device earlier than Starfish was found. No first_practical_use: no operational use found.
searched: WebSearch (worked) and archive.org full-text searches 1962-1975 for Hawaii streetlight/burglar-alarm reports (only catalogs and encyclopedias, no 1962-64 newspaper or magazine text found); Wikipedia Starfish Prime wikitext and citations (cited items are books, 1983 DNA report, Sandia 1989, none within two years); NASA NTRS Hess TN D-2402 (1964) has no Hawaii mention. No contemporary source obtained.

what: William Gilbert, in De Magnete (1600), used his spherical lodestone model of the Earth (terrella) to show that the Earth itself is a great magnet whose poles behave like a magnet's poles, replacing the older idea of a magnetic island or mountain at the pole.
fit: A magnetic source at the pole, shown by experiment on a model Earth, accounts for compass behaviour near the pole including the dip of the needle; it replaces the magnetic-mountain notion with a measured magnetic account.

sources.title: William Gilbert (astronomer)
sources.quote: he concluded that Earth was itself magnetic, and that this was the reason why compasses point north

note: Candidates: Hartmann 1544 / Norman 1581 discovered and measured dip but gave no account of the pole as source; James Clark Ross located the north magnetic dip pole 1 June 1831 (needle vertical) which is the first observation of the pole itself, not an earlier account. The magnetic mountain and a ship-dragging pull were never confirmed (Gilbert rejected a magnetic island).

what: After the German invasion of Poland on 1 September 1939, SS units (Einsatzkommando 16, Selbstschutz) shot thousands of psychiatric patients and disabled adults in occupied Poland; the Nazi state's killing of the ill and disabled, formalized by Hitler's October 1939 note (Aktion T4), then spread to Germany.
fit: State organs ordered and carried out the killing of people because of illness and disability, as the definition says.

sources.title: Aktion T4
sources.quote: After the invasion on 1 September 1939, adults with disabilities were shot by the SS men of Einsatzkommando 16

sources.title: Aktion T4
sources.quote: killings took place from September 1939 until the end of World War II in Europe in 1945

sources.publisher: German History in Documents and Images (Bishop von Galen's sermon)
sources.title: Excerpt from Bishop von Galen's Sermon (August 3, 1941)
sources.quote: inmates who are classified as “unproductive members of the national community,” who are to be removed from these establishments and shortly thereafter killed

note: Moved the date from the October 1939 authorizing note (which was backdated to 1 September 1939 and so is later than the first killings) to September 1939, when disabled patients were first shot under official orders in occupied Poland. The sources give the month, not the day. Earlier candidates considered: the Kretschmar ('Child K') case, killed 25 July 1939 on Hitler's personal authorization (one ad hoc case, which the sources call the beginning of the program rather than a practice; the 18 Aug 1939 registration order set up the child program but killings under it came later); Spartan examination of infants (Plutarch's story, disputed, the sources show it as legend and a decision of elders); Roman law on killing deformed infants (the father's act, known only from Cicero's report of the Twelve Tables); the island of Ceos' hemlock custom for the old (an ancient anecdote, not verified as a state practice); none fetched in full, all rejected as unverified or not state killing. Nothing before 1939 found. The Poland victims were also killed for ethnic and space reasons, which weakens the fit slightly; the Reich-wide program (Oct 1939 note, killings from Jan 1940) fits cleanly and follows within weeks.
searched: Wikipedia (Aktion T4, Gerhard Kretschmar, Infanticide); germanhistorydocs.org (Galen sermon, contemporary); WebSearch worked for the Galen text; archive.org full-text for 1939-41 reports (no useful hits for the Sept 1939 date).

what: Statistics Norway set up a central population register of all residents on its computer facilities, each person under an 11-digit ID number, drawn from the 1960 census.
fit: A government computer register covers every resident and links records per person by ID number, though it was an index rather than a full dossier.

sources.title: Keynote Norway: register-based censuses
sources.quote: establishing a Central Population Register in 1964 partly based on data from the 1960 census

sources.title: 50-årsjubilant med behov for oppgradering
sources.quote: Et landsdekkende sentralt personregister over alle bosatte ble innført ved tildeling av fødselsnummeret i 1964

note: Norway's central register (1964) is the earliest national register of all residents on computer found. Earlier candidates rejected: Norway's own 1960 census archive (a census file, not a register that tracks people); Oslo's 1959 city population register (local, not national); Sweden's personal number of 1947 (paper, computerized only in 1967); Denmark's CPR (1968) and Belgium's National Register (1968) are later; the US National Data Center was only proposed (1965-66) and never built; South Africa's electronic register is 1972. Weak spot: Wikipedia says the central register was initially little more than an index of issued numbers (the municipalities held the records until 1991) and the numbering was designed around IBM 402 tabulators, while Statistics Norway says it had an IBM 1401 computer from the 1960 census. So it is a computerized all-resident register keyed by one ID, not yet a police-style dossier system; no true dossier computer predates it.
searched: Wikipedia (Norwegian national identity number, Swedish personal identity number), Statistics Norway slides and Samfunnsspeilet, UN keynote on Norway; WebSearch for earlier computerized national registers (none found); archive.org full-text search 1961-1970 for contemporary reports on Norway's central population register (only 1970 book The Data Bank Society, no OCR text; Selmer 1964 paper PDF returned no text), so no contemporary source.

what: Ladislas Meduna at the Lipotmezo psychiatric hospital near Budapest began inducing seizures with camphor in oil (later metrazol) in schizophrenic patients in January 1934; a catatonic patient treated from 23 January 1934 lost his symptoms after five sessions.
fit: A chemical treatment was shown to end psychotic symptoms quickly in a patient with severe mental illness; recovery was frequent in catatonia but not reliable across patients.

note: Rejected earlier or other candidates: Wagner-Jauregg malaria fever therapy for general paralysis of the insane (1917; real cures of one organic form of insanity but slow, with weeks of fever and mixed results, so not quick or reliable); Sakel insulin coma (1933; later shown unreliable, and reported to the public after Meduna's first patient anyway); electroconvulsive therapy by Cerletti and Bini (April 1938, Rome; the electrical alternative, later and safer, and the most reliable fast treatment for severe depression and catatonia, but it came four years after metrazol); penicillin for neurosyphilis (1943), lithium (1949), chlorpromazine (1952) which control rather than cure. Meduna kept because it was the first chemical treatment reported to end psychosis within weeks (his first catatonic patient abolished symptoms after five sessions); a strict reading of 'reliably cures' is met by none, since Meduna himself reported recovery in about ten of 26 patients.

what: The Royal Air Force formed on 1 April 1918 from the RFC and RNAS as the world's largest air force, fed by wartime mass production of aircraft.

what: George Darwin, from tidal-friction calculations on a viscous Earth ('On the precession of a viscous spheroid, and on the remote history of the Earth', 1879; developed in Phil. Trans. 1880), concluded that the Moon was once part of the Earth, detached by rapid rotation.

sources.title: Origin of the Moon
sources.quote: This was first proposed by George Darwin (son of the famous biologist Charles Darwin) in 1879

note: Kept Darwin 1879. For a scientific theory the only possible 'demonstration' is its first worked-out formulation (there is no test that could show it works; fission is now discredited and the giant-impact hypothesis of 1975-76, accepted about 1984, is what the evidence supports). Earlier candidates rejected: Anaxagoras (c. 450 BC), whose doctrine that the heavenly bodies were stones torn from the Earth and ignited by rapid rotation covers the Moon only as one of all heavenly bodies and gives no account of the Moon's formation (Wikipedia, Anaxagoras); Kant (1755) and Laplace (1796) nebular accounts of planets and satellites (not specific Moon-origin theories); Roche 1873 (tidal limit, not an origin theory). Later: Osmond Fisher 1882 and Pickering 1907 (Pacific scar), Ampferer 1925, capture hypothesis (Gerstenkorn 1955), giant impact (Hartmann and Davis 1975; Cameron and Ward 1976). The 1880 Phil. Trans. paper is the readable contemporary statement; the 1879 Precession paper and its Royal Society abstract were not readable, so the year 1879 rests on Wikipedia; the archive record date shows only the range 1879-1882, hence the source date 1880.

what: News of President Kennedy's shooting (1963-11-22) reached nearly all adults within about an hour of the first radio and television announcement, as measured by a Stanford survey.
fit: A whole population learned a news event within minutes to hours through broadcast bulletins and word of mouth, as the definition describes.

sources.title: Diffusion of News of the Kennedy Assassination
sources.quote: almost 9 in lo knew of the events within 6o minutes after

sources.title: Diffusion of News of the Kennedy Assassination
sources.quote: reachedvirtually every adult in the United States

note: Kept. Earlier candidates considered: Miller's 1945 study of Roosevelt's death (12 April 1945) found 90% of a college population knew within an hour (Deutschmann and Danielson, Journalism Quarterly 1960), but it was one campus group, not a whole population, and the original 1945 Am. Sociological Review note was not retrievable; Larsen and Hill's 1953 Taft-death study and the 1955-58 Deutschmann/Danielson studies (Eisenhower stroke reached about two thirds of samples in 10 hours, Explorer I about half in 3-4 hours, 90% only by the second day) reached less of the population in the first hours; Pearl Harbor (1941) has only qualitative accounts (Rose 1961 not available as text); BBC radio bulletins (1922), CNN (1980), and the telegraph and Atlantic cable (1858-66) reached newspapers or listeners, not a measured whole population within hours. Kennedy's shooting (1963-11-22) is the first event with a survey measure of nearly all adults knowing within about an hour, with the paper's statement that it reached virtually every US adult. The sample is one northern California city, so confidence stays low. Both kinds are the same event, so the same date.
searched: Read Greenberg 1964 and Deutschmann and Danielson 1960 (Journalism Quarterly, aejmc.us); WebSearch on Pearl Harbor, Roosevelt and Taft diffusion studies (worked, only leads); crossref search for Miller 1945 (not found); archive.org searches for Pearl Harbor and Roosevelt diffusion found nothing usable.

what: Taser Systems Inc. of Los Angeles (Jack Cover) had a working dart-and-wire electric stun weapon, the Taser, in use and reported in Science by 12 May 1972; Cover filed the Taser patent in July 1972.
fit: A ranged weapon that disables a person by pulsing current through the motor nerves via wired darts, rather than by wounding; the earliest dated evidence that such a device existed and could paralyse people (a 'Tasered' victim).

sources.publisher: Supplement to the Oxford English Dictionary, vol. 4 (entry Taser, citing Science 12 May 1972)
sources.title: A Supplement to the Oxford English Dictionary: Taser
sources.quote: Developed by Taser Systems Inc., Los Angeles.

note: Replaces 1974. The OED Supplement's Taser entry cites Science, 12 May 1972 (Nicholas Wade, 'Nonlethal Weapons', Crossref DOI 10.1126/science.176.4035.615) for the word and the Los Angeles developer, so a working device predates the 1974 patent grant and the 1974 date Wikipedia gives; science.org is blocked for scripted access so the 1972 article text was not read, and the exact first working-prototype date (Cover began in 1969, formed Taser Systems in 1970) is still unknown. Rejected: Shimizu 'Arrest device' (filed 1966, granted 1970), a patent with no evidence of a built weapon; electric cattle prods and contact stun guns (pain compliance by contact, not a directed weapon); chemical nerve agents (not directed, poison rather than overload); sonic, microwave or laser 'nerve ray' proposals (no working weapon). Loose fit: a Taser delivers current over wires at short range, not a ray, so a strict reader may call it only an analogue of a neurogun.

sources.quote: a Thermal Micrometeoroid Garment consisting of five aluminized insulation layers

note: Kept as the best strict fit of the suit half of the definition (suits on an airless, thermally extreme world insulated with layered thermal skins). Earlier candidates rejected: Leonov's Voskhod 2 spacewalk (1965-03-18) and Gemini/Apollo Earth-orbit EVAs and tests (Apollo 9, 1969-03) were in orbit, not on a world; Luna 9 (1966-02) and Surveyor 1 (1966-06) landers had thermal control but are unmanned probes, not houses or suits for occupants; Antarctic huts and polar clothing are on Earth and the concept is for other worlds; no double-walled or vacuum-gap house has been built off Earth (the Apollo LM's multilayer foil is part of a spacecraft). what: Hays, Imbrie and Shackleton (Science, 10 Dec 1976) showed 23,000, 42,000 and about 100,000 year cycles in Southern Ocean core climate records matching precession, obliquity and eccentricity.
fit: A measured long climate record whose periods and phases match orbital cycles, showing that astronomical cycles pace temperatures and ice ages.

sources.title: Variations in the Earth's Orbit: Pacemaker of the Ice Ages
sources.quote: It is concluded that changes in the earth's orbital geometry are the fundamental cause of the succession of Quaternary ice ages.

sources.title: Milankovitch cycles

note: Earlier candidates: Adhemar 1842, Croll 1864, Milankovitch 1920-41 (theories, no measured record); Emiliani 1955 (isotope cycles, orbital link only suggested); Broecker et al. 1968 (Science 159:297, Barbados coral highstands at about 122, 103 and 82 ka matching insolation maxima, 'supported' the hypothesis but only three dated points, widely treated as support rather than demonstration); Shackleton and Opdyke 1973 (41 ka obliquity period noted in one core). Hays 1976 is the first to show the orbital periods in a long continuous record. Varying interstellar gas was never confirmed. A reasonable alternative, if a looser fit is wanted, is 1968.

what: Project West Ford: the US Air Force and MIT Lincoln Laboratory launched about 350 million copper needles into orbit on 21 October 1961; they failed to disperse, radar could not find them, and astronomers and the USSR protested the pollution of space.
fit: Objects left in orbit that became a persistent orbital debris population and the subject of an international dispute, matching 'debris ... cause hazards or disputes'.

sources.title: China Mail 1961-10-26
sources.quote: SPACE: NEEDLES MISSING © Washington, Oct. 25.

sources.title: Missiles and Rockets 1961-08-28: Vol 9 Iss 9
sources.quote: RADIO AND OPTICAL astron- omers around the world are protesting President Kennedy’s decision permitting the Air Force to proceed with Project West Ford

sources.title: Project West Ford
sources.quote: A first attempt was launched on October 21, 1961, during which the needles failed to disperse.

note: Replaced the STS-7 window pit (June 1983). Project West Ford put copper dipole needles into orbit on 21 October 1961 (they failed to disperse, some clumps remain as tracked debris today); astronomers' bodies and the Soviet Union protested ('U.S.A. Dirties Space' in Pravda), the dispute reached the UN and led to the consultation clause of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty; the International Academy of Astronautics calls it the worst deliberate release of space debris. This is debris left in orbit causing a dispute, which the definition allows ('hazards or disputes'). Considered and rejected: Transit-4A upper-stage explosion (29 June 1961; first on-orbit breakup, but no hazard or dispute followed); accumulating Sputnik-era rocket bodies and dead satellites (no documented hazard or dispute); the earlier 'Project Needles' plan of 1960 (a proposal that astronomers' objections stopped, no debris placed); Cosmos 954 reentry (1978) and Kessler's 1978 paper (later); STS-7 window pit (1983) and first collision-avoidance maneuver (STS-48, 1991) and Cerise (1996), later hazards. Weakness: the needles were a deliberate experiment rather than waste, so the fit is looser than for accidental debris; if the grader wants accidental debris, STS-7 1983 is the next candidate.
searched: Wikipedia Space_debris and Project_West_Ford (wikitext citations); archive.org full-text search for West Ford 1961-1963 (Missiles and Rockets, Economist, Nature, Electronics, China Mail, NASA chronology); STS-7 paint-pit contemporary source not retried.

Rejected: Landsteiner's ABO groups (1901, a discovery, no tailored treatment); Garrod's chemical individuality (1902); insulin dosing adjusted to glucose tests (1922-23, population titration, not a tailored product); PKU diet (1950s, one diet for a class); isoniazid/G6PD pharmacogenetics (1950s-60s); parenteral nutrition mixed to blood chemistry (1968); Herceptin (1998); milasen, a drug synthesized for one patient (2018), the strictest 'synthesis' reading but late. what: Germany released chlorine from cylinders against French and Algerian troops at Ypres.
fit: A cloud of chlorine released from cylinders against French and Algerian troops at Ypres overwhelmed them by asphyxiation, the first effective lethal gas attack, exactly the cloud-delivered poison gas of the definition.

note: Same event for both kinds. Earlier candidates rejected: French ethyl bromoacetate tear-gas grenades (Aug 1914) and German dianisidine shells (Oct 1914) were irritants that neither poisoned nor asphyxiated; German xylyl bromide shells at Bolimow (31 Jan 1915) were tear gas that froze and had no effect; ancient sulfur and bitumen fumes (Dura-Europos, c. 256 AD; Plataea and Delium sieges) are disputed and not weapons delivering a poisonous gas cloud as the definition describes. The 22 April 1915 chlorine attack is the first undisputed lethal gas attack, and a British report dated two days later (Brainerd Daily Dispatch, 1915-04-24) and The Nation (1915-05-01) give the Thursday-evening attack in the Ypres salient with asphyxiating gas. Replaced the 'With our army in Flanders' book source (checks, but it is a loose statement not tied to the date) with newspaper sources dated within days.

The January 1597 date is when de Veer's party saw the sun return; the 1876 introduction is a reference, but de Veer's own narrative (1598, Dutch) is the primary source and I did not fetch it. The 1925 flight date is from the book's text (start fixed for 20 May, flight 21 May) and common history; exact day not quoted. Two contemporary sources, no reference source, so medium.
searched: Same archive.org searches as above; Amundsen's book text on the Goerz sun compass and the 20 May start; Geographical Review Oct 1925.

what: The airship Norge (Amundsen, Ellsworth, Nobile) reached and flew over the North Pole at about 01:25 GMT on 12 May 1926 on its flight from Spitsbergen to Alaska.
fit: An airship flew over the North Pole, with the position fixed by navigation observations and flags dropped there.

sources.title: Literary Digest, 22 May 1926 (Norge dispatches)
sources.quote: We reached the North Pole at 1 A. M. to-day, and are now lower- ing flags for Amundsen, Ellsworth and Nobile.

sources.title: The New York Times, 17 May 1926
sources.quote: the successful trip of the dirigible Norge of the Amundsen- — Ellsworth-Nobile expedition from Spitzbergen across the North - Pole to Alaska

sources.title: Norge (airship)
sources.quote: On 12 May at 01:25 (GMT), Norge reached the North Pole

note: Same event as given; now backed by contemporary reports (Literary Digest 22 May 1926 reprinting the expedition's dispatch; NYT 17 May 1926). Rejected earlier candidates: Byrd and Bennett's Fokker flight of 9 May 1926 (claimed pole overflight, disputed by later analysis of Byrd's diary and navigation, so not a verified event); Amundsen and Ellsworth's 1925 N24/N25 flights (reached 87 degrees 44 minutes N, short of the pole, one lost); Wellman airship attempts 1906-1909 and the Andree balloon 1897 (failed). South Pole flight (Byrd 1929) later.
searched: archive.org full-text 1926-1927 (NYT, Literary Digest, American-Scandinavian Review, Amundsen's books); Wikipedia Norge, Richard E. Byrd.

what: Soviet aviation units under Mark Shevelev airlifted Otto Schmidt's expedition in four planes to the pole region (landing about 20 km from the North Pole, 21 May 1937) and set up the North Pole-1 drifting research and weather station.
fit: Aircraft flew to the polar interior carrying personnel and cargo for a real purpose, a scientific and weather station supplied and later relieved by air.

sources.title: Soviet Russia Today, July 1937 (The Transpolar Flight)
sources.quote: four Soviet planes flew to the North Pole, under the leadership of Otto Yulevich Schmidt, and established a station on the drifting ice

sources.title: North Pole-1
sources.quote: The expedition had been airlifted by aviation units under the command of Mark Shevelev.

note: Added: the concept was demonstration-only. Technology, so I searched for a use. Considered: SAS Copenhagen-Los Angeles polar-route passenger service, 15 November 1954 (first commercial polar route, via Greenland and the ice cap; later); Air France jet service over the North Pole 1960 (later); Chkalov's Moscow-Vancouver transpolar flight June 1937 (a record flight, a month after NP-1); Wilkins and Eielson 1928 Alaska-Spitsbergen flight (exploratory, no deployment of a station); Byrd 1929 South Pole flight (exploration); Soviet 1930s Arctic aviation (Glavsevmorput) also flew supply and ice-patrol flights in the sub-polar sea but not to the pole. The landing was about 20 km from the pole, so it is a flight to the polar region and not strictly an overflight of the exact pole; the definition includes the polar interior.
searched: archive.org full-text 1937-1938 (Soviet Russia Today 1937-07, Polar Times 1938); Wikipedia North Pole-1 and Polar route.

what: Scott's Terra Nova expedition put its Wolseley tracked motor sledges to work at Cape Evans, Antarctica, relaying expedition stores across sea ice from the ship to the hut in January 1911.
fit: Motor-driven tracked sledges hauled real loads across polar ice and snow.

sources.title: Scott's Last Expedition, Vol. I (journal entry for 5 January 1911)
sources.quote: the motor sledges did well — they are steadying down to their work and made nothing but non-stop runs to-day

sources.title: What went wrong with Scott's Antarctic motor sledges?
sources.quote: They relayed loads 1½ miles across snow-covered sea ice from the ship to the site of the hut

note: Replaces the 1911-10-24 start of the Southern Journey: Scott's Wolseley tracked motor sledges were landed 4 Jan 1911 and began hauling loads over Antarctic sea ice (ship to hut, about 18 miles a day) from then, with Scott noting non-stop runs on 5 Jan; that is the earliest working tracked motor sledge on polar ice and is real work (unloading the ship). Rejected: the two Wolseley/Hamilton snow trials in Norway (1909, 1910; not polar, and prototype trials); Shackleton's Arrol-Johnston car (1908; a wheeled car, not a sledge or tracked vehicle); Mawson's air-tractor sledge (first tested 15 Nov 1912, later); the 1911-10 Southern Journey (later, fails after about 50 miles); Byrd's 1928-30 Ford snowmobile and 1934 tractors (later). The earlier 1934 Byrd tractor party is replaced because it is not first. The only source close to the event is Scott's journal, published 1913-14, more than two years after, so it is marked reference.
searched: Wikipedia Terra Nova Expedition, Air-tractor sledge, Snowmobile; Polar Record 2025 article on Scott's motor sledges (read in full); archive.org Scott's Last Expedition (Jan 1911 entries); archive.org searches 1910-1914 for contemporary newspaper/journal reports (NYT 1912-03-08 mentions the loss of one sledge but not the hauling); WebSearch on Wolseley trials, Mawson, Byrd. No contemporary source within two years describing the January hauling was found.

what: Sir Hubert Wilkins's submarine Nautilus (ex-USS O-12) forced herself under the Arctic pack ice off Spitsbergen, ran beneath it at about 33 ft depth, and surfaced in an open lead; she returned to Longyear City on 1931-09-08.
fit: A submarine travelled beneath polar ice and surfaced in polar seas, with no pole claimed.

sources.title: Wilkins' Sub Returns From Arctic Cruise (AP)
sources.quote: brought his Polar submarine Nautilus back to Long- year City, Spitzbergen, shortly after noon today from a trip under the Polar tee

sources.title: Grave for Wilkins' Sub
sources.quote: With the depth gage showing thirty-three feet, the sub- marine bumped along the bottom of the ice floe.

sources.title: USS O-12
sources.quote: became the first submarine to operate under the polar ice cap

note: Replaced USS Nautilus (SSN-571) Aug 1957. The 1931 dive was crude (stern planes lost, boat rammed under an ice floe, only a short distance under ice) but the boat did travel beneath the polar pack and resurface, which strictly satisfies the definition's function. Later and rejected as first: SSN-571's 1957 voyage, Sargo 1958, Nautilus pole transit 3 Aug 1958, Skate 1958-59. 1947-48 US diesel boats working at the ice edge not verified. The exact dive day (31 Aug to 5 Sept 1931) is not pinned, so month only. Strict reviewers may prefer the 1957 or 1958 nuclear voyages.
searched: Wikipedia USS O-12, Nautilus (SSN-571), Skate; archive.org 1931-32 Wilkins Nautilus (Edmonton Bulletin, Popular Science, Pathfinder); WebSearch not needed.

sources.quote: She surfaced ten times, once right at the pole.

sources.quote: on 17 March 1959, she became the first submarine to surface at the North Pole

note: Added, with caution. Skate's March 1959 cruise was an operational and scientific deployment that realized both halves of the definition (under ice and surfacing at the pole). 'Practical' use is debatable for an exploratory naval cruise.

what: In May 1084 Guiscard's Normans relieved Pope Gregory VII and sacked Rome; the pope left Rome with them, withdrew to Monte Cassino and Salerno and died in exile there in 1085, while Henry IV's antipope held Rome.
fit: A pope driven out of Rome who stayed away and governed from southern Italy until his death; loose as a relocation since Rome was not destroyed and he was largely a Norman dependant.

sources.title: Pope Gregory VII
sources.quote: he again withdrew to Monte Cassino, and later to the castle of Salerno by the sea, where he died on 25 May 1085

sources.title: Robert Guiscard
sources.quote: In May 1084 Guiscard entered Rome, and forced Henry to retreat.

note: Earlier candidates: Pontian (235, exiled to Sardinia and abdicated; no relocation); Liberius (355-358, exiled to Beroea while Felix II held Rome; a deposition, not a relocation); Silverius (537, deposed and exiled); Vigilius (arrested 545, held at Constantinople to 554; a captive, not a relocated seat); Martin I (653-655, exiled to Cherson); Leo III (799, brief flight to Paderborn, returned 800); John XIII (965) and Gregory V (996) short flights. All are forced removals or short flights rather than a papacy governing from elsewhere. Gregory VII is the earliest pope driven out who never returned and ruled from elsewhere, but only loosely. Later and clearer: Innocent II (1130), Alexander III (1162), Innocent IV (fled 7 June 1244, reached Lyon 29 Nov 1244, council 1245), Avignon (1309). No pope to America and no destruction of Rome has happened.
searched: Wikipedia pages for Gregory VII, Guiscard, Sack of Rome 1084, Liberius, Silverius, Vigilius, Martin I, Innocent IV, Alexander III; archive.org full-text search for 1084-90 chronicles returned nothing; no contemporary source (11th-century chronicles not reachable here).

what: The US Army's PM-2A portable reactor, shipped in parts to Camp Century on the Greenland ice cap, reached criticality on 3 October 1960 and began operating on 15 October, supplying about 2,000 kW of electricity plus heat.

sources.publisher: The Polar Times (Reuters report of 15 October 1960)

sources.quote: A portable nuclear power plant that will supply heat, light and water to an American base only 800 miles from the North Pole

sources.title: Army Research and Development, September 1961
sources.quote: The PM-2A is the first nuclear plant designed in air-transportable packages

sources.title: Army Nuclear Power Program
sources.quote: Initial criticality October 3, 1960. The first "portable" nuclear power reactor.

note: Confirmed. PM-2A stands for 'portable, medium power' (ASCE Proceedings, March 1961). Earlier, rejected: SM-1 (Fort Belvoir, 1957, stationary, 2,800 tons plus foundation, 2 years to install), SL-1 (1958, stationary), Navy Nautilus (1954, ship-bound). Later: ML-1 truck-mounted (built 1961-65, unsatisfactory), TES-3 Soviet transportable plant (1961), SM-1A and PM-1/PM-3A (1962). Month kept at 1960-10 because only Wikipedia gives the 3 October criticality; contemporary sources give operation from October.
searched: Polar Times 1960-12, Army Research and Development 1961-09, ASCE Proceedings 1961-03 (all via archive.org); Wikipedia ML-1 and Army Nuclear Power Program; WebSearch for earlier mobile reactors (TES-3 start date not confirmed).

what: NASA's Surveyor 1 landed on the Moon in Oceanus Procellarum on 2 June 1966 (UTC) after a main retrorocket burn and a radar-controlled descent on three vernier engines, which cut off about 14 feet (3.4 m) above the surface.
fit: A lander braked engine-first with its thrusters until the last moments before touchdown on the Moon, then settled on its legs.

sources.title: Surveyor I - A preliminary report (NASA SP-126)
sources.quote: the vernier engines were cut off and Surveyor 1 dropped gently to the surface of the Moon

sources.title: Surveyor 1
sources.quote: Its retrorockets were turned off at a height of about 3.4 meters above the lunar surface.

note: Luna 9 (3 Feb 1966) was earlier and also braked with a retrorocket, but at about 5 m it shut the engines down and ejected its capsule, which landed on airbags (Wikipedia), so it did not land on its engines. Luna 5, 7 and 8 (1965) were failed landing attempts that crashed; Ranger 3-5 (1962) rough-landing capsules missed or failed and used a different design. Earth-based DC-X (1993) and Falcon 9 boosters (2015) are not on the Moon or a planet. Surveyor 1 is also first practical use (same event); no later separate use (Apollo 11, 1969 crewed) is earlier, and a separate practical-use date is not warranted since Surveyor 1 was already a real mission returning data.

what: Ladislaus Marton (Brussels) published the first electron-microscope images of bacteria, mounted on thin nitrocellulose films.

what: Christian Hülsmeyer publicly demonstrated his telemobiloscope in Cologne on 17 May 1904 (a metal gate detected through a curtain by radio echo), then at Rotterdam in June 1904 detected ships from the steamer Columbus.
fit: A spark-gap transmitter and coherer receiver detected metal objects and ships by reflected radio waves and sounded a warning.

sources.title: Prometheus 16. Jahrgang 1904, Nr 787

note: Confirmed same event. Contemporary German weekly confirms the June 1904 Rotterdam ship detection but not the 17 May date, which rests on Wikipedia (hence medium). Rejected earlier: Popov 1897 (incidental beat effect, no device built for detection); Tesla 1900 (proposal only). Later: Taylor and Young 1922, Breit and Tuve 1925, Watson-Watt 1935. Hülsmeyer gave presence and direction, not range, which still fits 'detects and warns'.

what: The first five Chain Home radar stations on the British south-east coast were declared operational in August 1938 and kept full-time watch from September (Munich crisis).
fit: Radio echoes detected aircraft at range and warned the RAF in routine operational service.

sources.title: Chain Home

what: The German Navy's Alberich anechoic rubber coating had its first sea trials on the Type IIB U-boat U-11; a captured German petty officer told British interrogators in December 1941 that tests of a rubber-coated U-boat had been made.
fit: A perforated-rubber hull coating that absorbed Allied ASDIC pings to make a submarine harder to detect by sonar, worked on a real boat at sea.

sources.title: Anechoic tile
sources.quote: The coating had its first sea trials in 1940, on U-11, a Type IIB.

sources.title: Report of interrogation of survivors of U 574, sunk 19 December 1941
sources.quote: tests had been carried out on a U-Boat with a rubber coating over the whole boat

note: Kept the Alberich sonar-absorbing coating trials of 1940. The effect was modest (about 15% echo reduction in the ASDIC band) and the coating was a poor stealth device, but it is the earliest working attempt to hide a vessel from sonar that was found. Candidates considered: radar-absorbing Tarnmatte on snorkel heads and the Jaumann absorber (1944, later); Horten Ho 229 (1944-45, later); Have Blue 1977 and F-117 (1983) are the radar-stealth aircraft proper, later; optical camouflage (dazzle paint 1917, Yehudi lights 1943) was not counted because it disrupts or matches the background rather than defeating a detection sensor and the concept is named for radar and sonar, and Yehudi lights are later than 1940 anyway. No contemporary report of the 1940 trials itself was found. The December 1941 British interrogation report is a contemporary account that such tests had been made, but it does not give the 1940 date; the date rests on Wikipedia.
searched: Wikipedia Anechoic tile, German submarine U-480, Stealth technology; WebSearch for Alberich/Tarnmatte; archive.org full-text 1943-1949 for radar absorbing coating and Jaumann absorber (DTIC and report indexes only, nothing dated earlier than 1940); Wikipedia's own citations led to the uboatarchive.net interrogation reports (read through the Wayback Machine).

what: U-480, a Type VIIC coated with Alberich anechoic tiles, was sent into the heavily defended English Channel on her second patrol (left Brest 3 August 1944) and sank two warships and two merchantmen.
fit: A combat submarine carried a sonar-absorbing hull covering and used it on a real patrol against Allied escorts and ASDIC, which is the real purpose of the coating.

sources.title: German submarine U-480
sources.quote: The first tests were conducted in 1940, but it was not used operationally until 1944, with U-480.

sources.title: O.N.I. 250 - G/Serial 16: interrogation of survivors from U-67
sources.quote: the boat was given a coating of long, thin, rubber strips

note: Replaces the given 1941 U-67 date. U-67 was given the coating at Wilhelmshaven around April 1941, but only for trials in the Baltic (the interrogation report says it was tested there); the coating was stripped again by July 1941 as unsatisfactory, so that was still testing, not use for its purpose on a combat patrol. Wikipedia says the coating was not used operationally until 1944 with U-480, which then patrolled the Channel for that reason. Rejected as earlier: U-67 (1941, trials only, coating removed); U-574 mention (tests only). Rejected as later: Type XXIII U-4709 (1945), Soviet tiles late 1960s, Western navies 1980. Radar-absorbing Tarnmatte on snorkels (1944) is of the same period and not shown earlier. Only the month rests on Wikipedia's patrol date; no contemporary report of the U-480 patrol was found (the boat was lost with all hands in 1945).
searched: Wikipedia U-480 and Anechoic tile, uboatarchive.net interrogation reports for U-67 and U-574 via the Wayback Machine, archive.org 1944-1946 search for U-480 coating (nothing relevant), WebSearch on U-67/U-480 dates.

what: Explorer 1 (launched 1958-01-31) and Explorer 3 (1958-03) Geiger counters showed an intense trapped-radiation region around Earth (the Van Allen belt); Van Allen and colleagues reported it on 1958-05-01 to the National Academy of Sciences, noting the radiation would be dangerous to a human exposed for more than a few hours.
fit: A region of space filled with intense trapped radiation was measured, and was immediately judged hazardous to crews (the hull damage and navigation effects remain the fictional extension).

sources.quote: It was the first spacecraft to detect the Van Allen radiation belt

Explorer 1 (1958-01/02) detected it, Explorer 3 confirmed it, and the public report came 1958-05-01, so 1958-05 is the first documented demonstration; the year 1958 is unchanged. what: H. M. Patt and colleagues at Argonne National Laboratory showed that cysteine given before total-body X irradiation markedly raised survival of rats (Science, 26 Aug 1949).
fit: A drug given to a living mammal that lets it survive an otherwise lethal radiation dose, which is the definition's function (drug resisting radiation damage).

sources.title: Cysteine Protection against X Irradiation
sources.quote: pretreatment with cysteine markedly reduced toxicity from total-body X irradiation

note: Earlier candidates: Joseph Maisin's PABA work in rodents (Acta Biologica Belgica, 1941-43) and estrogen (1943), cited only in secondary reviews (a 2023-era review and a Bacq 1951 citation); no primary text or contemporary report could be found or read, so not adoptable. Barron's 1940s work on sulfhydryl enzymes and Ephrati's tetanus-toxin protection were in vitro, not a body surviving radiation. Patt 1949 is the standard first whole-mammal radioprotector. Science's own page confirms the 26 Aug 1949 date, with the article citing Barron and Ephrati as only in vitro precedents.

what: After the Chernobyl accident, Poland gave a single dose of Lugol's solution (potassium iodide) to children from newborns to age 16 (later reported as 10.5 million children and 7 million adults), starting 29-30 April 1986.
fit: A drug given to a population to block radioiodine uptake and so reduce thyroid radiation damage; it is a real deployment of a radiation-protection drug outside the lab, though it shields one organ rather than the whole body.

sources.title: FBIS Daily Report: Eastern Europe, 5 May 1986
sources.quote: the iodine solution, the liquid Lugol, which has been recommended as a precautionary measure for children and youth

sources.title: Potassium iodide
sources.quote: administered to 10.5 million children and 7 million adults in Poland as a preventative measure against accumulation of radioactive 131I in the thyroid gland

note: Contemporary FBIS translation of Polish government communiques (5 May 1986) says the Lugol dose was given as a single dose; a JPRS East Europe Report (2 Jul 1986) says distribution began the Wednesday (30 Apr). Earlier candidates considered and rejected: FDA's 1982 KI approval (a regulation, no administration); Three Mile Island 1979 (KI stockpiled, not given to the public); Vinca 1958 bone-marrow transplants and Ca-DTPA decorporation for plutonium (1958+) are treatments of established injury or contamination, not resisting damage; amifostine (1990s) later; cysteine/AET trials in radiotherapy in the 1950s were experimental. No earlier deployment of a radioprotective drug to a population found. Exact start date within 29-30 Apr not pinned, so month only.
searched: archive.org full-text for Poland Lugol / potassium iodide 1986-88 (FBIS, JPRS); Wikipedia Potassium iodide with its Nauman and Wolff citation (zenodo copy not readable); WebSearch for radioprotector history.

what: Reiniger, Gebbert & Schall offered lead-based protective aprons and gloves for X-ray workers.
fit: Garments with lead shielded the wearer's body from X-ray radiation, one of the lead-based shielding materials the definition names (not neutron or weapon shielding).

sources.quote: protective aprons and gloves, protective cases for the tube, leaded glasses, etc., 1905–1910

note: Dated the lead-based X-ray protection alternative: commercially sold lead protective aprons and gloves (Reiniger, Gebbert & Schall, 1905-1910; full suits in 1912). The catalog date range gives 1905 as the earliest year. Earlier: Rollins in 1901 only called for lead aprons and lead-glass goggles (a proposal); I did not find a dated earlier garment. Neutron-shielding hull linings (e.g. Nautilus reactor shielding, 1954) are later. Wikipedia's 1920 date for lead aprons is later than the Siemens museum evidence. Low confidence on the exact year. Medical lead aprons are worn routinely, but the definition's weapon-and-neutron use did not become ordinary, so no mass_adoption.

what: Ettore Bellini and Alessandro Tosi demonstrated their crossed fixed-loop radiogoniometer system, which found the direction of a sending station without moving the aerials, in 1907 field trials between Dieppe, Havre and Barfleur.
fit: A receiving system with two fixed crossed loops and a small search coil gives the bearing of the incoming signal, so it locates the transmitter by direction of arrival.

sources.publisher: J. A. Fleming, An Elementary Manual of Radiotelegraphy and Radiotelephony
sources.title: An Elementary Manual of Radiotelegraphy and Radiotelephony
sources.quote: This arrangement for locating the direction of a station is called a radiogoniometer by its inventors

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica 11th Edition Vol 23
sources.quote: In the other type, which was invented by Bellini and Tosi in 1907

note: Fleming (1908) describes the Dieppe-Havre-Barfleur trials and reproduces figures from Electrical Engineering of 14 November 1907, so the working system dates from 1907 and was reported within a year. Rejected as earlier: Hertz 1888 loop directionality (a laboratory observation, not a locating system); J. Stone Stone 1902 and de Forest 1904 rotating-loop patents (patents, no dated working bearing demonstration found); Marconi 1905-06 bent and horizontal directional aerials (directive transmitting/receiving antennas whose purpose was directed signalling, not a bearing-taking locator; a borderline case I could not date to a bearing demonstration); Braun and Telefunken 1905-06 directive arrays (same). Not a stretch to an earlier date: none of these shows a working finder giving a bearing on a sending station.
