note: The 1954 date is now confirmed by two contemporary reports (Broadcasting, 1 Feb 1954, says the demonstration was 'last week'; Science News Letter, 6 Feb 1954). Earlier candidates: Moseley 1913 radon beta charging (150 kV but about 0.01 nA, no device powered; Discovery 1956 calls it the first conscious attempt to extract power); Linder and Christian 1952 Sr-90 high-voltage electrostatic generator (365 kV, about 10^-9 A, no device powered); P. H. Miller's 1945 proposal and Lobanev and Beliakov's 1945 machine (about 10^-9 A, unknown). Arguable earlier case, not adopted: Philip Ohmart (Mound Laboratory, then the Ohmart Corp.) claimed to have found in June 1950 that a gas-gap cell of dissimilar electrodes gives a small continuous current under nuclear radiation (J. Appl. Phys. 22, 1504, Dec 1951, received 5 Sep 1951); Aviation Week of 24 Dec 1951 reported these 'atomic batteries' in production for gamma-measuring instruments. That is a radiation-driven cell whose current serves as an instrument signal rather than a power source for devices, and the 1950 date is only Ohmart's claim, so it was not taken; if the user counts it, the dates would be 1951-09 (demonstration) and 1951-12 (practical use). what: A Mr Squires of Soho revived a three-year-old girl, Sophie Greenhill, pronounced dead after falling from a window, by electric shocks through the chest (Royal Humane Society report).

sources.quote: A 3 year-old girl, Sophie Greenhill, was pronounced dead after a fall, but a Mr Squires

note: Case reported to the Royal Humane Society (founded 1774): a three-year-old pronounced dead after a fall from a window was given electric shocks through the chest and began to breathe. Historians dispute whether it was true cardiac revival or arousal from coma, and the account is retrospective, so confidence is low. Rejected as later or not revival of the dead: Beck's 1947 human defibrillation (a heart in fibrillation on the table), Gurvich 1939 and Negovsky 1930s animal resuscitation, Brukhonenko's 1920s dog experiments, Kouwenhoven CPR 1960. Wikipedia lists Prevost and Batelli 1899 defibrillation in dogs, which is later.
searched: Web search on Greenhill/Squires 1774; Wikipedia Defibrillation, Claude Beck, Brukhonenko; RCP and Cryonics Archive pages.

what: Discoverer 14 (CORONA KH-1, US Air Force/CIA) was launched 18 Aug 1960; its film capsule was ejected on 19 Aug and caught in mid-air by a C-119 near Hawaii, the first film recovered from an orbiting satellite.
fit: An Earth-orbiting satellite carrying a panoramic camera photographed the Soviet Union and returned the film, the function and mechanism of a surveillance satellite.

note: Confirmed. Earlier candidates: Discoverer 13 (1960-08-11) was recovered but carried no camera; earlier camera-carrying Discoverers (1959-60) failed to return film; Navy GRAB (1960-06) intercepted radar signals (not imaging); Midas 2 (1960-05) was an infrared missile-warning test; Korabl-Sputnik 1 (1960-05) was a Vostok test and did not return; TIROS-1 (1960-04) and Explorer 6 (1959-08) took civilian weather or crude cloud pictures. The NASA summary of the time hides the camera (cover story: 'recovery techniques'), so it dates the capsule recovery but not the photography; that comes from the later references, hence medium not high.

what: Walter Kaufmann measured the deflection of fast beta-ray electrons and found their charge-to-mass ratio fell as speed rose, showing mass increases with velocity.

searched: Crossref and archive.org (JOSA 1938-07 full text) for Ives-Stilwell; Wikipedia Ives-Stilwell, Time dilation, Tests of special relativity.

what: The Denver Mad Scientists Society ran the first Critter Crunch, a rules-governed fighting contest between remote- or cable-controlled robots, at the MileHiCon science fiction convention in Denver.
fit: Robots fought each other in a rules-governed competition run at a public convention, matching the sport as defined (human operators standing in for trainers).

sources.publisher: Robot Battles (history page, written by the Denver organizers' circle)
sources.title: A Brief History of Robot Battles
sources.quote: So, in 1987, Bill and his mad scientist cohorts developed a simple set of rules for cable and RC-controlled robots and launched the very first

sources.title: Pyro Technics 41
sources.quote: the rules for the "Critter Crunch," an un- usual competition at the last MileHiCon.

note: Considered: First Robot Olympics, Glasgow 1990 (peacetime contest, later and not combat); Robot Battles, Atlanta 1991 (later); Robot Wars, San Francisco 1994 (later, the famous one); Japanese robot sumo and robot contests of the late 1980s (not found earlier, and not fighting under trainers' control); the 1964 Rock'em Sock'em Robots toy (human-operated toy, not a competitive sport). Critter Crunch rules (rules-governed fights between remote- or cable-controlled vehicles, last one still moving on the table wins) fit the definition acceptably though the 'reflexes tuned by trainers' part is loose (human operators). Date: the organizers' own history gives 1987. Contemporary evidence only reaches back to 1988: Pyro Technics 41 (April 1989) reports the rules from Con News for the competition 'at the last MileHiCon' and says its editors 'missed the 1988 competition', so the event existed by late 1988; Pyro Technics 47 (1991) calls the 1990 event the '2nd annual' and Wikipedia's Critter Crunch article says first event 1989, which conflict. 1987 rests on the organizers' retrospective account; 1988 is the contemporary-attested bound.
searched: Wikipedia Robot combat and Critter Crunch articles; robotbattles.com history (Wayback); archive.org full-text for 'Critter Crunch' 1986-1995 (Pyro Technics 41, 42, 47 found); archive.org searches for robot fighting contests 1975-1987 and robot sumo 1988-91 (nothing earlier and fitting); Wikipedia citations list for Robot combat.

what: The 'Electric Dog' designed by John Hays Hammond Jr. and built by Benjamin Miessner and Joseph Broich in 1912: a three-wheeled box with selenium-cell 'eyes' that followed its master's lantern, turning as he turned.
fit: A self-propelled machine that reacts on its own to a stimulus and behaves like a dog following its master, an animal imitation by reflex mechanism rather than a clockwork routine.

sources.title: John Hammond and his electric dog (Cleveland Moffett)
sources.quote: If you walk before him carrying a lantern, he will follow you, turning to the right or left as you turn

sources.title: Electric Dog - 1912
sources.quote: designed in 1912 and constructed in the USA by researchers John Hammond, Jr. and Benjamin Miessner

note: Replaces Grey Walter's 1948 tortoises with the earlier Electric Dog. The year rests on Miessner's own later account (his 1964 recollection, quoted at cyberneticzoo) and the Hammond patent filing of April-June 1912; the contemporary McClure's report of March 1914 shows it working and is within about two years of a 1912 build, but gives no year of construction. Miessner's own article on it is Scientific American Supplement 14 June 1919 (reference, too late to count as contemporary). Candidates considered: Walter's Elmer and Elsie 1948-49 (later, kept as a fallback only); clockwork automata such as Vaucanson's duck (1739), Tipu's Tiger and the medieval animal automata, rejected because they replay a fixed mechanism and do not sense or respond (the definition's robot dog, cat and insect examples are reactive machines), and Vaucanson's digestion was faked; Tesla's 1898 teleautomaton boat (not an animal); Theseus the maze mouse (Shannon, 1950, later).
searched: cyberneticzoo (both Electric Dog pages), davidbuckley.net, Wikipedia Robotic pet and Grey Walter; archive.org full-text 1912-14 (found McClure's March 1914, The World's Advance 1914) and 1915-19 (Scientific American Supplement 1919, Radiodynamics 1916); WebSearch (worked). what: Volvo's Kalmar car plant (Sweden) opened and began production with a fleet of about 250 computer-guided battery carriers run from the factory's central computer.
fit: Volvo's Kalmar plant (inaugurated June 1974) moved bodies and engines on about 250 battery-powered carriers that were computer-guided and, per a 1975 book, could be controlled from one central data computer, the plant's 'heart and brain'; the carriers are driverless mobile robots in all but name.

sources.title: Architecture Plus, November 12, 1974
sources.quote: battery-powered and computer-guided, that creep silently about the factory bearing body assemblies

sources.title: Volvo
sources.quote: carriers at Kalmar can be controlled from a central data computer which is the heart and brain of the factory

sources.publisher: Associated Press (Washington Court House Record Herald)
sources.title: Volvo workers enjoy challenge
sources.quote: It is connected to the factory computer system, but can also can be operated by the workers via a switch panel.

note: Same event for both kinds, since the plant opened already in production (AP, 1974-06-08: 'inaugurated this week'). Confirmed with a third contemporary source (AP) tying the carriers to the factory computer. Rejected: 1950s Barrett wire-guided driverless tractors (guided by a wire loop, no computer directing a population); Tetra Pak Lund 1976 and Kiva 2006/2007 (later); Computer Integrated Manufacturing (1974) mention of dispatching trucks from a central computer (lending book, unreadable, and no earlier proof); industrial-robot lines (Unimate, 1961 and GM Lordstown 1971) were individually controlled, not directed by one computer. Fit remains partial: the carriers are AGVs rather than humanoid robots, but they are autonomous computer-run machines directed as a fleet, which matches the definition's function and mechanism. Earliest found, not proven earliest; confidence medium.

what: Luna 1 (USSR), launched 2 Jan 1959, passed the Moon and became the first spacecraft to leave Earth's orbit into solar orbit, returning scientific data by radio on the way.
fit: An uncrewed robot spacecraft explored interplanetary space beyond Earth orbit and reported measurements back, the minimum for a space probe.

sources.quote: the Soviet Moon rocket will become a satellite of the Sun, the first artificial planet

sources.title: Luna 1
sources.quote: was the first spacecraft to reach the vicinity of Earth's Moon, the first spacecraft to leave Earth's orbit

note: Contemporary report (TASS of 3 Jan 1959, reprinted in US hearings) agrees with the Wikipedia reference. sources.quote: perfume was wafted into the auditorium synchro- nized with scenes

sources.quote: Vogue Theatre in Detroit, Michigan in 1940 with Boom Town and The Sea Hawk

note: Replaced Scentovision/Mein Traum (1940-10-10) and AromaRama (1959-12-09). The Mein Traum screening rests only on Wikipedia citing a 1993 Guinness book; Variety of 1940-09-11 reports Laube and Barth arriving in New York with scent reels and says the first showing 'would probably be given' at the Swiss Pavilion, so no contemporary source confirms a screening, and Science Digest 1958-03 says Scentovision 'first appeared on the scene two years ago' (c.1956). The Aromatix Co. of Detroit's 'Dramatic Zephyrs' gave public, paid theater audiences perfume synchronized with scenes at the Vogue (first tryout reported 1940-11-12, a full week of Boom Town by 1940-11-26): a working, scene-synchronized system used in a real theater. It is also the first contemporary-documented event, so it is the date for both kinds. Rejected as loose or manual theater stunts with no scene-keyed system and no contemporary source found: 1906 Rothafel rose-oil fan (1958 trade-paper claim), 1916 Rivoli scent equipment for 'Story of the Flowers' (only a 1940 Variety reminiscence by a manager, so not contemporary), 1929 Lilac Time perfume in the ventilation, 1933 Rialto smell system, 1868 London spray. AromaRama (1959) and Smell-O-Vision (1960) are later. Sources by Wikipedia's 'Mein Traum' date could still make Oct 1940 correct; a one-month gap, so the choice matters little.
searched: archive.org full text 1916-1941 for Scentovision, Laube, Rivoli Story of the Flowers, Lilac Time Fenway, Rialto Mayer odors (nothing contemporary for the pre-1940 stunts); Variety 1940-09, 1940-11-13, 1940-11-27; International Projectionist 1940; Wikipedia Smell-O-Vision and its citations. Candidates considered: the ice-age fall of world sea level (about 120 m at the last glacial maximum), which exposed continental shelves; the idea dates from Charles Maclaren in 1842 as a proposal, and I found no dated demonstration that strictly fits, so it is not used. Earlier hypotheses of Mediterranean desiccation from seismic salt layers (1960s) were proposals before the cores, rejected as not demonstrations.

Earlier candidates: Vernam's teleprinter cipher (1917-19) later; Wheatstone/Playfair 1854 telegraph cipher was a proposal, not shown in use; pre-war commercial telegraph code books were abbreviation codes for cost, not found as secrecy links; ancient devices (scytale, Caesar and the Great Cipher of Louis XIV) are message ciphers on couriers, not a scrambled communication link in the technology sense. Plum (1882) calls Stager's cipher 'doubtless the first telegraph cipher used for war purposes'. The Principia (1862) shows ciphered telegrams in wartime use and being intercepted a year later, corroborating practice but not the 1861 event itself, so confidence is medium. Same event serves as demonstration and practical use. Spring 1861 given as the year only.

what: Edward Jenner took cowpox matter from the sore on dairymaid Sarah Nelmes's hand and inserted it into the arm of eight-year-old James Phipps, who then resisted variolous matter (1 July 1796); published in Jenner's Inquiry (1798).
fit: Protection was passed from one person to another by injecting body material from a person carrying a harmless contagion (cowpox), as the definition's 'injection of body material' clause says; Phipps's lesion was then used to pass it on (arm-to-arm chains).

sources.publisher: Edward Jenner, An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae (London)

sources.quote: The matter was taken from a fore on the hand of a dairymaid

sources.quote: On 14 May 1796, he tested his hypothesis by inoculating James Phipps, the eight-year-old son of Jenner's gardener.

note: Replaces the 2000 Barcena myxoma-vector rabbit work, which is the narrow 'self-spreading by contact' case but not the whole definition, which also covers a person passing protection or cure by injection of body material. Candidates: (1) Barcena 2000, a genuine self-spreading vaccine and the first designed one (kept as the strict self-spreading reading, not the milestone, because the definition's injection-of-body-material route is met 200 years earlier); (2) variolation (Chinese, Indian, Ottoman/Boston 1721): material from a smallpox case, a dangerous not harmless contagion, so rejected; (3) Benjamin Jesty 1774 and Plett 1791: cowpox taken from cows, not from a person, rejected; (4) convalescent serum 1890s-1920s: later; (5) oral polio vaccine spread to contacts (1960s): incidental. Jenner 1796 is the first documented person-to-person transfer of a harmless contagion that protected the recipient. The 1798 book is just over two years after the event, so it is marked reference. A loose-fit risk remains: a strict reader may want the self-spreading reading only (2000).

what: SLAC-MIT deep inelastic electron-proton scattering experiments at Stanford (results 1968, published October 1969) showed the proton contains point-like constituents, later identified as quarks.
fit: First measurement showing the proton has smaller sub-particles, the definition's second alternative.

sources.publisher: Proceedings of the Boulder Conference on High Energy Physics (1969 meeting)
sources.title: Proceedings of the Boulder Conference on High Energy Physics
sources.quote: the electron as scattering incoherently from pointlike constituents within the proton

sources.title: Quark
sources.quote: there was little evidence for their physical existence until deep inelastic scattering experiments at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center in 1968

note: Same event as given. The earlier source quote (a paper title) did not support the claim and was replaced by a 1969-70 conference report on pointlike constituents. Candidates rejected: Prout 1815 (hypothesis only, later contradicted by isotopes), Thomson 1897 electron (a universal constituent of atoms, but atoms also have nuclei, so not one primitive substance), Rutherford 1917-19 proton knock-out (nuclei also hold neutrons, Chadwick 1932), Hofstadter 1950s proton form factors (extended charge, not shown to have sub-particles), Gell-Mann/Zweig quark proposals 1964 (theory). Quarks as real particles were only widely accepted after 1973-74.
searched: Wikipedia Quark, Deep inelastic scattering; Semantic Scholar and Crossref records for the 1969 PRL paper (title only); archive.org full-text search for pointlike constituents 1968-1970, finding the Boulder proceedings; High Energy Collisions 1969 proceedings (not used).

what: Lerner and Fitzpatrick (JAMA, 13 June 1953) reported that 20 percent monobenzyl ether of hydroquinone (Benoquin) ointment left two Black vitiligo patients completely depigmented except hair and eyes.
fit: A topical drug that permanently destroys pigment, here turning dark skin pale, is a drug that permanently changes skin pigmentation between racial appearances.

sources.title: Treatment of melanin hyperpigmentation (JAMA 1953-06-13, vol 152 iss 7)
sources.quote: used these preparations on a single arm for long periods of time and became completely depigmented, except for the hair and eyes

sources.title: Monobenzone
sources.quote: Monobenzone may cause destruction of melanocytes and permanent depigmentation.

note: Earlier candidates: (a) 1939-40 occupational leukoderma from rubber gloves (Oliver, Schwartz, Warren, Arch Dermatol Dec 1940): accidental, not a treatment; (b) Sulzberger and Schwarzschild's c.1940 deliberate patch tests on mostly Black volunteers in a city institution: reported in 1949 discussion as irregular, some got depigmentation, some dermatitis, they concluded it could not be used reliably (Arch Dermatol Nov 1951), so not a working demonstration; (c) 1949 chloasma trials of 2-5 percent MBEH (Pollock, Fisher; Bronx Dermatological Society Oct-Nov 1949): lightening of hyperpigmentation, not permanent change of skin color, and often failed; (d) hydroquinone creams: lighten only. The 1953 paper also cites 'personal communication' cases (Stolar, Schwartz) of total depigmentation, undated, which may predate June 1953.
searched: archive.org full text 1939-1960 for monobenzyl ether of hydroquinone and agerite alba; read JAMA 1953-06-13 (two items), Arch Dermatol Dec 1940 and Nov 1951 (Bronx society transactions), Arch Dermatol 1954-11 discussion. Contemporary source found: the JAMA paper itself, quote checked.

what: Benoquin ointment was in clinical use by dermatologists; by June 1953 it had been used to depigment 84 patients with hyperpigmentation, and total depigmentation of Black vitiligo patients was reported.
fit: Applied to real patients to remove pigment, with complete permanent depigmentation in vitiligo, matching a drug that changes skin pigmentation.

sources.title: Treatment of melanin hyperpigmentation (JAMA 1953-06-13, vol 152 iss 7)
sources.quote: used these preparations on a single arm for long periods of time and became completely depigmented, except for the hair and eyes

sources.title: Monobenzone
sources.quote: Monobenzone may cause destruction of melanocytes and permanent depigmentation.

note: Same report as the demonstration. The paper says some dermatologists had used crude MBEH ointment therapeutically for years ('occasional reports'), so use may predate 1953; those uses were for hyperpigmentation (chloasma, freckles), irregular and not racial recoloring. Mass adoption never occurred.
searched: As for the demonstration.

what: NASA's unmanned Apollo 4 command module re-entered at lunar-return speed, skipped back up to about 241,600 ft and made a second entry, steered by lifting-entry guidance.
fit: The returning spacecraft shed speed by skipping out of the upper atmosphere and re-entering a second time, as the definition describes.

sources.publisher: NASA Langley (Entry aerodynamics at lunar return conditions obtained from the flight of Apollo 4)
sources.title: Entry Aerodynamics At Lunar Return Conditions Obtained From The Flight Of Apollo 4 (AS-501)
sources.quote: at a time near the maximum skip altitude of 241 602 feet, the FINAL ENTRY pase was entered.

sources.title: Apollo 6 Mission Report
sources.quote: did not skip out to as great an altitude to allow an ablator cool-down phase

note: Replaced Zond 6 (1968-11-17) with Apollo 4 (unmanned, launched 1967-11-09): its command module entered at simulated lunar-return speed (about 11,168 m/s), pulled out, skipped up to about 241,600 ft (a first entry, a coast out, then a 'second entry') and re-entered, steered by the Apollo UPCONTROL guidance; the NASA flight report calls this the skip and second entry and the Apollo 6 report compares its own shorter skip with Apollo 4's skip out and blackout periods. That is a working skip entry a year before Zond 6, and the Apollo skip was lift-guided rather than a bounce, as was Zond 6's. Rejected earlier: AS-202 (1966-08) and Gemini lifting entries (no skip out found); Zond 4 (1968-03, planned skip but destroyed after failed orientation); Zond 5 (1968-09, ballistic). Apollo 4's purpose was heat-shield test at lunar-return conditions and skip also served range control, so the fit is looser than a pure speed-shedding bounce; Zond 6 (1968-11-17, AP: 'double dip') is the next dated case and fits equally. No practical use added: Apollo 11 (1969-07) flew the skip-up control routine (P65) on a crewed return to extend range, and Zond 7 landed safely in 1969-08, but both are later and the skip was for range or g-load control on test or mission returns; I could not find Apollo 8 evidence.
searched: Wikipedia Zond 4, 6, 7, 8, Apollo 4, Atmospheric entry; archive.org full-text for Apollo 4/6/8/10/11 mission reports and NASA entry reports 1967-1970, and 1968 newspapers on Zond 6 (AP 'double dip'); NTRS search (unhelpful).

sources.title: Vasari Corridor

what: Stephane Leduc of Nantes produced electric sleep with interrupted low-voltage current through head electrodes, first in rabbits and dogs and then on himself (1902; published 1903).
fit: An apparatus passing a pulsed current through the head puts the subject into a sleep-like, dream-like state and the subject wakes refreshed, so it matches an apparatus that induces sleep.

sources.title: Harper's Weekly 1904-02-13: Vol 48 Iss 2460
sources.quote: The patient is said to awaken instantaneously from the electric sleep and to experience a feeling of refreshment.

sources.title: Electronarcosis: a New Treatment of Schizophrenia (Paterson and Lippert)
sources.quote: In 1902 a French physician called Leduc produced a narcotic-like state in rabbits and dogs by applying a unidirectional pulse current

note: Kept Leduc 1902 (self-test the same year, published 1903). Earlier candidates considered: 1870s static-electricity ('Franklinic') baths for nervous disorders (Arthur 1874) mention sleep only as a side benefit of treating neuralgia and stomach disease, not as a sleep apparatus, rejected; chloral hydrate and bromides are drugs, not apparatus; Mesmer-era devices and hypnosis are not apparatus that induces sleep; ether and chloroform anesthesia (1840s) is unconsciousness for surgery, not restful sleep. Weak spots: Leduc's state is closer to electro-anesthesia than restful sleep, but contemporaries called it 'electric sleep' and described the sleeper waking refreshed. Sleep sprays or gases were not found.
searched: archive.org full text for Leduc electric sleep 1902-1905 (Journal of Advanced Therapeutics 1902, Harper's Weekly 1904, Lancet-Clinic 1904, Progressive Medicine 1904); static electricity and electric bath insomnia 1870-1895; Wikipedia Electrosleep page not found.

what: Tietz and colleagues in the US treated 47 schizophrenic patients with electronarcosis, an electric-current sleep produced by a head-electrode machine (1945-46); British trials (Paterson, 1947) followed, and by 1948 'prolonged electric sleep' was in use for mental patients in the US, Canada and Britain.
fit: Patients were put to sleep with an electric apparatus as a treatment to calm mental disturbance, the clinical use of the device that Leduc demonstrated.

sources.title: The American Journal of Psychiatry 1948-07: Vol 105 Iss 1
Electronarcosis: a New Treatment of Schizophrenia (Paterson and Lippert)
sources.quote: Owing to the simplicity and relative safety of electro- narcosis, it may possibly take the place of insulin-coma

sources.title: Coronet 1948-03: Vol 23
sources.quote: Under this method the patient suffering from mental difficulties is put to sleep and kept asleep

note: Replaces the 1948 date with 1946, the earlier clinical series that a 1948 journal states. Earlier candidates: Leduc 1902-1907 and Tuffier's 1907 surgical electro-anesthesia (experimental or surgical anesthesia, not sleep for calming); static electricity baths of the 1870s (no sleep device). Soviet electrosleep for neuroses (Gilyarovsky, Livenstev, 1948-49) is a better fit for 'soothes nerves' but could not be dated earlier than 1948 from sources reached. Electronarcosis was a strong current producing unconsciousness and sometimes convulsion, so the fit to 'restful sleep' is loose; the quoted AJP line gives the date, and the 1948 review describes the series as 47 patients. Electrosleep stayed a niche therapy.
searched: archive.org full text for electronarcosis and electric sleep 1946-1955 (Lancet 1947, AJP 1948, Belmont Hospital report 1949, Coronet 1948); Soviet electrosleep 1950-1962 (only abstracts and copyright entries found, none earlier than 1948).

what: Zust et al. (University of Bern) played recorded pseudoword/German word pairs to young adults in slow-wave sleep and found they had formed and kept new word associations that showed up on an implicit test after waking.
fit: Recorded vocabulary was played to sleeping people and they retained new verbal associations from it, so teaching by recorded sound during sleep worked, though only for implicit word-pair associations and not for general lessons.

sources.title: Implicit Vocabulary Learning during Sleep Is Bound to Slow-Wave Peaks
sources.quote: While in slow-wave sleep during a nap, a series of word pairs comprising pseudowords, e.g., "tofer," and actual German words, e.g., "Haus" (house), were played

note: Second pass gave nothing. This is the earliest strictly fitting result I found. Rejected: Saliger's Psycho-Phone (1927, patented 1932, sold as a sleep-teaching phonograph) and 1950s-60s commercial sleep-learning records, because there was no evidence they worked (the Wikipedia history says Emmons and Simon's 1956 EEG studies found material presented during sleep was not recalled and called it 'impractical and probably impossible'); Arzi et al. 2012 (Nature Neuroscience, 'Humans can learn new information during sleep') showed learning of tone-odour associations in sleep, which is conditioning rather than teaching with lessons, so earlier but a loose analogue; Schreiner and Rasch 2015 only cued words learned while awake. Hypnosis tapes: no controlled evidence found. The abstract itself says earlier evidence 'is inconclusive'. Hence low confidence.
searched: Wikipedia Sleep learning; Crossref for Zust 2019, Arzi 2012, Emmons/Simon 1955-56; Semantic Scholar abstract for Zust 2019 (Arzi abstract not returned); no archive.org full-text search made for 1950s sleep-learning newspapers.
check_note: checker proposed 1942-07 (Lawrence LeShan (College of William and Mary) played a phonograph record of 'My finger nails taste terribly bitter' to 2); rejected in review: The checker's replacement, LeShan's 1942 nail-biting study, played a suggestion rather than a lesson, did not establish that the boys were asleep, and was not borne out once sleep was measured (Emmons and Simon 1956, cited in the checker's own note), so it does not show that teaching during sleep works. The 2019 milestone stays.
tier2_overruled: replaced 1942-07: The pilot's review (pilot/computing/report3.md §3.2) rejected LeShan's 1942 nail-biting study: a suggestion, not a lesson; sleep was not established; later studies that measured sleep found no learning. Tier 2 was not given that review.

what: The U.S. Army fired a Davy Crockett M388 round with a W54 nuclear warhead from a 155 mm recoilless gun 1.7 miles in the Little Feller I shot at the Nevada Test Site (the warhead alone was tested 1962-07-07 in Little Feller II).
fit: A nuclear warhead small enough for an infantry crew was launched from a recoilless smoothbore gun and detonated, the definition's recoilless-rifle case.

sources.title: Palm Springs Desert Sun 1962-07-18
sources.quote: is the smallest atomic weapon known. It is designed to be carried by three men or on a Jeep

sources.title: W54
sources.quote: In Little Feller I (17 July), the warhead was launched as a Davy Crockett device from a stationary 155-millimeter launcher

sources.title: Davy Crockett (nuclear device)
sources.quote: actual firing of the Davy Crockett from a distance of 1.7 miles (2.7 km) in the Little Feller I test shot on July 17, 1962

note: Confirmed. The 17 July 1962 Little Feller I shot at the Nevada Test Site (a Tuesday, with Attorney General Robert Kennedy watching and 901 troops taking part, per UPI of 1962-07-18) is the first detonation of a nuclear round fired from an infantry launcher. Earlier candidates rejected: Little Feller II (1962-07-07), the warhead alone on a stand, which does not show the delivery system; the 280 mm atomic cannon Grable shot (1953-05-25), artillery not infantry; Gnat and Scarab (1950s) were device designs and primaries, not weapons; the SADM backpack demolition munition (B54) went into production 1964, later. Earlier non-nuclear Davy Crockett firings of the M388 round (1950s-1961 at Fort Greeley, Yuma) did not detonate a nuclear charge. No earlier infantry-fired nuclear detonation was found. The UPI report is hedged ('possibly involving' the Davy Crockett), so the Wikipedia pages carry the firing detail.
searched: Wikipedia Davy Crockett (nuclear device) and W54; archive.org full-text search 1961-1962 for Davy Crockett atomic (Palm Springs Desert Sun 1962-07-18 found and read; Illustrated Guide to U.S. Missiles and Rockets 1962 also hits but not read); no earlier infantry-fired nuclear test found.

what: Polaroid variable density windows (two polarizing discs, the inner one turned by the passenger) were fitted in the observation lounge car Copper King of the Union Pacific streamliner City of Los Angeles; announced in August 1938 and reported in service by 30 December 1938.
fit: A window whose light transmission the passenger changes on command by turning a polarizer, from clear to fully dark, matching windows that change opacity or filter mechanically on command.

sources.title: Science 1938-12-30, Vol 88 Iss 2296
sources.quote: can now control the brightness of light coming through the window by turning a knob

sources.title: Commercialization of the polarizer (Polaroid history)
sources.quote: could adjust the amount of light coming in by rotating the inner window pane

note: Replaces the 1964 Corning photochromic glass, which is a later and looser fit (first sold as eyeglass lenses). Candidates considered: Land's 1930s polarizer light-valve and variable-density window patents (patents; the ones I could date were filed 1940-41), Polaroid Variable Day Glass eyewear (1940, later), electrochromic tungsten oxide films (Platt 1961 observation, Deb 1969, later), liquid crystal and SPD panels (later working devices), and Corning photochromic glass (1964, later). No dated working window earlier than the 1938 railcar found; Land demonstrated rotating polarizer discs in 1936 but not as a window. The Corning 1964 glass remains the first automatic light-responsive glass if only that mechanism counts.
searched: archive.org full text (Science 1938, Railway Age Aug 1938, Franklin Institute 1940), Harvard Business School Polaroid history, Google Patents US2260220, WebSearch (worked), Wikipedia Smart glass, Photochromic lens and Electrochromism.

what: U.S. Army ordnance captain Alfred Mordecai tested Schonbein's gun-cotton as a charge in a musket and reported that its combustion is unattended with smoke.

what: The US National Bureau of Standards (radio propagation work that became the Interservice Radio Propagation Laboratory) began broadcasting short-wave radio disturbance forecasts over its standard-frequency station, replacing earlier radio disturbance warning notices.
fit: An instrument-based government service forecast and warned of ionospheric and radio disturbances caused by solar outbreaks and geomagnetic storms, in regular operational use.

sources.title: American Scientist 1942 (NBS notice)
sources.quote: Standards will broadcast new short-wave radio disturbance forecasts via the NBS standard frequency

sources.publisher: Interservice Radio Propagation Laboratory, National Bureau of Standards
sources.title: IRPL Radio Propagation Handbook, Part I
sources.quote: Regular warnings or forecasts of radio disturbances.

sources.title: Early History of Space Weather Forecasting
sources.quote: it was not until World War II that routine forecasts of the ionosphere related to radio propagation were made.

note: Replaced the 1965 date. Earlier candidates: (1) URSIgram radio-cosmic bulletins broadcast from the Eiffel Tower from 1928-12-01 and from Arlington from 1930 (data reports of solar, magnetic and auroral conditions, not forecasts or warnings, so rejected); (2) Giovanelli's 1939 flare-probability formula and Ellis's 1879 note on sunspot cycles (scientific methods, not an instrument-based forecast or warning service); (3) the 1942 NBS service: a notice in American Scientist (1942) says the Bureau will broadcast new short-wave radio disturbance forecasts on its standard frequency and that this replaces earlier radio disturbance warning notices, so some warning notices pre-date 1942 but I could not find a dated source for them; (4) the Interservice Radio Propagation Laboratory (founded 1942) listed regular warnings or forecasts of radio disturbances as a regular service in its 1943 handbook, and the NBS Technical News Bulletin of April 1946 shows these warnings issued for a solar outbreak and great geomagnetic storm of 1946-02-07 (Warnings of the radio-transmission conditions expected because of this solar outbreak were issued by the Interservice Radio Propagation Laboratory); (5) the Australian Ionospheric Prediction Service (late 1947), later. 1942 is the earliest dated warning/forecast service I could source; the 1965 Boulder service is a later daily public forecast. The disturbance forecasts were radio-propagation oriented, so the fit to solar storms and magnetic storms is partial but the warnings were explicitly tied to solar outbreaks and geomagnetic storms.
searched: WebSearch (worked); archive.org full-text for ionospheric storm warnings 1930-1950 (American Scientist 1942, IRPL handbook 1943, Ionospheric Data 1944-46, NBS Technical News Bulletin 1946-04, Circular 462 found); read spaceacademy.net.au history and HGSS ASFC history, Hildner NOAA talk; searches for pre-1942 NBS 'radio disturbance warning' notices found nothing dated.

what: ATS-5 (launched 1969-08-12) at synchronous orbit charged to several thousand volts negative on entering Earth's shadow, measured by the UCSD plasma detector (DeForest); up to 12,000 V was seen later.
fit: A spacecraft built up a large electric charge in space (kilovolts, far above the tens of volts seen before), the charging that later explained discharge anomalies on other satellites.

sources.publisher: NASA Technical Reports Server (ATS bibliography, quoting DeForest's 1970 AGU abstract)
sources.title: Applications technology satellites: A continuing bibliography with indexes
sources.quote: The Applications Technology Satellite (ATS-5) charges to several thousand volts negative when the satellite passes into the earth's shadow

sources.title: Final Technical Report for the 3 DLE Instrument on ATS-5
sources.quote: The whole spacecraft charges up to thousands of volts (12,000 maximum to date) at certain times of the year

sources.title: Photon and particle interactions with surfaces in space (6th ESLAB Symposium, 1972)
sources.quote: ATS-5 was launched into synchronous orbit on August 12, 1969

note: Kept 1969. The abstract naming the kilovolt charging (DeForest, 1970 AGU meeting, reprinted in a 1972 NASA bibliography) puts the first observation in ATS-5's first eclipse seasons after its 1969-08 launch; a flux plot in the ESLAB volume is labeled 10/16/69, but I could not tie the first charging event to a day. Earlier candidates rejected: Johnson and Meadows 1955 rocket potential of about -20 V, Sagalyn 1963 satellite potentials of -0.4 to -1.7 V, Whipple 1961-65 theory (tens of volts at most, no discharges: Garrett's 1985 Handbook of Geophysics chapter 7); Echo-series and Aerobee rocket electron-beam flights of 1969-72 (tens of volts, deliberate and beam-driven); ion-engine tests SERT I (1964) and SERT II (1970), whose thrusters expel charge but do not charge the craft as a propulsion means; later DSCS anomalies (1973) and SCATHA (1979) come after. Nothing within two years of the event could be fetched, so no source is marked contemporary.
searched: Garrett Handbook of Geophysics chapter 7 (NOAA NGDC PDF); NASA NTRS report 1973 and the 1972 ATS bibliography via archive.org; archive.org full text 'spacecraft charging' 1969-1972; NTRS search; Semantic Scholar/Crossref for DeForest 1971 and 1972 (titles only); WebSearch worked. JGR and AGU pages not fetched.

what: Apollo 9: two astronauts left the command module in the lunar module Spider, flew it separately in Earth orbit, then rendezvoused and redocked.
fit: A small crewed craft carried by the larger spacecraft was used by the crew to leave it and return, the mechanism of a detachable lander.

sources.title: Astronautics and aeronautics, 1969
sources.quote: McDivitt and Sehweiekart reentered lm on fifth day to perform CSM-lm rendezvous.

sources.title: Apollo 9
sources.quote: Spider was released. After spending about 45 minutes near Gumdrop

note: Replaced. The definition is 'a small craft carried by a larger ship that the crew can use to leave it in an emergency or for landing' (aliases include detachable lander), so the lunar module, carried by the Apollo CSM and used by two crewmen to leave it, fits. The earlier researcher's Apollo 13 (1970-04, LM Aquarius used as lifeboat) fits only the emergency branch and is later than events that fit the landing branch; kept as a later candidate. Demonstration: Apollo 9, March 1969, first crewed flight of the LM: McDivitt and Schweickart left the CSM in LM Spider, flew it apart and rendezvoused and redocked (fifth day, 7 March per the usual accounts; the chronology gives only March 3-13), so month precision. Rejected earlier: Gemini and Vostok ejection seats (a seat, not a carried craft); Apollo 5 (uncrewed LM, January 1968); Soviet LK never flew crewed; aircraft escape capsules (not spacecraft). Apollo 10 (1969-05) LM descent to about 15 km is a closer rehearsal but later than Apollo 9. Strictness: Apollo 9 did not land or escape, so this is a loose demonstration of the craft; medium confidence.
searched: NTRS Astronautics and Aeronautics 1969 chronology (Apollo 9 and Apollo 11 entries, quotes checked); Wikipedia Apollo 9, Apollo 11 and Apollo Lunar Module; earlier NTRS Apollo 13 lifeboat source reviewed from the prior pass. Searched archive.org for Spider/Gumdrop reports; no better full-text hit.

what: Gemini III (Grissom and Young) flew with the IBM Gemini onboard digital computer, which fed navigation and reentry bank guidance to the crew.
fit: An onboard digital computer navigated the spacecraft and computed reentry steering, with the crew closing the loop.

sources.title: Gemini Midprogram Conference Including Experiment Results
sources.quote: Gemini III was planned and flown so that a fixed-bank angle

sources.title: Gemini Titan 3 Press Kit
sources.quote: insert landing area parameters in the spacecraft computer, retrofire, and descend to a planned recovery area

sources.title: Gemini Guidance Computer
sources.quote: Project Gemini was the first with an on-board computer, as Project Mercury was controlled by computers on Earth.

note: Kept Gemini III (1965-03-23), the first crewed flight with the IBM Gemini onboard digital computer (computer operated 4.7 hours per the NASA Midprogram Conference table). Gemini II (1965-01-19, unmanned, 0.2 hours of computer time) had an unguided ballistic reentry, so it did not steer. On Gemini III a fixed bank angle was held; its lift shortfall meant the guidance did not fully steer to the target. Gemini 4's computer reentry was lost to a memory problem. Earlier candidates rejected: Mercury (ground IBM computers), Vostok (analog Globus), Atlas/Titan/Thor launch-vehicle guidance (steers rockets, mostly ground-based), submarine inertial navigators (analog, no burns); Soviet Voskhod/Soyuz systems and unmanned probe sequencers (Ranger, Mariner) not checked in depth.

what: On Gemini 6A (Schirra and Stafford) the onboard computer was put in charge of the burns and navigation for the first crewed rendezvous, with Gemini 7, on 15 December 1965.
fit: The computer calculated the orbit-changing burns and guided the spacecraft through them to reach another spacecraft, the guidance computer's real purpose, not a test of the hardware.

sources.title: Gemini 6A
sources.quote: Schirra put Gemini 6A's computer in charge of the rendezvous.

sources.title: Gemini Midprogram Conference Including Experiment Results
sources.quote: the iner- tial guidance system was utilized for attitude control and reference, for precise translation control, and for navigation and guidance in closed-loop rendezvous

note: Replaced the earlier same-day Gemini III date. Gemini III was a short test flight whose reentry guidance fell short because of lower lift than planned, and Gemini IV's computer reentry was lost to a memory fault; Gemini V (August 1965) flew the computer for 16 hours but reentry landed off target. Gemini 6A is the first flight in which the computer's core task, calculating and steering burns to a destination, was done for the mission's objective. Rejected: Gemini III, IV, V as tests or partial use.
searched: Same as the demonstration; Wikipedia Gemini 6A for the computer's role in the rendezvous, Midprogram Conference text on closed-loop rendezvous.

note: Confirmed Apollo 8 (1968-12-21 to 27), now at medium-high with a contemporary source: Lovell made over 200 sextant sightings on the way to the Moon and the on-board state vector was kept only by these measurements for long periods (ground values were loaded before each burn). Candidates rejected: Gemini XII (1966-11), where Aldrin used a hand-held sextant for rendezvous after the radar failed and NASA's 1966 report calls it still an experiment confirming 'potential' of the sextant; Apollo 7 (1968-10, orbital determination by sextant, but an Earth-orbit development flight); Gemini X (sextant unusable). Apollo 8 is the first operational star-sighting navigation toward another world.

what: After the big proton solar flare of 29 Sept 1989 and three more by 24 Oct, Mir's radiation-safety service had cosmonauts Viktorenko and Serebrov stay in the most protected zone of the station's working section while crossing high-radiation orbit sections, cutting their flare dose two- or three-fold (TASS, 26 Oct 1989).
fit: A crew used the best-shielded part of their spacecraft as a shelter from solar flare radiation, the shelter function and shielding mechanism of the definition, and it measurably lowered the dose.

sources.title: Countermeasures Against Solar Flare Radiation (TASS, 26 Oct 89)
sources.quote: the cosmonauts were to stay in the most protected zone of the Mir working section when crossing orbit sections with enhanced radi¬ ation.

sources.publisher: JPRS Report, Science and Technology, USSR: Space (TASS, 26 Oct 1989)
sources.title: Countermeasures Against Solar Flare Radiation (TASS, 26 Oct 89)
sources.quote: its recommendations enabled the cosmonauts to lower the radiation impact of the flares by two- or three-fold

fit: Ground controllers sent radio commands that directed the spacecraft's operations and received its transmissions and pictures during the flight.

sources.title: Spaceflight 1960-07
sources.quote: Two-way communication was maintained with Lunik III’s instrument container throughout the flight, and the Earth operator had remarkable control over the vehicle’s operation.

sources.title: Luna 3
sources.quote: Commands from the Earth were then given to move the film into a flying-spot scanner

note: Kept Luna 3. Earlier candidates rejected: Sputnik 1 (1957-10) and Explorer 1 (1958-01) only transmitted tracking/telemetry that ground stations received, with no commands to guide them; Sputnik 2 and 3 (1957-58) likewise, with no ground command found and the Sputnik 3 tape recorder failing; Luna 1 (1959-01-02) had its rocket stage cut off by a radio signal from the ground (late, causing the miss) but the spacecraft itself was not commanded; Pioneer 1 (1958-10) carried a command receiver but no use of it was found. Contemporary Spaceflight (1960-07) confirms two-way contact and a ground command starting the photography. A one-time earlier ground command to some 1958 probe cannot be ruled out.
searched: Wikipedia Sputnik 1/2/3, Luna 1, Pioneer 1, Explorer 1/6, Vanguard 1; archive.org full text 1958-1961 for Lunik III command, Pioneer I ground command, Sputnik III command; NTRS query (no hits); read Spaceflight 1960-07 and Aviation Week 1958-11/12.

what: TIROS 1, the first weather satellite, launched 1 Apr 1960 and was run from ground stations: its picture tapes were read out on ground command and its weather pictures used by forecasters.
fit: Ground controllers commanded an operational spacecraft by radio and received its telemetry and pictures, for the real purpose of observing weather.

Candidates: Luna 3 (1959, demonstration), Transit/Discoverer 1959-60 (military, ground-commanded but later or less documented), Vostok 1 crewed flight (1961-04) and Mercury Control (1961) are later. Whether TIROS 1 is the first operationally used commanded satellite is not proven.
searched: archive.org full text 1960-1961 for TIROS command ground station; Wikipedia TIROS-1.

what: Alexei Leonov left Voskhod 2 in a Berkut suit with a backpack oxygen supply and spent 12 minutes 9 seconds outside, the first spacewalk.
fit: A sealed suit carrying its own oxygen (backpack tanks) kept a person alive in vacuum outside a spacecraft, with the spacecraft's radio link and television covering the walk.

sources.title: In open space - Voskhod-2 spacecraft design

sources.title: Voskhod 2
sources.quote: The white metal EVA backpack provided 45 minutes of oxygen for breathing and cooling.

note: Earlier candidates rejected: Wiley Post's 1934 pressure suit and later aircraft and Navy Mark IV high-altitude suits (flown in aircraft, not outside a spacecraft); 1950s Litton hard-shell suit and other vacuum-chamber suit tests (chamber tests only, no own-air-supply spaceflight use); Gagarin's SK-1 (1961) and Mercury suits, worn inside the cabin as a backup and never exposed to vacuum. Ed White's Gemini 4 EVA (1965-06-03) came after Leonov and relied on an umbilical air hose. Radio: the 1966 text lists the spacecraft's transmitters and television system observing the walker; the suit's own radio link is not separately quoted.

what: Yevgeny Khrunov and Alexei Yeliseyev, wearing Yastreb suits with chest-mounted regenerative life-support units, spacewalked from Soyuz 5 to Soyuz 4 to transfer crews between two docked spacecraft.
fit: Self-contained sealed suits with their own life support and communication were used outside the spacecraft to do the mission's actual job, moving two men from one ship to the other.

Later: Apollo 9 (1969-03) PLSS test and Apollo 11 (1969-07-20), the first work on another world.
searched: Wikipedia Soyuz 4, Voskhod 2; archive.org full-text search 1965-69 for Khrunov and Yeliseyev (Red Bluff Daily News AP report of 1969-01-16 read and quote checked); the Gemini umbilical point rests on general knowledge, not a fetched page.

what: Alexei Leonov left Voskhod 2 through an inflatable airlock and floated outside on a tether for 12 min 9 s.
fit: A person in a spacesuit exited a spacecraft via an airlock and moved in open space, which is the definition's function and mechanism.

what: Michael Collins, outside Gemini 10 in his second EVA, used a handheld maneuvering gun and tether to reach the dormant Agena 8 and retrieve its micrometeorite collector.
fit: The first spacewalk in which a person left the spacecraft and did real work in open space (retrieving hardware from another vehicle) rather than only floating or testing.

sources.title: Gemini 10
sources.quote: Collins then retrieved a cosmic dust-collecting panel from the side of the Agena

what: Sandra Pruzansky at Bell Telephone Laboratories published a computer pattern-matching procedure that identified which of ten talkers spoke a test utterance, with 89% recognition.

sources.quote: A pattern-matching procedure for automatic recognition of talkers was used to study the effects of variations in patterns upon recognition performance.

note: Added: the input had no demonstration. Pruzansky 1963 is an automatic computer identification of talkers from voice patterns, working on ten speakers (laboratory). Rejected: Kersta's 1962 voiceprints (visual matching by people). Authentication proper (verification) was shown later, 1960s-70s (Luck 1969, Bell Labs 1972, TI/RADC 1972-74); not used since identification by voice already fits the definition.

what: An early laboratory model of the Bell Laboratories sound spectrograph (R. K. Potter and colleagues) was demonstrated to the National Defense Research Committee in March 1941, turning speech into a visible frequency-time-intensity pattern.
fit: The device converts speech into a visible pattern (frequency, time, intensity) that can be read by eye.

sources.publisher: NDRC Summary Technical Report, Division 13, Vol. 3
sources.title: Speech and Facsimile Scrambling and Decoding
sources.quote: In March 1941 an early laboratory model of the sound spectrograph was demonstrated

sources.title: Visible Speech (R. K. Potter)
sources.quote: This was before the war, and subsequently military

note: Date made precise to March 1941 (the 1946 NDRC report gives both 'early in 1941' and 'March 1941'). Earlier candidates rejected: Scott's phonautograph (1857) and oscillograms or Dayton Miller's phonodeik, which show waveform only, so frequency and intensity cannot be read (Potter 1946 says an oscillogram does not make speech visible in this sense); A. M. Bell's Visible Speech (1867), a hand-written phonetic notation, not a device converting speech. Potter says the concept predates the war, but no working pre-1941 instrument was found. The Bell Laboratories Record quote is only partial support (concept before the war, so wartime machine); no contemporary source within two years of March 1941 was found, as the work was classified.
searched: archive.org full-text search for sound spectrograph 1943-1947, visible speech 1941-1944, sound analyzer 1935-1940 (no 1941-43 hits); read NDRC Div. 13 vol. 3, Science 1945-11-09 (Potter), Bell Laboratories Record 1946-01.

note: Replaced the 1963 dye test. The definition covers channels carrying sea water 'from the sea to underground regions' as well as between seas, and John Davy's 1835 report (Dr White's letter of 26 May 1835) documents four streams of sea water descending into the ground at Argostoli, Cephalonia, long known to locals; this is the earliest report found, and the mill that Stephens was erecting on one stream harnessed the flow. Rejected or later: Maurin and Zoetl's 1963 dye test (Argostoli to Karavomylos at Sami) proved the sea-to-sea link, which a strict reading of the name 'linking seas' might prefer, but it is not the first demonstration of sea water entering underground passages; ancient katavothres such as Lake Copais carry lake water, not sea water; the Gibraltar undercurrent is an open strait, and built canals (Suez, Panama) are open cuts. No built subterranean sea channel exists.

what: F. S. Southerland, a former US Navy man known as the 'Human Fly' or 'Jack the Steeple Climber', was reported by the St. Louis Post-Dispatch (16 July 1899) to climb building walls and smokestacks with his own invention: rubber coverings for hands and feet that gripped by air-pump suction.
fit: Worn hand and foot pads that cling to a wall by suction so a person can climb it, exactly the definition's suction shoes and gloves; a 1901 newspaper report has him walking up a room wall to the ceiling in them before Post Office officials.

note: Replaces the 2015 Stanford gecko-adhesive paddle paper, which is 116 years later and used hand-held paddles. what: Hans Bethe's 'Energy Production in Stars' (Physical Review 55, 434, 1 March 1939) showed that the carbon-nitrogen cycle, with the proton-proton chain, matches the Sun's observed energy production.
fit: It shows that stars shine by converting matter through nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium, with the energy released over very long times, an atomic process matching the definition.

sources.title: Energy Production in Stars (H. A. Bethe)
sources.quote: The agreement of the carbon-nitrogen reactions with observational data (§7, 9) is excellent.

sources.title: Stellar nucleosynthesis
sources.quote: Hans Bethe analyzed the different possibilities for reactions by which hydrogen is fused into helium

note: Bethe's paper (received 7 Sept 1938, published 1 March 1939) is the first to show quantitatively that known nuclear reactions (the carbon-nitrogen cycle, with the proton-proton chain) give the Sun's observed energy output, its summary calling the agreement with observation excellent. Earlier candidates: Eddington 1920 (hydrogen to helium as the stellar source, a hypothesis only); Atkinson and Houtermans 1929 (calculated reaction rates of proton capture); Bethe and Critchfield, Physical Review 15 August 1938 (the p-p reaction gives about 2 ergs/g/s, 'almost but not quite' enough for the Sun, and their paper says nuclear energy for stars was already generally accepted, so the general idea predates 1938 but was not yet shown to match the Sun); Rutherford/Joly/Curie c. 1903 radioactivity as the source (refuted by the Sun's low radium content and later by nuclear physics); Einstein 1905 mass-energy (no stellar model). The idea itself (as opposed to a demonstration) was proposed and widely held earlier, mostly after Eddington 1920.

what: Mortimer and ten co-authors published 'Zealandia: Earth's Hidden Continent' in GSA Today (10 Feb 2017), arguing that Zealandia, about 94 percent submerged continental crust that subsided after leaving Gondwana, meets all the criteria of a continent; the BBC reported it on 17 Feb 2017.
fit: A continent-sized landmass of continental crust that subsided beneath the Pacific, with New Zealand and New Caledonia as the remnants above water, matches a vast land that sank and left remnants (no 'ruins' in the Atlantis sense).

what: IBM demonstrated the Naval Ordnance Research Calculator (NORC) to the press on 1954-11-30 and presented it to the US Navy on 1954-12-02, a machine about 20 times faster than the best previous computer for large scientific problems.
fit: A computer built to be far faster than any other, for large scientific and ballistic calculations beyond hand calculation.

sources.quote: For the largest sci- entific problems this machine is about 20 times faster than the best previous computer.

sources.title: IBM NORC
sources.quote: At the presentation ceremony, it calculated pi to 3,089 digits, which was a record at the time.

note: Judgment call on fit: 'supercomputer' is a retrospective label, but the NORC was built to be the fastest machine for the largest scientific problems (Eckert: about 20 times faster than the best previous computer) and Columbia's history site calls it the first supercomputer. Rejected earlier: ENIAC (1945-46) and Harvard Mark I (1944), first-generation general computers, not the frontier machine of their time in the sense of the name; EDSAC/Whirlwind/IBM 701 (1951-53) not built as far-faster scientific machines. Later: UNIVAC LARC (1960), IBM 7030 Stretch (1961), Atlas (1962), CDC 6600 (1964), usually cited retrospectively as first supercomputers. Date refined: public demonstration to the press 1954-11-30, formal presentation to the Navy 1954-12-02 (Wikipedia); testing began early Dec 1954.

what: NORC, reassembled at the Naval Proving Ground, Dahlgren, Virginia, went into productive operation in early July 1955, computing ballistics and ordnance problems (main computer there until 1958).
fit: The machine was put to work on the Navy's large scientific and ordnance calculations.

sources.title: Digital Computer Newsletter Vol 7 No 4

what: General Electric built a demonstration computer from thin-film cryotrons (arrays of 2000 devices operated), following John Bremer's 1957 planar cryotron.

sources.title: Cryotron
sources.quote: In the next few years, a demonstration computer was made and arrays with 2000 devices operated.

note: The page gives only 'the next few years' after 1957, so the year 1960 is approximate (1958-1961). Buck's 1953-55 cryotron was a single switching element, not a computer. No machine described as a working superconducting computer was found in other sources. No practical use: cryotron work was abandoned by the mid-1960s and, per Wikipedia, there are no commercial superconducting computers as of 2016. No mass adoption.

what: Brookhaven National Laboratory built and tested a 10 m coaxial Nb3Sn superconducting 60 Hz cable cooled by supercritical helium (first in a series of 10 m test cables, reported Sept 1978).
fit: A cryogenically cooled superconducting cable was built and operated, with current, ac loss and fault-current measurements.

sources.publisher: OSTI / IEEE Transactions on Magnetics (Applied Superconductivity Conference)
sources.title: 10 m Nb3Sn Cable for 60 Hz Power Transmission
sources.quote: A 10 m Nb 3 Sn cable for 60 Hz power transmission was constructed.

note: Considered: Garwin and Matisoo 1967 (design study, rejected); Brookhaven 100 m cable operated 1982-86 (later, though more complete). Earlier short laboratory superconducting cables of the 1960s-70s (Union Carbide, Siemens, Karlsruhe, IBM) probably exist but none could be found or fetched. Brookhaven's first 10 m cable is documented, but whether it is the very first cable demonstration is not established.
searched: WebSearch and OSTI for Brookhaven cable history; archive.org search for 1966-75 cable tests found nothing usable; BNL pdf blocked.

what: Southwire energized a 30 m HTS (liquid-nitrogen-cooled) cable feeding three facilities at its Carrollton, Georgia plant, 18 Feb 2000.
fit: A cryogenically cooled superconducting cable carried real plant electric power in industrial service.

sources.title: ORNL, Southwire achieve superconducting milestone
sources.quote: Three facilities at the 2,000-employee Carrollton, Ga., plant now receive electricity through a high-temperature superconductor (HTS) power system

sources.title: Development and Test of World's First Industrial HTS Power Cable
sources.quote: Southwire Company has installed the world's first industrial high-temperature superconducting cable system to power three of its main manufacturing plants.

note: Earlier candidates: Brookhaven's 115 m Nb3Sn liquid-helium cables operated 1982-1986 but only as a test system, serving no load, so a demonstration not a practical use; IBM Garwin-Matisoo 1967 proposal (design); LIPA Holbrook 2008 is later (first in a utility grid). Southwire is the first to feed real loads.
searched: ORNL and OSTI pages fetched, BNL history pages, WebSearch for pre-2000 superconducting cables; no evidence of an earlier cable feeding a load.

what: Mesopotamian celestial omen series (Enuma Anu Enlil prototype) in use in the Old Babylonian period, reading eclipses and sky phenomena as warnings for cities and kings.
fit: Eclipses and sky signs were taken as reliable forecasts of events affecting regions, cities and the king.

sources.title: Enuma Anu Enlil
sources.quote: there was certainly some form of prototype Enuma Anu Enlil current in the Old Babylonian period (1950–1595 BCE)

sources.title: Enuma Anu Enlil
sources.quote: Tablets 15 to 22 are dedicated to lunar eclipses.

what: The Soviet Tupolev Tu-144 airliner prototype exceeded Mach 1 for the first time in a flight test (Concorde 001 first went supersonic on 1969-10-01).
fit: A prototype of a passenger airliner, built for passenger service, flying faster than sound.

sources.title: Astronautics and aeronautics, 1969 Chronology on science, technology, and policy
sources.quote: U.S.S.R.’s Tu-144 supersonic aircraft exceeded mach 1 for first time during flight test, according to Tass.

sources.title: Tupolev Tu-144
sources.quote: The Tu-144 first went supersonic on 5 June 1969, four months before Concorde

note: Same event as given. Candidates rejected: Tu-144 first flight 1968-12-31 (subsonic; the NASA chronology notes the second flight on 1969-01-10 did not go supersonic); the public Tu-144 demonstration flight of 1969-05-21 (Pravda pilot said it had not yet exceeded the speed of sound); Concorde 001 (first supersonic 1969-10-01, later); earlier supersonic aircraft such as the Bell X-1 (1947) and military jets, which are not passenger aircraft; the Tu-144 prototype built in the MiG-21 analogue form is a test rig, not an airliner. The contemporary NASA entry sits under early June 1969 and cites Interavia Air Letter of 1969-06-09; the exact day 5 June comes from the Wikipedia reference.
searched: archive.org full-text search for Tu-144 supersonic 1969-1970; NASA Astronautics and Aeronautics 1969 chronology read in full for Tu-144 entries (works); Wikipedia Tu-144.

what: Concorde entered scheduled passenger service: Air France Paris-Rio and British Airways London-Bahrain, on the same day.
fit: Fare-paying passengers carried on scheduled supersonic cruise flights, the airliner's purpose.

sources.title: Jeppesen Sanderson Aviation Yearbook 1977 Ed
sources.quote: A passenger from Germany for the first scheduled Concorde flight to Rio

sources.title: Concorde
sources.quote: Concorde entered service on 21 January 1976 with Air France from Paris-Roissy and British Airways from London Heathrow.

note: Same event as given. Rejected: Tu-144 Aeroflot service from 1975-12-26 (Moscow-Alma-Ata) carried only mail and freight; its passenger flights began 1977-11-01, after Concorde; the Tu-144 as a passenger type but with no passengers is not a use as an airliner. The yearbook (published 1977) names the first scheduled Concorde flight to Rio; it also says air transport would not be the same after January 21, 1976 (the Air France Rio flight left that day).

what: The Eiffel Tower in Paris, an iron lattice tower about 1,000 ft (300 m) high, was completed on 31 March 1889 when Eiffel led officials and press to the top; built for the Exposition Universelle.
fit: A free-standing giant lattice tower far taller than any earlier structure, built for observation and display.

sources.title: The Electrical World 1889-04-20
sources.quote: looms up in the sky for 1,000 feet, or just twice as high

sources.title: Eiffel Tower
sources.quote: on 31 March, Eiffel celebrated by leading a group of government officials

note: Earlier candidates: Washington Monument (1884, 169 m, obelisk, not far taller than Cologne Cathedral's 157 m, rejected), Gothic cathedral spires such as Lincoln and Strasbourg (not free-standing observation towers), Great Pyramid (tomb), unbuilt proposals (Trevithick 1832 1,000-ft column, Philadelphia 1876 Centennial Tower). Eiffel's tower, about 1,000 ft (300 m), was nearly twice the Washington Monument. Completion: structural work done and Eiffel's flag-raising on 31 March 1889 (Wikipedia, reference), reported by The Electrical World on 20 April as 'opened a few days ago'.
searched: archive.org full text 1889 for Eiffel Tower (Electrical World, Engineering News, Builder), Wikipedia Eiffel_Tower; checked date 31 March from Wikipedia, with the contemporary source dating completion only to 'a few days ago' in April.

what: The Eiffel Tower opened to the public nine days after the Exposition opened on 6 May 1889; visitors climbed the stairs before lifts began on 26 May.
fit: A tower used for its real purpose of public observation and display.

sources.title: Engineering News 1889-06-15
sources.quote: was the first visitor to ascend the Eiffel tower and record his name in the Wg visitors’ book

sources.title: Eiffel Tower
sources.quote: the tower was not opened to the public until nine days after the opening of the exposition on 6 May

note: Public opening date (15 May, nine days after 6 May) is Wikipedia's; contemporary Engineering News (15 June 1889) reports first visitor to ascend after opening, and The Builder (18 May 1889) found it closed to the public on the Tuesday it visited (14 May), consistent with opening on 15 May. Earlier: the 31 March ascent by officials and press was a ceremony, not public use; no earlier structure was a supertall tower.
searched: as for first_demonstration; Builder 1889-05-18 and ENR 1889-06-15 read.

what: Synod of Sens at Paris forbids reading Aristotle's natural philosophy under penalty of excommunication
fit: Church authority banned and punished study of a body of natural-science writing.

sources.title: Condemnations of 1210-1277
sources.quote: are to be read at Paris in public or secret, and this we forbid under penalty of excommunication.

what: Gracchus Babeuf, journalist and leader of the Conspiracy of the Equals, was condemned and guillotined at Vendome by the French Directory.

sources.title: Conspiracy of the Equals

what: Thebans attacked Plataea at night in peacetime, before any declaration, opening the Peloponnesian War.
fit: One power opened a war by attacking another's territory (a city) with no declaration or diplomatic warning.

sources.title: Peloponnesian War
sources.quote: The first attack was by the Thebans on the Athenian outpost at Plataea, on 4 April 431 BC.

sources.title: Declaration of war
sources.quote: Thucydides condemned the Thebans, allies of Sparta, for launching a surprise attack without a declaration of war against Plataea

note: Earlier undeclared attacks surely exist in antiquity but I found no documented earlier war opened this way. Later, more famous candidates rejected as not earliest: Japan at Port Arthur 1904, Pearl Harbor 1941, Britain at Copenhagen 1807. Fleet attack specifically (as the aliases say) would be later; I dated the earliest on territory.
searched: Wikipedia Peloponnesian War, Declaration of war.

what: Walter Mantell obtained from sealers the skin of a live-caught takahe (Notornis) from Dusky Bay, Fiordland, New Zealand, late 1849; the genus was known only from fossil bones and presumed extinct like the moa.
fit: A bird known only as an extinct fossil was found still living in a remote region, matching the extinct-bird-found-alive clause.

sources.publisher: Gideon Mantell, Notice of the discovery of a living Notornis
sources.title: Notice of the discovery by Mr Walter Mantell ... of a living specimen of the Notornis
sources.quote: Towards the close of last year, on Mr. Walter Mantell’s second visit to the south of Otago, he obtained from some sealers the recent bird

sources.title: Takahē
sources.quote: realised this was Notornis, a living bird known only from fossil bones

note: Replaces the 1948 Orbell rediscovery. The takahe had already been found alive in 1849 (Owen named it from fossils in 1848 as extinct; live bird captured late 1849, announced 1850; second specimen 1851). The 1948 event is a second rediscovery after the 1898 last specimen. Other candidates (cahow 1951, noisy scrub-bird 1961) are later; no giant roc or moa found.
searched: archive.org full text 1849-1852 (Notornis); Mantell 1850 pamphlet; Wikipedia Takahe; Lazarus taxon lists.

what: Tarquinius Priscus (traditional) had Etruscan and plebeian workers build drainage channels (the Cloaca Maxima) and fill the Forum valley and Velabrum marsh, turning swamp into building ground in Rome.
fit: Engineered drainage channels plus fill drained a marsh so the land could be built on and settled, matching drainage of a swamp for settlement.

sources.title: Cloaca Maxima
sources.quote: worked to transform the land by the Roman forum from a swamp into a solid building ground

sources.title: Cloaca Maxima
sources.quote: it was constructed in Ancient Rome in order to drain local marshes and remove waste from the city

note: Date is traditional (around 600 BC), not archaeologically firm. Considered Faiyum Twelfth Dynasty scheme (about -2000) and Copaic Basin drainage (Middle Helladic, about -1900): those drained lakes or lake margins, not clearly swamps or marsh, so rejected as looser fits. Pontine Marshes works (312 BC) are later.
searched: Wikipedia: Cloaca Maxima, Land reclamation, Lake Copais

what: Patrick Geddes at Roscoff found the green planarian Convoluta (algae living in its tissue) evolved oxygen and held starch in sunlight, showing animal and alga living as one benefiting partnership.
fit: An animal hosts another organism inside its body in a mutually beneficial association, matching the literal definition.

sources.publisher: Proceedings of the Royal Society of Edinburgh
sources.title: On the Nature and Functions of the Yellow Cells of Radiolarians and Coelenterates
sources.quote: It was only necessary to expose a quantity of these animals to direct sunlight to observe the rapid evolution of bubbles of gas

note: Loose: it matches animals plus alga, not the fictional sapient or human symbiote, and algae are acquired, not inherited, in Convoluta. Brandt 1881 and de Bary's 1879 term are neighbors I did not source; Hydra viridis was known earlier as green without the benefit shown. Gut microbiota is a human case but dated later.

fit: A state organized on corporations of workers, employers and professions instead of parties matches the corporatist definition; it was a short-lived city-state under a dictator.

sources.title: Italian Regency of Carnaro
sources.quote: The constitution established a corporatist state, with nine corporations to represent the different sectors of the economy

sources.title: Italian Regency of Carnaro
sources.quote: On 8 September 1920, D'Annunzio proclaimed the city to be under the Italian Regency of Carnaro

note: Considered fascist Italy's syndical and corporative system (1926-27) which fits the single-union idea better but is later; Soviet and Hungarian council republics (1917-19) are council states without employer-worker syndicates and were not examined.

what: ASEA in Vasteras/Stockholm, Sweden, made the first known synthetic diamonds (secret project QUINTUS) in a split-sphere high-pressure apparatus, two years before GE announced its own.
fit: Real diamond crystals (genuineness checked by X-ray) were grown artificially from carbon at high pressure and temperature.

sources.title: Science 1955-05-20: Vol 121 Iss 3151
sources.quote: the first synthetic diamonds were those produced in February 1953 by the Swedish ASEA electric company

sources.title: Synthetic diamond
sources.quote: The first known (but initially not reported) diamond synthesis was achieved on February 16, 1953, in Stockholm by ASEA

note: Confirmed. The best period source (Science news note, May 1955, 2 years 3 months after the event, so just outside the contemporary window and kept as a reference) says the Swedish diamonds were genuine by X-ray and the synthesis repeated. Rejected: Hannay 1880, Moissan 1893, Parsons and others (never confirmed; Lonsdale's 1944 reassessment doubted); the GE 1951 Strong-Bundy attempt in which a diamond was a natural seed; GE Hall synthesis 16 Dec 1954 (announced 15 Feb 1955) is later and the first reproducible published one, but ASEA is earlier. ASEA stones were small and not gem quality, which the definition does not require for a demonstration.
searched: Wikipedia Synthetic diamond; archive.org full-text search for ASEA diamonds 1955-1957 (found Science 1955-05-20); Crossref Nature 1955 earlier. ASEA kept the work secret until after GE's Feb 1955 announcement, so no report within two years of the event exists.

what: General Electric's Detroit plant made man-made industrial diamonds in quantity (100,000 carats by Nov 1957) and began supplying them to industry for grinding wheels, lapping and dressing; by March 1958 GE offered them in unlimited quantities.
fit: Synthetic diamond was manufactured and put to its real industrial work (diamond grinding wheels for carbide tools, lapping, wire-drawing dies).

sources.title: Grinding and Finishing 1957-11
sources.quote: By the end of the year a substantial quantity will be in use.

sources.title: G.E. Offers Man-Made Diamonds in Quantity
sources.quote: General Electric Co.’s Metallurgical Products Depart- ment is now offering industry its man-made diamonds in unlimited quantities.

note: Confirmed. Rejected earlier candidates: ASEA 1953-55 stones (tiny, never put to use; ASEA kept secret); GE pilot-plant output of 1955-56 (Tooling & Production July 1956 and Mechanical Engineering Sept 1956 say only limited pilot quantities, cost still above natural stones, no commercial supply); gem-quality stones (GE 1970) are a later separate step but the definition is met by real diamond made artificially and used commercially. A web-search snippet (not fetched) says C&EN reported GE Detroit making diamonds commercially since October 1957, consistent with 1957.
searched: archive.org full-text search for man-made diamonds 1955-1958 (Grinding and Finishing 1957-11, Tooling & Production 1956-07 and 1958-02, Mechanical Engineering 1956-09, Mining Journal 1956-05, Purchasing Week 1958-03-31); WebSearch for first GE sales; ACS C&EN pages returned 403/not-found term.

fit: Gem-quality synthetic diamonds, indistinguishable by eye and cheaper, were bought by ordinary jewelry shoppers.

sources.title: Synthetic diamond
sources.quote: In 2023, synthetic diamonds were 17% of the diamond jewelry market.
