what: Burke (Shriners Burns Institute, Boston) and Yannas (MIT) reported in Annals of Surgery that their bilayer artificial skin (silicone epidermis over a collagen-chondroitin sulfate dermis) closed excised burn wounds in ten patients with 50 to 95 percent burns.
fit: A manufactured, non-living skin that physiologically closed burns and was populated by the patient's cells to form a neodermis matches artificial skin used for repair (a template that regenerates dermis, so only a partial match to 'replicates living tissue').

sources.title: Successful use of a physiologically acceptable artificial skin in the treatment of extensive burn injury
sources.quote: has been used to physiologically close up to 60% of the body surface following prompt excision of burn wounds in ten patients

sources.title: Artificial skin
sources.quote: In 1981 Burke and Yannas proved that their artificial skin worked on patients with 50 to 90 percent burns

note: Same event as before, now with the primary 1981 paper (the actual patient treatments may have begun slightly earlier, but no earlier dated report was found; Yannas and Burke's 1980 'Design of an artificial skin I' was animal and design work). Rejected: Green's cultured epidermal sheets 1975-79 (living cells, not synthetic); Biobrane and other nylon-silicone or polymer burn coverings of the 1970s (temporary dressings that do not replicate tissue, a loose stand-in); porcine and amnion biological dressings (not synthetic). Artificial skin for disguise or robot bodies has not been demonstrated; electronic skin for prostheses is experimental.
searched: Wikipedia Artificial skin and its citations; PMC1345315 (Ann Surg 1981) abstract; Crossref abstract of Yannas Science 1982; archive.org 1975-84 searches (DTIC 1977-78 synthetic burn covering reports, DTIC ADA117879 1982 which lists the Burke/Yannas artificial skin as under clinical trial, Western J Med 1984 Biobrane).

what: The US FDA granted premarket approval (PMA P900033) to Integra artificial skin for life-threatening burns, the first marketed artificial skin of this type.
fit: A commercially marketed artificial skin used on patients to repair skin loss after burn excision.

sources.title: P900033/S042 Summary of Safety and Effectiveness Data
sources.quote: Integra Template was first granted FDA Premarket Approval for use in life-threatening thermal injuries under PMA P900033 on March 1, 1996.

note: Date made exact (1996-03-01) from the FDA's own summary. The 1981 patient series and 1980s trials (e.g. 1988 multicenter trial) were experimental, so not counted as routine practical use. Biobrane (early 1980s) is a temporary synthetic dressing that does not replicate tissue; Apligraf (1998) contains living cells and is later. No contemporary 1996-97 report of the approval was found.
searched: Wikipedia Integra LifeSciences; WebSearch (worked) found the FDA summary; archive.org 1996-97 search for contemporary reports returned nothing relevant.

what: Arthur Imhausen and Werner Prosch (Märkische Seifenindustrie / Deutsche Fettsäure-Werke, Witten) made edible fat by oxidizing coal-derived Fischer-Tropsch paraffin to fatty acids and esterifying them with glycerin; in 1936 the product was fed to people and animals in tests.
fit: An edible fat manufactured chemically from coal, a non-agricultural input, shown to work as food in feeding tests.

sources.title: German synthetic fat
sources.quote: in 1936, immediately after obtaining the result and the product, they began experiments on people

note: Moves the demonstration from the 1939 approval to the 1936 working product and feeding tests, which the Topwar retrospective dates; Evonik's history page dates Imhausen's marketable fatty acid process to 1935 (soap first). No contemporary 1936 report found. Earlier candidates rejected: saccharin (1879) and synthetic vanillin (1870s) are coal-tar additives, not food or staples; Berthelot's 1854 synthetic fats were lab curiosities not tested as food; WWI German yeast and ersatz foods used agricultural inputs (sugar, molasses). Later: single-cell protein from hydrocarbons (1960s), Solein (2020s).
searched: Topwar, Evonik history page, Wikipedia Fischer-Tropsch process, WebSearch (worked) for Imhausen and WWI synthetic fat (no WWI edible synthetic fat found), archive.org searches 1936-1946 (newspaper and Science News Letter items found from 1939-40 only).

what: After the Reich health office cleared synthetic fat for food in September 1939, German industrial production of edible fat from coal-derived paraffin began just before the war and was eaten as margarine and cooking fat; by late 1940 it was reported at about 40,000 tons a year.
fit: Chemically made fat from coal supplied part of the national food fat ration, a staple made from non-agricultural inputs on an industrial scale.

sources.title: Science News Letter 1940-12-28
sources.quote: Germany gets 40,000 tons of edible fats a year from coal

sources.title: German synthetic fat
sources.quote: large-scale industrial production of synthetic fats, both technical and food, began just before the war

note: Same event as the earlier researcher's 1939 date, now backed by a 1940 contemporary report (the tonnage may be inflated). Evonik says synthetic margarine came during the war years, so 1939 to 1940 is the range; 1939 kept since the retrospective puts large-scale production just before the war. Rejected: 1936 feeding tests (demonstration, not supply), saccharin 1879 (sweetener additive, not food), WWI ersatz foods (agricultural inputs). A Dec 1939 newspaper item says Germany was 'prepared to make' fats from coal, so not yet confirming production then.
searched: archive.org full text for coal butter 1939-1943 (Kingston Daily Freeman 1939-12-29, Science News Letter 1940-12-28, Quote 1941); Topwar; Evonik history page; WebSearch.

what: Thomas Midgley Jr. at General Motors Research (Dayton, Ohio), working under Charles Kettering, found on 9 December 1921 that tetraethyl lead in very small proportion suppresses knock in gasoline engines.
fit: A compact additive mixed into gasoline at about 1 part in 1,300 raises the fuel's performance in engines (the 'gasoline additive' alternative of the definition).

sources.title: Tetraethyllead
sources.quote: was the first to discover its effectiveness as a knock inhibitor on 9 December 1921

note: Earlier candidates considered: iodine and aniline as anti-knock additives (Kettering and Midgley, 1916-1920; SAE Journal 1920 and 1921 describe them, but no dated first demonstration; iodine was a costly dye-theory additive and aniline a poor one, neither used as a fuel additive in service); ethanol blends (known as anti-knock by 1921 but a different, lower-energy fuel); benzol and toluene blends in aircraft and motor spirit (WWI, a blending component, not a new compact fuel); Bergius coal hydrogenation (1913) and Fischer-Tropsch (1925), which make gasoline-like fuel that is not more powerful. Later: high-octane aviation fuel (1930s) and liquid-oxygen rocket propellants (1926). TEL kept as the earliest additive that gave a strong, practical gain.
searched: Wikipedia Tetraethyllead, Thomas Midgley, Engine knocking, Leaded gasoline; archive.org full text 1919-1925 for tetraethyl/lead tetraethyl with anti-knock (SAE Journal 1920-09, 1921-11; Science 1923-06 and 1923-12; Chemical & Metallurgical Engineering 1923-09). Contemporary papers describe the effect but none found states the 9 December 1921 date, so the date rests on the reference source.

what: Leaded 'ethyl' gasoline was first sold to motorists at a filling station in Dayton, Ohio, on 2 February 1923; a November 1924 paper says it had then been on sale one year and nine months.
fit: Gasoline treated with a compact additive was in routine retail sale for ordinary engines.

sources.title: Xenia Evening Gazette (1924-11-13)
sources.quote: For one year and nine months ethylized gasoline has been on sale

sources.title: Famous First Facts
sources.quote: Ethyl gasoline was marketed in Dayton, Ohio, February 2, 1923

note: Date sharpened from 1923-02 to 1923-02-02 by Famous First Facts (record date shown as 1923 by the checker; it is a later compilation, so kept as a reference), which agrees with the 1924 newspaper's 21-months count. Earlier candidates considered: 1920-21 iodine/aniline fuels (laboratory only), ethanol-gasoline blends and benzol motor fuels (blends, not a new compact fuel), Bergius/Fischer-Tropsch synthetic gasoline (not more powerful, and not in this sense). Not the 1924 Ethyl Gasoline Corporation national rollout.

what: Edmond Frémy and Charles Feil made crystal corundum (ruby) from which small stones could be cut.

what: J. Craig Venter Institute (Gibson et al.) assembled a Mycoplasma mycoides genome from chemically synthesized DNA, transplanted it into a Mycoplasma capricolum cell, and obtained replicating cells controlled only by the synthetic genome (JCVI-syn1.0); published online in Science on 20 May 2010.
fit: A living, self-replicating cell run entirely by a chemically synthesized genome matches making a living cell from chemicals and controlling it, though the cell body came from a recipient cell.

what: At the State Bank of Barneston, Nebraska, in October 1923, tear gas installed to protect the safe was released when robbers blew the safe doors and drove them off without any loot.

sources.title: Lamberto Dini

what: Sputnik 1, launched 4 October 1957, radioed continuous beeps to ground stations on 20.005 and 40.002 MHz whose length and pauses varied with the temperature and pressure inside the satellite.
fit: A spacecraft's radio transmitter streamed internal measurements (temperature, pressure) continuously to ground receivers, the spacecraft-telemetry meaning of the concept's name.

sources.publisher: Information Department, USSR Embassy in India
sources.title: Sputniks - Breaking Into Cosmos
sources.quote: the length of the signal and the pause also changed within definite limits

sources.title: Sputnik 1
sources.quote: Temperature and pressure were encoded in the duration of radio beeps.

note: Replaced Explorer 1 (1958-01-31) with Sputnik 1, which carried a working telemetry link four months earlier; the 1958 booklet (second edition February 1958) is contemporary and agrees with Wikipedia. Considered and rejected: radiosonde of Robert Bureau (1929-01-07) and Pavel Molchanov (1930-01-30), real radio links streaming measurements from a remote balloon instrument, which the definition's 'or remote instrument' could admit, but the concept's name is 'Spacecraft telemetry link' and I found no contemporary source for either (Nature 1932-12-31 dates Molchanov's tests to January 1930, two years too late to count); V-2 rocket flights of 1942-44 and US V-2 and Aerobee rocket telemetry of 1946-49, sounding rockets and not spacecraft, with no sources fetched. If the definition's 'remote instrument' branch is wanted, the radiosonde date 1929-01 is the earlier alternative.
searched: archive.org full text 1957-1959 (Electronics 1957-11-20, Missiles and Rockets, Sputniks - Breaking Into Cosmos, Soviet Sputniks); Wikipedia Sputnik 1, Radiosonde, Telemetry; archive.org 1929-1933 for radiosonde/radio-meteorograph (Nature 1932-12-31 found; nothing on Bureau). NTRS search returned no results.

what: Sputnik 2, launched 3 November 1957, radioed its instrument readings, including Laika's pulse, respiration and blood pressure, back to Earth by a radio-telemetering device.
fit: The telemetry link served its real purpose of returning scientific and biomedical measurements from a spacecraft to ground stations (at fixed intervals, not strictly continuously).

sources.title: Soviet Sputniks
sources.quote: radio-telemetering device ensured the transmission of all these 14 readings and those of the instruments installed in the sputnik, to the Earth

sources.title: Sputnik 2
sources.quote: for the first time, returning scientific data from above the Earth's atmosphere

note: Replaced Explorer 1 (1958-01-31) because Sputnik 2 returned scientific data from orbit three months earlier (Wikipedia says for the first time). Sputnik 1 (1957-10-04) returned only housekeeping readings and ionospheric propagation information from its beeps, which I treat as the demonstration, not a use for its real purpose. Explorer 1's cosmic-ray data and the Van Allen discovery (announced 1958-03) are later. Radiosondes (routine weather service from the 1930s) are the remote-instrument alternative, not dated here.
searched: Wikipedia Sputnik 2; archive.org 1958 booklets (Soviet Sputniks, Sputniks - Breaking Into Cosmos); Electronics 1957-11-20 (confirms multiplexed Sputnik II signals but is not quoted).

what: Scotland Yard engaged Dutch clairvoyant Peter Hurkos to hunt for the stolen Stone of Scone; he toured London sites with a police sergeant and car.
fit: A police force (Scotland Yard, per contemporary press) put a self-described clairvoyant on an active theft case with a police car and sergeant at his disposal, i.e. police using a psychic for investigation, though not a genuine telepath or interrogation.

sources.title: China Mail 1951-02-09
sources.quote: Scotland Yard send Peter Hurkos

sources.title: The Round Robin, v6 n6, Mar-Apr 1951
sources.quote: Scotland Yard Consults Peter Hurkos', well-known cleirvoyant, for help in finding the Coronation Stone

note: Earlier candidates: (1) W. de Kerler, 1914, claimed psycho-criminologist who solved crimes that baffled police (only parapsychology sites repeating Mishlove; no archival record found, so rejected as unverified); (2) Gerard Croiset consulted by Dutch police after WWII (Wikipedia, undated and success disputed; likely earlier than 1951 but no year or contemporary record found); (3) August Drost, Germany 1925, clairvoyant tried to help officials, tried for fraud (not shown to be police use). Hurkos 1951 is the earliest dated, contemporary-documented case found; the true first police use of a psychic may be earlier. Later: CIA/SRI remote viewing 1972, Army GRILL FLAME operational 1978 (intelligence use of psychics) is a later, better-organized government use. Telepathy proper has never been shown to work; this dates the use of self-described psychics/clairvoyants, the alternative named in the definition.
searched: Wikipedia (Psychic detective, Gerard Croiset, Stargate Project); WebSearch on first police psychics; archive.org full text search for Hurkos, Croiset, SCANATE, GRILL FLAME 1900-1985; CIA reading room INSCOM memo 1979.

note: Date moved from 1919 to 1920-01: the March 1919 paper measured dissipation in the Irish Sea; the step that links it to the slowing of Earth's rotation is the January 1920 MNRAS paper (Nature, Dec 1920, summarizes both and Jeffreys's follow-up). Earlier candidates rejected: Halley 1695 and Dunthorne 1749 (found the Moon's apparent acceleration, no cause), Kant 1754, Adams 1853, Kelvin 1860s, Delaunay and Ferrel 1860s (tidal retardation proposed, not measured), G. Darwin 1879 (theory of tidal friction), Spencer Jones 1939 (Earth's rotation variable, cause unsettled). The Moon's locked face was known long before and Mercury's 1965 radar result was 3:2 resonance, not locking, so neither dates the process. Judgment call: Taylor's is a calculated sufficiency, not an observation of spin-down, so Wells 1963 is the alternative.

what: Streptomycin, discovered by Schatz, Bugie and Waksman, was shown by Feldman and Hinshaw at the Mayo Clinic to act against TB in guinea pigs.
fit: A drug that kills the tuberculosis bacillus and arrested experimental and then clinical tuberculosis, the first with real curative effect.

sources.quote: Streptomycin was the first effective antibiotic against M. tuberculosis.

sources.quote: Hinshaw and Feldman* have carried out experiments to test the therapeutic value of streptomycin in the treatment of clinical tuberculosis.

note: Streptomycin (Waksman lab, Rutgers; Schatz, Bugie, Waksman 1944) was the first antibiotic active against TB, tested by Feldman and Hinshaw at the Mayo Clinic in guinea pigs in 1944 and in patients from late 1944. It arrested rather than reliably cured disease because resistance appeared; reliable cure came with streptomycin plus PAS (1946-49), isoniazid (1952) and rifampin (1970s). Earlier candidates: sanatorium rest (1850s, Brehmer), BCG vaccine (1921, prevention not cure), sulfones/Promin (1940s, weak). Dated the first effective anti-TB drug, with low confidence that it fits "cure" strictly.

Conshelf II (Precontinent II) in June-July 1963 was the first multi-structure sea-floor complex (Starfish House at 10 m, Deep Cabin at 27-30 m, diving-saucer hangar) occupied for a month by oceanauts who went out daily to do scientific work and tasks meant to test commercial work on the sea floor, partly funded by the French petrochemical industry. what: On builders' and official trials in early 1900 the Parsons turbine destroyer HMS Viper (Hawthorn Leslie, Hebburn) reached about 35.5 knots with 11,000 indicated horse power; in July 1900 the Admiralty mean of six runs was 36.581 knots.
fit: A warship running at more than 35 knots, faster than the 30-knot destroyers of the day.

sources.title: The Engines of the Torpedo Boat Destroyer Viper
sources.quote: On her re- cent official trial the " Viper " attained a speed of 35 J£ knots with 11,000 indicated horse power.

sources.quote: On her builders’ trials a speed of 35 knots was attained

sources.title: HMS Viper (1899)
sources.quote: Reports indicate that Viper may have reached even higher speeds during trials, variously reported as 35.5 knots

note: Confirmed and now backed by two contemporary 1900 reports that agree with the reference. The official figures Wikipedia quotes (31.0 and 33.57 knots, August 1900) came from later acceptance trials in poor conditions; Marine Engineering (June 1900) reports a 34.25-knot mean in May 1900 but also 35 knots on the builders' trials, and The Engineer of 20 July 1900 (quoted in US Naval Institute Proceedings, Sept 1900) gives an Admiralty mean of 36.581 knots. Earlier candidates rejected: Turbinia (1897), estimated 34.5 knots at the Spithead review, below 35; Chinese torpedo boats built by Schichau (32-35 knots only 'reputed' per Scientific American 1900, small craft, no trial record); 1890s reciprocating destroyers and torpedo boats (27-31 knots). Exact month of the first 35-knot run (early 1900, before April) not pinned, so the date is the year.
searched: archive.org full text for Viper turbine trials 1900 (Scientific American Apr 1900, Marine Engineering Jun 1900, USNI Proceedings Sept 1900 quoting The Engineer Jul 1900, Army and Navy Gazette 1900, Page's Weekly 1902, Nature Mar 1900); Wikipedia HMS Viper, Turbinia.

what: Kay Lab of San Diego developed a TV-telephone (TV-T) intercom: each station a 17-inch television with a handset, both parties' pictures shown on every screen, picture and sound both ways over coaxial cable, as many stations as desired in one system.
fit: A two-way screen-and-speaker link between nearby stations on a local cable lets people see and talk to one another, with guard-post and door identification named as uses.

sources.title: TV-Telephone Intercom
sources.quote: television telephone (TV-T) inter- com system has been developed by Kay Lab

sources.title: TV-Telephone Intercom
sources.quote: Picture and sound are carried in both di- rections between stations over an inexpen- sive coaxial cable

note: Rejected earlier candidates: Bell Labs two-way television-telephone (April 1930, between 195 Broadway and West Street, New York): an inter-building telephone-service demonstration over a city, not a local room-to-room intercom, so it belongs to a videophone concept; Theremin 1927 Kremlin courtyard viewer (picture only, undated installation, unverified); Siemens Peenemuende 1942 and Vericon 1949 (one-way monitoring, no talk, and not door/room intercoms); Radio & Television Nov 1940 'R&T Videophone' (a construction article for a home-built camera/monitor pair, a design not a deployed system); Talk-A-Phone 1950 video intercom (Financial World 15 Mar 1950: only 'in the development stage'); 1947 Mechanix Illustrated 'visual intercommunication' (a forecast). what: Japan's Hi-OVIS experiment began in July 1978 in 156 homes at Higashi-Ikoma, Nara, an optical-fiber two-way system whose services included a video request service letting subscribers call up programs from the center.
fit: Subscribers chose a program from the system's video library and had it sent to their home television, over a working two-way network.

sources.title: Hi-OVIS Project
sources.quote: The phase 1 experimet, which started in July on 1978

note: Replaces Bell Atlantic 1993 (the Wikipedia 'first outside the lab' claim is contradicted by earlier field trials). Hi-OVIS: the video request service is listed among Hi-OVIS services in Wired Cities (1987) and described as video on demand by the system's own association, but I found no 1978-80 report showing the video request function ran in phase 1 rather than later, so the month is the experiment start and the date may be a few years late. Rejected: Tama CCIS (1976) fixed-image request service (still pictures only, not video); Qube (1977) and hotel or cable pay-per-view (fixed schedules); near video on demand; videotape rental; Westminster Cable video library (1980s, later); Bell Atlantic 1993 and GTE Cerritos 1990 (later). Possibly earlier 1960s-70s university dial-access video systems exist but I found no source showing viewers choosing from a video catalogue.

what: British Telecom's Westminster Cable network in London operated an interactive video library, letting customers choose a film from videodisc players on request, described in June 1988 as the world's first commercially operational full-bandwidth video library service.
fit: Customers pressed a library button, chose a title from a catalogue, and had a free videodisc player allocated to play it for them alone, on a cable network serving paying customers.

Hi-OVIS (1978-86) ran a video request service in real homes but as a government experiment, so it is kept as the demonstration. Rejected: Bell Atlantic 1993 and GTE 1990 trials; pay-per-view, hotel and cable services with fixed schedules; videotape rental.
searched: BT Journal 1987-07 and 1988-06, British Telecommunications Engineering 1987-04 (Kerr, On-Demand Interactive Video), Wikipedia Full Service Network, Video on demand; archive.org full text 1982-1990.

what: Ivan Sutherland and students built a head-mounted display whose computer generated a stereo perspective view that changed as the wearer moved his head (the Harvard system described in his 1968 report and paper).
fit: A computer draws a three-dimensional world in each eye and updates it from head tracking so the user sees it as if it were around him, though only as crude wireframe lines; the report notes observers remark on the realism of the stereo images.

sources.publisher: Harvard University / ARPA report (Computer History Museum archive)
sources.title: Final Report (Part II: A Head-Mounted Three-Dimensional Display), I. E. Sutherland
sources.quote: present the user with a perspective image which changes as he moves

sources.title: The Sword of Damocles (virtual reality)
sources.quote: The system was created in 1968 by computer scientist Ivan Sutherland with the help of his students Bob Sproull

note: Kept. Earlier candidates rejected: Heilig's Sensorama (1962, pre-filmed, not computer-generated); Heilig's Telesphere Mask (1960 patent, a design); Philco Headsight (1961, camera-fed remote viewing, not computer-generated); Sutherland and colleagues' first head-mounted-display experiments at Lincoln Lab from 1966 (experiments with different displays, no documented computer-generated head-tracked world before the 1968 system); Sutherland's 1965 'Ultimate Display' (a proposal); 1960s computer-generated-image flight simulators (GE NASA II 1967 and similar, projected or screen displays, not a head-tracked world around the user). The fit is partial because the picture is wireframe, so 'convincing enough to feel real' is only loosely met; it is still the first working head-tracked computer-generated world.
searched: archive.org full text 1966-1991 for head-mounted display, virtual environment; read the Sutherland report PDF at the Computer History Museum archive; Wikipedia Sword of Damocles; contemporary source attempted and found (the 1968 report itself).

what: Tsutomu Sato (Juntendo, Tokyo) reported anterior and posterior corneal incisions (an early radial keratotomy) that flattened the cornea to correct myopia; his first patients were military pilots.
fit: Eye surgery on patients that reduced myopia so spectacles were less needed, by reshaping the cornea.

sources.title: Tsutomu Sato (ophthalmologist)
sources.quote: In 1939, Sato became the first physician to report the use of radial keratotomy for myopia.

note: Replaced 1936 with 1939: 1936 is when Sato began research, 1939 is his first report (Acta Soc Ophthalmol Jpn 43:544, per Wikipedia). Rejected earlier candidates: Schiøtz 1885 (corneal incision for post-cataract astigmatism, a theoretical proposal, not a myopia cure), Lans 1898 (animal experiments), Fukala 1890 (lens extraction for high myopia, which still left strong aphakic glasses), Barraquer keratomileusis 1949 (later). Sato's result is real but dated only from secondary sources; his 1953 English paper (Am J Ophthalmol 36, 'A new surgical approach to myopia', Crossref record 1953-06) is later and gave no text to quote. Sato's own endpoint, freedom from glasses, was reached only for some patients, hence low.
searched: Wikipedia (Radial keratotomy, Tsutomu Sato, Refractive surgery); archive.org full-text 1939-1945 and 1950-1960 for Sato keratotomy (only index hits); Crossref for Sato 1953. No contemporary 1939-41 source was readable.

what: Svyatoslav Fyodorov in Moscow developed anterior radial keratotomy and began operating on myopic patients so they could do without eyeglasses; about 1000 Americans had it by 1980.

sources.title: Radial keratotomy

Later: Bores performed the first US RK in 1978; PRK 1987-88; LASIK around 1990-92. No contemporary 1974-76 report found.
searched: Wikipedia; archive.org full-text 1975-1982 for Fyodorov keratotomy (Pulse 1980, DTIC 1980-81, Time 1980 index only; Time 1980 text printed no hits for 'keratotomy'); Cumulated Index Medicus 1979 lists Fedorov papers; Sato/Crossref.

what: Mount Pelée's pyroclastic surge destroyed the town of Saint-Pierre, Martinique, killing almost all of its roughly 28,000 people.
fit: A volcanic eruption destroyed a town and killed nearly everyone in it (only a handful survived).

sources.title: 1902 eruption of Mount Pelée
sources.quote: Almost everyone within the city proper—about 28,000 people—died, most burned or buried by falling masonry.

sources.title: The volcano's deadly work, from the fall of Pompeii to the destruction of St. Pierre
sources.quote: St. Pierre, Martinique, volcanic eruption, 30,000 killed

note: Earlier candidates: Vesuvius AD 79 (Pompeii/Herculaneum; most inhabitants are thought to have escaped, only a minority died, so it does not 'kill most of its people'); the Minoan eruption of Thera c. 1600 BC (island destroyed, but Akrotiri was evidently evacuated, no mass death recorded); Tambora 1815 (page lacked a clear town-wide kill figure; not verified); Krakatoa 1883 (uninhabited island). Rejected on the 'kills most of its people' clause. An earlier unfetched case is possible.
searched: Wikipedia Pelée, Vesuvius 79, Pompeii, Tambora, Minoan eruption; archive.org search St. Pierre 1902.

what: Before the July 1910 eruption of Mount Usu, Hokkaido, police chief Seiichi Iida predicted it from preceding earthquakes and had residents within 12 km evacuated; no lives were lost.
fit: Warning issued ahead of an eruption from precursor signs (earthquakes), acted on before it happened.

sources.title: The Eruption of Usu-san and the Formation of a New Mountain (C. Davison)
sources.quote: the police wisely took precautions in time and removed all the inhabitants of the disturbed region beyond the reach of danger

sources.title: Recent Eruptions after the 19th Century (Mount Usu)
sources.quote: The chief of the police station, Seiichi Iida, had attended Professor Omori's lectures and predicted the eruption from the preceding earthquakes.

note: Contemporary 1912 account (Davison, Knowledge) confirms the police evacuated the district in time with no loss of life. Rejected: Palmieri at Vesuvius 1871-72 (said he had often predicted an explosion from seismograph changes, but no warning to the public or evacuation documented, and Mallet in 1873 called prediction impossible); Mont Pelee 1902 and Vesuvius 1906 (no warnings); Taal 1911 (signs neglected, 1,100 died); Nevado del Ruiz 1985, Pinatubo 1991 (later).
searched: archive.org 1910-1913 (Knowledge 1912-05 and 1913-03, Omori's Usu-san report listings, Bulletin of the American Geographical Society), Vesuvius 1872 Palmieri memoir (Mallet 1873), Wikipedia Mount Usu; museum page.

what: During the 1669 Etna eruption the priest Diego Pappalardo and about fifty men broke open the side of the lava flow near Catania to divert it; the diversion worked at first until townspeople of Paterno drove them off.
fit: Engineering work (breaching the flow channel) redirected an active lava flow, which matches redirecting or venting lava, though only for a short time and on a small scale.

sources.title: 1669 eruption of Mount Etna
sources.quote: The first recorded attempt to divert a lava flow occurred when priest Diego Pappalardo and fifty others worked to break up a lava flow

note: Considered the 1973 Heimaey (Iceland) seawater cooling and 1983 Etna explosives/earth-barrier diversion: both later and larger, not earlier. The 1669 attempt was cut short, so it is the earliest working redirection, not a lasting one. Not dated: flooding a crater or extinguishing an eruption, for which no event was found.
searched: Web search for first lava diversion; Wikipedia 1669 Etna, Eldfell, Mount Etna; archive.org full-text for Heimaey cooling.

what: J. R. Tarchanoff (Pflueger's Archiv 35:109) showed that a student could voluntarily raise his heart rate from 70 to 105 beats per minute, by concentrating on his heart, with respiration ruled out as the cause.
fit: A person consciously altered an involuntary function (heart rate) in a measured laboratory test.

sources.publisher: Centralblatt fuer klinische Medicin (review of Tarchanoff)
sources.title: Zentralblatt fuer klinische Medizin, Jahrgang 6, 1885
sources.quote: Der von T. untersuchte Student S. accelerirte seinen Herzschlag willkürlich z. B. von 70 auf 105 Schläge pro Minute

sources.title: Biofeedback
sources.quote: In 1885, J.R. Tarchanoff showed that voluntary control of heart rate could be fairly direct

note: Contemporary review of the paper (1885) confirms the event, the numbers and that breathing was excluded. Considered and rejected: Bair 1901 (ear muscle, skeletal); Schultz 1932 autogenic training, Miller and DiCara 1967, Kamiya 1968, Green 1970s (all later); anecdotal reports of individuals who could slow or stop their pulse, such as Col. Townshend in Cheyne's 1733 account, or of yogis (uncontrolled, no measured test; not checked here). The same paper notes that Tarchanoff found several other people with the ability.
searched: Wikipedia Biofeedback; archive.org full text 1885-1892 (found Zentralblatt review and Pflueger's Archiv citations); Crossref (no record for the 1885 paper).

what: Johannes H. Schultz, a Berlin neurologist, published 'Das autogene Training' (Thieme, Leipzig, 1932), a clinical practice manual of a training method built over twenty years, in which patients learn by exercises of heaviness and warmth to bring body states under conscious influence.
fit: A training method used in treatment to let patients consciously influence involuntary bodily states (warmth, relaxation).

sources.title: Buddhistisches Leben und Denken 1932-10-12 (review of Das Autogene Training)
sources.quote: In mehr als zwanzigjähriger Arbeit hat der Verfasser ein Übungsverfahren ausgebildet, das in erster Linie therapeutische Zwecke verfolgt

sources.title: Autogenic training
sources.quote: Autogenic training is a relaxation technique first published by the German psychiatrist Johannes Heinrich Schultz in 1932.

note: The date is that of the clinical book. Wikipedia says Schultz first presented the method in 1926 to a Berlin medical society, and the 1932 review says twenty years of work, so clinical use was earlier but undated by any source found; 1932 is kept as the first documented use. The fit is moderate: it is a relaxation and warmth-suggestion method rather than direct control of pain or temperature. Considered and rejected: Coue autosuggestion (1910s; suggestion, not trained control); Jacobson's progressive relaxation (skeletal muscle, 1929 book, later than Schultz's work anyway); yoga (undated, no documented clinical service); biofeedback clinics (1960s-70s, later).
searched: Wikipedia Autogenic training and Biofeedback; archive.org full text 1926-1935 for Schultz 'autogene Training' (reviews in Buddhistisches Leben und Denken 1932, Zentralblatt fuer Psychotherapie 1933-35).

what: Convair XFY-1 Pogo, flown by J. F. 'Skeets' Coleman at Brown Naval Auxiliary Air Station near San Diego, made the first full transition from vertical takeoff to horizontal wing-borne flight (21-minute flight) on 2 November 1954, and flew again for the press on 4 November.
fit: A tail-sitting turboprop aircraft rose vertically on its propellers then flew forward on its wings like an airplane, matching the definition's function and mechanism.

sources.title: Convairiety San Diego Edition 1954
sources.quote: The initial transition from ver¬ tical to horizontal flight meant the XFY-1 had become the first fully successful vertical takeoff fighter in history

sources.title: Convair XFY
sources.quote: On 1 August 1954, Coleman logged two outdoor test flights

note: Date corrected from 1954-11-05 (Wikipedia) to 1954-11-02: the contemporary Convair paper and a quoted Navy BuAer message both give the first complete transitional VTO flight as the morning of 2 Nov 1954; 4 Nov was the press demonstration. Rejected earlier candidates: Lockheed XFV-1 (June 1954) never made a vertical takeoff or landing, only in-flight transitions on a ground-roll airframe; Transcendental Model 1-G (1954-55) never made a complete transition; McDonnell XV-1 (1955), Fairey Rotodyne (1958-04-10, compound gyrodyne), Ryan X-13 (1956-57), Bell XV-3 (1958) all later; Rolls-Royce Flying Bedstead (1954) had no wings. No earlier aircraft was found that both lifted off vertically and flew on wings.
searched: Wikipedia Convair XFY, Lockheed XFV, Transcendental 1-G, Fairey Rotodyne; archive.org full-text search 1954-56 (Convairiety, Aviation Week, Leatherneck, Aircraft Year Book hits); read Convairiety San Diego Nov 1954 text.

what: The Hawker Siddeley Harrier GR.1 officially entered RAF service on 1 April 1969, with No. 1 Squadron converting at RAF Wittering that month.
fit: A jet VTOL aircraft (vectored-thrust Pegasus) that takes off vertically and flies on wings, in operational front-line military service.

sources.title: Hawker Siddeley Harrier
sources.quote: it officially entered service with the RAF on 1 April 1969

note: Considered: XFY-1 and XFV-1 (never operational, cancelled 1955-56); Kestrel Tripartite Evaluation Squadron 1965 (evaluation, not operational use); Fairey Rotodyne (never entered service, compound gyrodyne); Soviet Yak-36/Yak-38 (1976 service, later); USMC AV-8A (1971, later); Bell V-22 (2007, later). what: General Electric's Walking Truck (Cybernetic Anthropomorphous Machine, Ralph Mosher), a four-legged hydraulic walker with a seated operator, was built for the Army and ARPA and shown on national television in 1968; a December 1968 NASA survey reports prototype hardware built and the feared instability not encountered.
fit: A legged vehicle that walks while carrying its operator, meant to haul cargo over rough ground.

sources.title: Teleoperator control: An AEC-NASA technology survey
sources.quote: The instability predicted by Rock Island Arsenal engineers has not been encountered in this design.

sources.title: Walking truck
sources.quote: In 1968, Walter Cronkite covered the Walking Truck in a segment of The 20th Century.

note: Press in March-June 1966 (AP, Circleville Herald, Appleton Post-Crescent) and June 1967 still call it 'in model stage' or 'being built', so it was not shown walking then; the earliest contemporary report of a working prototype is the December 1968 NASA survey, with Cronkite coverage in 1968. The exact first walk (somewhere 1966-68) was not found. Rejected earlier: Pedipulator study (1962, a proposal), Pedipulator/Hardiman (not a walking cargo vehicle), Dederick Steam Man 1868 (patent, no evidence it walked unsupported), Rygg mechanical horse 1893 (unverified), Chebyshev plantigrade machine 1878 (not a rider carrier). No practical use: Walking Truck remained a prototype.

what: Esso Research and Engineering showed a preliminary model of a magnetic-tread robot painter that drove up vertical metal surfaces (reported 4 Sept 1961).
fit: A tracked vehicle whose rubber treads contain magnets grips and climbs vertical steel surfaces under its own power, matching climbing by grip/power.

sources.title: Toy Gives Peek Preview Of Robot Painter on Wall

Nishi's 1966 negative-pressure (suction cup and fan) wall-climbing robot (cited only secondhand in a 2020s impeller paper; later than 1961); a LSBU keynote that dates the first wall-climbing robot to the late 1980s in Moscow (later, and disagrees with the 1960s date, so unreliable); rock/ice climbing vehicles and steep-slope tracked vehicles (not vertical-surface climbers). what: A German hot-water (steam) rocket was used to drive a rocket sled to Mach 1.2.
fit: Superheated water flashing to steam through a nozzle served as the rocket reaction mass, matching water/steam as propellant.

sources.title: Astronautics 1959-12
sources.quote: As early as 1939, a hot-water rocket was used to drive a rocket sled to Mach 1.2.

note: Single retrospective source, no place or builder named. Same article says James Perkins patented a hot-water rocket toy in 1824 (rejected: patent/toy described only as patented, no demonstration documented in a fetched page). Heron's aeolipile is a steam reaction device but not a rocket. V-2 75% ethanol/25% water is a fuel diluent, loose. Article says Germans used hot-water RATO on the Me 262 in WWII, undated, so no first_practical_use given. Definition's 'extend fuel or feed an engine' read as water/steam as reaction mass; alternative reading (water mixed into fuel) not dated.

what: North German Lloyd's express liner Kronprinz Wilhelm was fitted with Prof. Dorr's system of watertight bulkhead doors worked from the bridge, with a demonstration closing all twenty doors below the waterline from the bridge.

sources.title: Marine Engineering (Bulkhead Doors note)

what: Drs. Geffchen and Richter of Leipzig built a walk-through electric metal detector (gate-coil wicket) for the exit of a German factory, where it was in successful operation by April 1926 to search every worker leaving for hidden metal tools and parts.
fit: An electric scanner at a doorway that detects hidden metal objects on each person passing through without contact, the same mechanism as walk-through weapon detectors; applied to stolen goods rather than weapons.

sources.title: Radio Oscillator Detects Thieves (Radio News, April 1926)
sources.quote: it is possible to make an effective search of every person leaving the premises

sources.title: Radio Oscillator Detects Thieves (Radio News, April 1926)
sources.quote: where the apparatus described in this article is in suc- cessful operation

sources.title: Walk-Through Metal Detectors Were Invented to Catch Thieving Employees
sources.quote: In the mid-1920s, H. Geffchen and H. Richter of Leipzig invented the walk-through metal detector

note: REPLACED the 1970 New Orleans date. Doorway metal detector (a gate-coil wicket whose oscillator pitch changes when a person carrying metal passes through, with a hand search coil to locate the object) invented by Drs. Geffchen and Richter of Leipzig and in successful operation at a German factory exit by April 1926; the stolen tools and small manufactured articles it was built to find are hidden goods carried out of premises. Fit caveat: it finds stolen metal goods, not weapons or smuggled goods as such, and a human attendant listens for the pitch change, so judgment is needed; if only weapon screening should count, the fallback is Eastern Air Lines' magnetometer plus behavior-profile screening at some terminals by about October 1969 (Smithsonian Air and Space: 'Eastern Air Lines ... had magnetometers in place, at some of its terminal operations'; Salem News 1970-07-17: Eastern 'was the first to use the system' after '10 months operational experience'), then New Orleans on 1970-07-17, the first airport-wide system. Other candidates rejected: Fisher 1931 and Garrett hand-held detectors (not a doorway scanner); FAA/Lockheed magnetometer development reported in Science News 1968-08-31 (development, not use); Outokumpu and 1972 US airport mandate (later). Date is the 1926 publication year, as the article says the apparatus was 'recently' worked out; the exact installation date is not given.
searched: archive.org full-text search 1955-1969 for walk-through detectors and magnetometers/hijack (Salem News 1970-07-17, Facts on File 1969 via search snippet, DTIC AD0688766 Hijacking references 1969); archive.org 1926 search for the Radio News article (found); Smithsonian Air and Space and Gizmodo pages fetched; WebSearch for pre-1969 walk-through detectors (found the 1926 Leipzig factory detector, nothing for prisons or courthouses before 1969).

what: France launched the ironclad Gloire in 1859 and Britain answered with the iron-hulled armored HMS Warrior, starting the ironclad naval race.

sources.quote: over half-a- million women are now directly replacing men

sources.title: Women in World War I
sources.quote: The vast majority of these women were drafted into the civilian work force to replace conscripted men or to work in greatly expanded munitions factories

note: The date moves from the war's start (1914) to 1915: the 1916 report shows women did not recover pre-war employment until April 1915 and that most replacement of men came in the war's second year (from August 1915), with the first replacement felt from the skilled-labor shortage of November 1914. Earlier candidates rejected: US Civil War 1861-65 (women took government clerical and some factory and farm jobs, but not a systematic replacement of drafted men; could not source it), Crimean War (nursing only), Dahomey and other women's military units (not replacement of drafted men in industry), Franco-Prussian war. The 'all trades' and 'serve alongside men' parts came later (Women's Army Auxiliary Corps 1917, Second World War), so WWI replacement is the first strict match of the wartime-replacement mechanism.
searched: archive.org full text 1914-1916 for women replacing men (read Labour, Finance and the War 1916 and a 1915-1920 'Women and World War I' periodical set); Wikipedia Women in WWI, Women in the American Civil War, Women in the workforce. No source found that dates a mass replacement earlier than late 1914.

what: In WWII women filled industry in all belligerents and the Soviet Union integrated about a million women directly into army units.
fit: Women worked across trades replacing drafted men and served alongside men in the military.

sources.title: Women in World War II
sources.quote: The Soviet Union integrated women directly into their army units; approximately one million served in the Red Army

note: WWI rejected for mass_adoption: women's roles largely reverted afterwards and military service was auxiliary. Year is the Soviet entry into WWII; broader adoption varied by country (US 1942).

what: Wyoming Territory's first legislature passed, and Governor Campbell signed on 10 December 1869, an act granting women the right to vote and to hold office; Esther Morris was appointed a Justice of the Peace in early 1870 and women served as jurors.
fit: A real community (a US territory) put equal suffrage and office-holding for women into practice, the same pair of rights as the definition, though at territorial not national level.

sources.title: Women's suffrage in Wyoming
sources.quote: An Act to Grant to the Women of Wyoming Territory the Right of Suffrage, and to Hold Office

sources.title: The Revolution 1870-03-17: Vol 5 Iss 11
sources.quote: your Aunt Esther Morris is a Justice of the Peace

note: Added as the first working trial on a real community. Considered: Pitcairn Island 1838 and Isle of Man 1881 (property-limited or no parliament seats), Utah Territory (vote only, Feb 1870, after Wyoming), Franceville 1889 (a brief self-declared commune). Wyoming is sub-national, so it is not the practical use for a national-parliament concept; the date is the signing of the act (the Wikipedia source states the 10 Dec 1869 signing, not quoted here).
searched: Wikipedia Women's suffrage in Wyoming; archive.org full-text search 1870-71 (The Revolution) for the Wyoming justice of the peace and juror reports.

what: The Commonwealth of Australia's Commonwealth Franchise Act 1902 (No. 8, 1902) gave women equal federal voting rights and the right to stand for the federal Parliament; women voted and stood in the December 1903 federal election (Vida Goldstein ran for the Senate).
fit: A national law gave women the vote and eligibility for seats in a national parliament on the same terms as men, which is the definition's pairing at national level.

sources.title: Commonwealth Franchise Act 1902
sources.quote: The act gave Australian women the right to vote and stand for parliament at the federal level

sources.title: The Independent 1904-06-09: Vol 56 Iss 2897
sources.quote: legally qualified to act in the Federal elections of last Decem-

note: Replaces Finland 1906. Earlier candidates: Wyoming Territory 1869 and Utah 1870 (territories, not national); Isle of Man 1881, Pitcairn 1838 (tiny, no real parliament seats); New Zealand 1893 (vote only; women could not sit until 1919); South Australia 1894-95 (vote and stand, but a colonial parliament, not national; its women also voted in the 1901 federal election only in SA and WA); Australia 1902 (uniform national law with vote and eligibility). Finland 1906-07 is the first where women were actually elected (19 in March 1907) and its parliament was equally of an autonomous Grand Duchy, so it adds nothing earlier; Australia elected no woman until 1943, so a stricter reading that requires seats actually held would keep Finland (1907-03). Racial exclusions in the Australian act applied to men and women alike. The 12 June 1902 date is the Register's start date for the Act.
searched: Wikipedia (Women's suffrage, Women's suffrage in Australia, Commonwealth Franchise Act 1902); Federal Register of Legislation; archive.org full-text 1902-04 (Woman's Journal, The Independent, Parliamentary Debates, Daily Public Ledger on Goldstein); legislation text itself not retrievable.

what: Fenwick Weavers' Society formed in Fenwick, Ayrshire, by local weavers to sell discounted oatmeal to workers; later added savings, loans and education.
fit: A workers' own society running a store cooperatively matches cooperative ownership of stores; it is not a producer firm with employees sharing management.

sources.title: Cooperative
sources.quote: In 1761, the Fenwick Weavers' Society was formed in Fenwick, East Ayrshire, Scotland to sell discounted oatmeal to local workers.

note: Wikipedia's Consumers' co-operative article dates the same society to 1769; the Cooperative article says 1761, taken here. Considered Owen's New Lanark store (1810s) and Rochdale 1844 (both later). Religious communal groups (Harmony Society) and Mondragon 1956 not dated as earlier; not searched deeply. No mass_adoption given.
searched: Wikipedia Cooperative, Consumers' co-operative, Worker cooperative.

what: Lyon silk workers (canuts) rose in arms after manufacturers refused a minimum price tariff and held the city for days.
fit: A violent uprising of workers against manufacturers and property owners.

sources.title: Canut revolts
sources.quote: They were among the first well-defined worker uprisings of the period known as the Industrial Revolution

note: Earlier: Luddite machine-breaking 1811-1812 and Swing Riots 1830 (sabotage and protest rather than a defined uprising against capitalist order); rejected as looser. Lyon 1831 is cited as among the first well-defined worker uprisings. Not exhaustively searched for earlier ones.
searched: Wikipedia: Canut revolts.

what: Ford Motor Company's Five Dollar Day came with intrusive company investigations of employees' home lives and spending (the Sociological Department).
fit: A company managing employees' private lives and rating their conduct to impose a standard of behavior matches the private-life alternative of the definition; there is no sociability ranking or dissent suppression shown.

sources.title: Henry Ford: Sociological Department
sources.quote: rather intrusive company investigations to insure that workers would not spend their money on riotous living

note: Earlier loose analogue: Pullman company town (1880s) where George Pullman set behavioral standards workers had to meet to live there; it is housing-based, not employer management of employees' own lives, so rejected. Not dated: Lowell mill boardinghouses. Aptitude testing and sociability rankings not found.
searched: Henry Ford museum page; Wikipedia Pullman, Chicago.

what: In AD 536 a dust or aerosol veil, probably from a volcanic eruption, dimmed the sun across Europe and Asia for months; Procopius and Cassiodorus recorded the sun giving light without brightness.
fit: The sun was darkened over a large region (Mediterranean and beyond) by ash/aerosol for a long period; dimmed rather than fully hidden.

sources.title: Extreme weather events of 535-536
sources.quote: For the sun gave forth its light without brightness

note: Earlier candidate: the 44-43 BC dimming after Etna/Okmok eruptions (Virgil, Plutarch; the Okmok and Etna pages describe famine and a volcanic winter but no fetched text gave the sun-dimming duration), rejected as under-documented, though it may be the earlier fit. Later: New England Dark Day 1780 (one day, smoke). The 536 event is a dimming, not full darkness; the fit is partial.
searched: Wikipedia 535-536 events, Okmok, Etna, Volcanic winter, Dark Day 1780, Death of Julius Caesar.

what: World War I became a war of most great powers on 4 August 1914, when Britain declared war on Germany (Germany was already at war with Russia and France; Austria-Hungary joined against Russia on 6 August); fighting reached Africa on 6-7 August and Asia and the Pacific that month.
fit: Most of the great powers were at war, with modern navies and aircraft, spreading over several continents within days, which is the scale the definition names.

sources.title: Europe in the Melting Pot: The Historical Background of the Great War
sources.quote: August 4 — England declared war on Germany and began to mobilize her army and navy

sources.title: Chronicle of International Events
sources.quote: Great Britain formally declared war on Germany

sources.title: World War I
sources.quote: On 6–7 August, French and British troops invaded the German protectorates of Togoland and Kamerun.

note: Changed the date from 28 July 1914 (Austria-Hungary's declaration on Serbia, a war of one great power against a minor state) to 4 August, when the war first involved most of the great powers (Germany, Russia, France and Britain, with Austria-Hungary at war with Serbia and then Russia on 6 August); the scale the definition names was reached within the week and the 7-day difference is small. Earlier candidates rejected: Seven Years' War (1756-63), Napoleonic Wars and the Crimean War (great-power wars with no aircraft or modern fleets), the 1900 Eight-Nation Alliance in China (most great powers but a police action against one state, no aircraft, one continent), the Russo-Japanese War of 1904-05 (two powers). Aircraft were in use from the first month; this is background knowledge not separately sourced.
searched: archive.org full-text 1914-15 (Europe in the Melting Pot, Chronicle of International Events, Current History, newspapers); Wikipedia World War I.

what: John P. Maynard used liquid collodion as a film that sealed incised finger wounds, first on his niece and then on himself, in Dedham, Massachusetts.
fit: A liquid that dries to a protective film and holds a cut closed, matching a liquid wound sealant.

sources.title: Collodion (J. P. Maynard)
sources.quote: I used it as such on a little niece of mine, who had cut her finger, and then on my own hand

sources.title: Collodion (J. P. Maynard)
sources.quote: keeping the incised surfaces together until they healed

note: John Parker Maynard, a Dedham, Mass., medical student, brushed collodion (nitrocellulose in ether) over the closed edges of a cut and held it with a cotton strap; the account was published in March 1848 and the year 1847 is from later histories, not from the page, so the date is approximate. Earlier candidates: gum and resin plasters, court plaster and sutures (not a sealed film), and the Boston Medical and Surgical Journal says these were the first surgical uses of the mixture. Later: cyanoacrylate glue (Coover 1951-58, used on wounded soldiers in Vietnam in the 1960s, Dermabond approved 1998).
searched: archive.org full-text search collodion Maynard 1847-50; Wikipedia Collodion and Cyanoacrylate

what: Leveaux's spring-driven tram car, built 1874 by Middleton and Co., pulled a passenger car at the Lillie Bridge depot, London; a 5 hp stationary steam engine wound its coiled springs.
fit: Large coiled springs wound by an engine stored the mechanical energy that ran a machine.

sources.title: The Clockwork Tram
sources.quote: It was demonstrated pulling a passenger car at the Lillie Bridge depot of the Metropolitan and District Railway in May 1875.

sources.title: The Clockwork Tram
sources.quote: A small stationary steam engine of about 5 horsepower wound a series of compound coiled springs in barrels

note: Reference source only. Ordinary clockwork and small spring motors are far older but are not large engine-wound storage. Philadelphia spring-car proposals (1883-85) were not built. No spring-powered dynamo or hoist found.
searched: WebSearch on spring tramcars; tramwayinfo.com; archive.org search 'spring motor' street car 1870-1900.

what: NTT (Japan) reported to have developed a working wristwatch-size mobile telephone with voice recognition, to be tested at the Nagano Winter Olympics in February 1998.
fit: A telephone worn on the wrist like a watch that makes calls over a mobile network, the function and form the definition names.

sources.title: Amateur Radio Newsline 1066
sources.quote: A mobile telephone the size of a wristwatch has been developed by the Japanese state telephone company and will be tested at the Winter Olympics.

note: Replaces Samsung SPH-WP10 1999 as the first demonstration. Earlier candidates rejected: Brunetti wrist-watch radio transmitter (Radio-Craft 1948-04) is voice transmitter only with no receiver, so no calls; US Signal Corps wrist radio (Tele-Tech 1953-11) is a receiver only; 1947-48 Dick Tracy wrist radios were toys; 1970s NASA wrist radio-telephones were concepts only. NTT's prototype (a 1999 book also gives it as a prototype) predates Samsung's Comdex unveiling in Nov 1999. Exact date of the first working NTT unit not found; 1998-01 is the date of the report.
searched: archive.org full-text: wrist radio, wrist telephone, wristwatch telephone, wristwatch phone, watch phone, 1946-2001; read Radio-Craft 1948-04, Tele-Tech 1953-11, Newsline 1066 (1998-01), Monitoring Times 2000-01, W5YI Report 2000-06. Could not read the lending-library book on NTT directly.

what: Giovanni Domenico Cassini investigated the zodiacal light and explained it as sunlight scattered by dust around the Sun (some sources credit Fatio de Duillier, 1684).
fit: The explanation attributes the glow to sunlight reflected by orbiting dust, as defined.

sources.title: Zodiacal light
sources.quote: The phenomenon was investigated by the astronomer Giovanni Domenico Cassini in 1683.

sources.title: Zodiacal light
sources.quote: Zodiacal light is produced by sunlight reflecting off dust particles in the Solar System known as cosmic dust.

note: This is an explanation dated by a reference; spectroscopic confirmation (solar spectrum, early 1900s) was not sourced, and Gegenschein backscatter explanation was not separately dated. Joshua Childrey 1661 only reported the light.
